questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Restitution is best described as:
options: Passive movement of head due to untwisting of neck
Movement of the head by 1/8th of the circle due to torsion
Stretching of the vulval outlet by the head
External rotation after delivery of shoulder
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Passive movement of head due to untwisting of neck

Restitution describes a passive adjustment of the head to untwist the neck after internal rotation.

The most common position of the fetus is the left occipito-lateral position where the vertex occupies the left anterior quadrant of the mother's pelvis.

During internal rotation, there will be anterior rotation of the occiput by 2/8th of a circle, placing the occiput behind the symphysis pubis. There is always an accompanying movement of descent with internal rotation. (Option B)

Torsion of the neck occurs during internal rotation of the head. The neck cannot withstand such a high degree of torsion, so the shoulders will rotate in the same direction to the extent of 1/8th of a circle, placing the shoulders in the oblique diameter with one-eighth of the torsion still left behind. Torsion refers to the twisting forces applied to the fetal head and neck during internal rotation to align the head with the birth canal.

In restitution, these twisting forces are released, allowing the head to return to its anatomical alignment with the shoulders.

Other Options:

Option B: Movement of the head by 1/8th of the circle due to torsion: While the head typically does rotate by about 1/8th of a circle (45°) during restitution, this is a passive as the tension in the neck resolves. The phrase "due to torsion" is misleading because torsion refers to twisting forces exerted during internal rotation, not restitution. Restitution is about the release of torsion, not its application.

Option C: Stretching of the vulval outlet by the head: This describes a process that occurs during the crowning stage of labor, not during restitution. At crowning, the fetal head stretches the vulval outlet as it emerges. Restitution occurs after the head is delivered and involves the passive rotation of the head to align with the shoulders.

Option D: External rotation after delivery of shoulder: Once the shoulders are delivered, the head undergoes a second adjustment to align with the shoulders as they rotate to fit through the maternal pelvis. This is an active movement that happens post-delivery of the shoulders, while restitution occurs before shoulder delivery.
questions.learning: Passive movement of head due to untwisting of neck Restitution describes a passive adjustment of the head to untwist the neck after internal rotation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are the characteristic features of Meigs’ syndrome in a female? 1. Right sided hydrothorax 2. Ascites 3. Genital warts 4. Fibroma ovary Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Meigs’ syndrome is the triad of:

• Benign ovarian fibroma
• Ascites
• Pleural effusion (usually right-sided hydrothorax)

The ascites and pleural effusion resolve after surgical removal of the ovarian tumor.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Right-sided hydrothorax: Correct. Pleural effusion is typically right-sided.
• 2. Ascites: Correct.
• 3. Genital warts: Incorrect. Unrelated to Meigs’ syndrome.
• 4. Fibroma ovary: Correct. The ovarian tumor is classically a fibroma (may also rarely be thecoma or Brenner tumor).
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Meigs’ syndrome is the triad of: • Benign ovarian fibroma • Ascites • Pleural effusion (usually right-sided hydrothorax) The ascites and pleural effusion resolve after surgical removal of the ovarian tumor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient has a cavernous sinus infection affecting the nerve located medially within the sinus. To assess involvement of the abducens nerve, in which direction should you ask the patient to move their eye?
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus contains several cranial nerves (III, IV, , , and VI). The abducens nerve (CN VI) is unique because it travels through the center of the sinus, medially placed near the internal carotid artery, while the others are in the lateral wall. As established previously, the abducens nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which is responsible for abducting the eye. Therefore, to test its function and confirm involvement, the clinician must ask the patient to look laterally (away from the midline). Looking superiorly (Option A), inferiorly (Option B), and medially (Option C) primarily tests the muscles innervated by the oculomotor nerve (CN III). In cavernous sinus thrombosis, the abducens nerve is often the first nerve affected due to its central location. Patients will present with an inability to move the eye outward and will experience double vision when trying to do so. This clinical correlation is a classic "must-know" for medical examinations
questions.learning: The cavernous sinus contains several cranial nerves (III, IV, , , and VI). The abducens nerve (CN VI) is unique because it travels through the center of the sinus, medially placed near the internal carotid artery, while the others are in the lateral wall.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Lipotrophic factors are all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arginine

Arginine is not a lipotropic factor.

Lipotropic factors are those factors that mobilize triacylglycerol from the hepatocytes. Following are the example :

* Choline

* Folic acid

* Betaine

* Vitamin B12

* Methionine

* Glycine

* Inositol

* Serine

Lecithin (option b) is a phospholipid (phosphatidylcholine) that is important for VLDL formation and its secretion from the liver. So the best answer is arginine
questions.learning: Arginine Arginine is not a lipotropic factor. Lipotropic factors are those factors that mobilize triacylglycerol from the hepatocytes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is not used for the identification of the facial nerve trunk?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inferior belly of omohyoid muscle

The inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle is not used as an anatomical landmark for the identification of the facial nerve trunk.

There are two methods for localization of the facial nerve trunk:

1. Anterograde method: The facial nerve trunk is identified based on the anatomical landmarks after it exits from the stylomastoid foramen. This includes:

• Tragal pointer/Conley's pointer - It is the inferior portion of the cartilaginous canal. The facial nerve trunk lies 1 cm deep and inferior to its tip.
• Posterior belly of digastric - The facial nerve lies superior to the upper border of the muscle.
• Squamotympanic fissure - It is a fissure in the temporal bone, which runs from TMJ to the tympanic cavity. The facial nerve runs through this fissure.
• Styloid process - The facial nerve lies superficial to it.
• Mastoid process - Upon drilling it, the nerve is identified proximally.

2. Retrograde method: The main branches of the facial nerve trunk are identified and are then traced proximally until the main tunk is identified. Some branches used for tracing the facial nerve trunk include:

• Buccal branch - It lies in relation to the parotid gland.
• Marginal mandibular branch - It lies in relation to the facial vessels.
questions.learning: Inferior belly of omohyoid muscle — The inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle is not used as an anatomical landmark for the identification of the facial nerve trunk.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A female patient presented with fatigue. Routine complete blood count analysis showed hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, MCV 60fL, and RBC count of 5.2 million. A peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia. Which of the following is the next best investigation for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HbA2 levels

The next best investigation for this patient would be determining the HbA2 levels, as the history of reduced hemoglobin, reduced MCV (microcytic anemia) and normal to high RBC count is suggestive of thalassemia.

The MCV count divided by the RBC count is called the Mentzer index, which is lower than 13 in thalassemia due to the normal to high RBC count in the denominator. In iron deficiency anemia, it is higher than 13 as the MCV and the RBC count both are reduced.

Alpha- and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively. This leads to precipitation of the excess (unpaired) chains, interfering with red blood cell (RBC) production and survival.

Clinical features in thalassemia include anemia, jaundice, skeletal deformities including facial deformities, changes in body habitus, growth impairment, and hepatosplenomegaly. Due to frequent blood transfusions, iron overload is also seen.

Peripheral smear is likely to show microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, teardrop cells, and some coarse basophilic stippling in certain cases.

The image given below shows peripheral smear findings in thalassemia.

An X-ray of the skull shows a crewcut appearance due to expansion of hematopoetically active marrow.

Thalassemia is usually managed by blood transfusions every 2-4 weeks and chelation therapy with deferoxamine, deferasirox, and deferiprone for iron chelation. Splenectomy is indicated when the transfusion requirement to maintain ideal hemoglobin increases. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the only known curative treatment for thalassemia.

Other options:

Option A: Serum ferritin level is used to diagnose iron-deficiency anemia (IDA). They are usually low in IDA.

Option C: Serum folate level is used to diagnose macrocytic anemia due to a deficiency of folic acid.

Option D: Serum homocysteine levels are increased in vitamin B12–deficient macrocytic anemia.
questions.learning: HbA2 levels — The next best investigation for this patient would be determining the HbA2 levels, as the history of reduced hemoglobin, reduced MCV (microcytic anemia) and normal to high RBC count is suggestive of thalassemia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding inguinal hernias in children? I. It is more common in full-term boys. II. It should be repaired promptly. III. It is always indirect. IV. It may frequently be transilluminant. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

Inguinal hernias in children are congenital and occur due to failure of obliteration of the processus vaginalis. This creates a persistent communication between the peritoneal cavity and the inguinal canal, allowing abdominal contents to herniate. Because of the risk of incarceration and strangulation, all diagnosed pediatric inguinal hernias should be repaired promptly.

The following statements are true:

• II. It should be repaired promptly: Pediatric inguinal hernias do not resolve spontaneously and have a high risk of incarceration, especially during infancy. Early herniotomy is the treatment of choice.
• III. It is always indirect: Almost all inguinal hernias in children are indirect, occurring through a patent processus vaginalis. Direct inguinal hernias are extremely rare in children.
• IV. It may frequently be transilluminant: Because a patent processus vaginalis is often associated with a communicating hydrocele, the swelling may transilluminate when fluid predominates. Clinically, differentiating a communicating hydrocele from an inguinal hernia can sometimes be difficult.

Why is I incorrect?

• I. It is more common in full-term boys: Although inguinal hernias are more common in boys, they are more common in premature infants than in full-term infants, making this statement incorrect.
questions.learning: II, III and IV Inguinal hernias in children are congenital and occur due to failure of obliteration of the processus vaginalis. This creates a persistent communication between the peritoneal cavity and the inguinal canal, allowing abdominal contents to…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient is planned for laparoscopic surgery under general anesthesia as a day care procedure. Which of the following factors would make him unsuitable for day care surgery?
options: Home is 45 minutes away from the hospital
The surgical procedure is expected to last slightly over 1 hour
No attendant is available at home to care for the patient postoperatively
The patient has had general anesthesia in the past without complications
questions.explanation: The presence of a responsible adult attendant at home for the first 24 hours is a non-negotiable safety requirement for day care (ambulatory) surgery under general anesthesia. Post-anesthesia patients may have impaired judgment and a risk of falls or adverse reactions to pain medication. Living 45 minutes away (Option A) is generally acceptable as it allows for timely return if complications arise. A 1-hour surgery (Option B) is well within the typical limits for day care procedures. A previous history of uncomplicated anesthesia (Option D) is a positive indicator of suitability rather than a contraindication. Without a caregiver to monitor the patient, they cannot be safely discharged on the day of surgery
questions.learning: The presence of a responsible adult attendant at home for the first 24 hours is a non-negotiable safety requirement for day care (ambulatory) surgery under general anesthesia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40 year old male patient presented with pain and hearing loss after trauma to his right ear. Otoscopy reveals the presence of blood clots along with irregular perforations in the tympanic membrane. What is the next step in management in this case?
options: Keep ear dry with systemic analgesics
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keep ear dry with systemic analgesics

In this case, the presence of blood clots and irregular perforations in the tympanic membrane suggests traumatic injury to the ear. The initial management involves keeping the ear dry to prevent infection and further damage.

When a patient presents with pain and hearing loss after trauma to the ear, it's important to manage the condition appropriately. Systemic analgesics can be prescribed to alleviate pain.

Other options:

* It's important to avoid introducing any foreign substances into the ear canal, such as ear drops or irrigation, as this can exacerbate the injury and increase the risk of infection.

* Aspirating and performing audiometry may be considered later in the management process, once the acute phase has resolved and the extent of damage needs further evaluation.

* Giving gentamicin and levofloxacin or other antibiotics is not indicated at this stage unless there are signs of infection, as prophylactic antibiotic use is generally not recommended due to the risk of promoting antibiotic resistance.
questions.learning: Keep ear dry with systemic analgesics — In this case, the presence of blood clots and irregular perforations in the tympanic membrane suggests traumatic injury to the ear.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 15-year-old boy presents with swelling in the upper diaphyseal part of the tibia. X-ray of the swelling showed a periosteal reaction. A histopathological image of the biopsy is given below. Immunohistochemistry was positive for synaptophysin and mic 2. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ewing sarcoma

The given clinical scenario along with the image showing small round blue cells and immunohistochemistry (IHC) positive for synaptophysin and mic-2 point to a likely diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma.

Ewing sarcoma is the 2nd most common bone sarcoma in children. The majority of the patients affected are usually <20 years of age. It has a slight male predominance.

It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus and flat bones of the pelvis. The majority of Ewing sarcomas have a balanced translocation between the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 and the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11.

Patients present with painful enlarging mass, fever, and anemia. The affected area is usually tender, swollen, and warm. Laboratory findings may show an elevated WBC count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).

A histopathological examination of Ewing sarcoma shows sheets of uniform, round cells arranged in Homer-Wright rosettes. These cells are of neuroectodermal origin and have minimal cytoplasm and abundant glycogen. When they are arranged around a central fibrillary core in the form of clusters, the appearance is termed Homer-Wright rosettes. Immunohistochemistry is usually positive for synaptophysin and mic-2.

Given below is the histopathological appearance of Ewing sarcoma.

As tumor cells are rich in glycogen, they stain positive for periodic acid Schiff (PAS) stain however, they stain negatively for reticulin.

The image given below shows PAS staining done in Ewing's sarcoma:

Radiological examination of Ewing sarcoma shows a destructive lesion in the diaphysis of long bones. Deposition of periosteal reaction in layers gives an onion-peel appearance (shown below).

Other options:

Option A: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignancy of bone. The histological features of osteosarcoma include pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant mitoses. The diagnosis is definitive with the presence of malignant tumor cells producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone arranged in a typically fine, lacelike pattern.

Given below is the histopathological image of osteosarcoma:

X-ray shows periosteal reaction and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunray appearance as shown below.

Option C: Neuroblastoma is a tumor of the sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla. It is derived from primordial neural crest cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor in childhood. On histopathology small round blue cells are seen. These cells are concentrically arranged around a faintly eosinophilic fibrillary material (neuropil). This appearance is called Homer-Wright pseudorosettes (shown below).

Option D: Osteoclastoma is also known as a giant cell tumour. The tumor cells are primitive osteoblast precursors and express high levels of RANKL. Histologically, the tumors consist of osteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei. These cells are usually present against a backdrop of mononuclear stromal cells.

The image given below shows the histopathological appearance of giant cell tumour/osteoclastoma:

The image below shows an X-ray of a giant cell tumour showing the typical soap bubble appearance.
questions.learning: Ewing sarcoma — The given clinical scenario along with the image showing small round blue cells and immunohistochemistry (IHC) positive for synaptophysin and mic-2 point to a likely diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which procedure poses the greatest risk of duodenal ulcer recurrence?
questions.explanation: A duodenal ulcer primarily occurs due to excess gastric acid secretion. Surgical procedures aim to reduce acid production or remove the ulcer-prone area. Gastro-jejunostomy is only a bypass procedure that connects the stomach to the jejunum without reducing acid secretion or addressing the underlying cause. Therefore, the stomach continues to produce acid, and the ulcer can recur at the stoma (stomal ulcer), making recurrence most likely with this procedure. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Gastrectomy: Removes acid-producing part → ↓ recurrence (B) Highly selective vagotomy: Preserves function but reduces acid → low recurrence (C) Truncal vagotomy: Significantly reduces acid secretion → lower recurrence than GJ
questions.learning: A duodenal ulcer primarily occurs due to excess gastric acid secretion. Surgical procedures aim to reduce acid production or remove the ulcer-prone area.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following cells is responsible for the destruction of bacterial foreign bodies in liver sinusoids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Kupffer cells

Kupffer cells, also known as stellate macrophages and Kupffer-Borowicz cells; are specialized macrophages of the liver that are responsible for the destruction of bacterial foreign bodies. These cells are present in the walls of the sinusoids and not in the perisinusoidal space (Space of Disse). They are responsible for removing cellular and microbial debris from the circulation, and also for secreting cytokines involved in defense.

Macrophages can be divided into:

* Blood macrophages (monocytes) are the largest of the lymphoid cells in the peripheral blood. Life span: 3 days.

* Tissue macrophages survive for months.

2 main functions of macrophages:

* Phagocytosis.

* Antigen presentation.

All the options given are various types of cells present in an adult liver.

Option A: Hepatocytes are polyhedral cells with a central spherical nucleus, arranged in a single-cell layer. Every hepatocyte has contact with adjacent hepatocytes (with gap junctions for intercellular communication), bile canaliculus, and the space of Disse/perisinusoidal space (hepatocytes project multiple microvilli into this space for active transport of substances.)

Option B: Ito cells or hepatic stellate cells are present in the space of Disse and store vitamin A. They are mesenchymal in origin and take part in the development of hepatic fibrosis.

Option C: Sinusoidal endothelial cells are flat cells with a central nucleus and are joined to each other by junctional complexes. Their cytoplasm contains numerous transcytotic vesicles. These are separated from hepatocytes by the space of Disse (perisinusoidal space).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A student presented with urticaria after she ate some seafood. She wants a non-sedating drug as she has an exam to study for. Which of the following drugs would you prefer to prescribe to her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fexofenadine

The student is suffering from urticaria and fexofenadine can be prescribed to her. This is preferred as it is a second-generation antihistamine having minimal/no sedative effects as it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier easily.

Pheniramine, promethazine, and hydroxyzine are first-generation antihistamines that should not be prescribed to drivers and heavy machine workers because these can cause sedation.

Highly sedative first-generation antihistamines:

* Diphenhydramine

* Dimenhydrinate

* Promethazine

* Hydroxyzine

Second-generation antihistamines- They are less sedative because of less central nervous system penetration and do not block autonomic receptors. They include:

* Fexofenadine

* Loratadine, Desloratadine

* Cetirizine, Levocetirizine

* Azelastine, Mizolastine, Ebastine

* Olopatadine

* Rupatadine
questions.learning: Fexofenadine — The student is suffering from urticaria and fexofenadine can be prescribed to her. This is preferred as it is a second-generation antihistamine having minimal/no sedative effects as it cannot cross the blood-brain barrier easily.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about corneal epithelium?
options: Regeneration is limited to the limbus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bowman's membrane regenerates

Bowman's membrane is acellular. Hence, it will not regenerate but heals by scarring when damaged.

Corneal stem cells are located at the corneoscleral limbus (Option A), so the regeneration is limited to the limbus.

The cornea comprises distinct layers:

1. Corneal epithelium is lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (Option C), with microvilli on the apical layer (Option D) to enhance surface area and tear film attachment. It consists of basal, columnar, wing, and squamous cells.
2. Bowman’s membrane, a superficial stromal layer, is acellular, collagen-based, and incapable of regeneration.
3. The stroma, the thickest layer constituting 90% of corneal thickness, houses collagen fibrils with ground substances such as chondroitin sulfate and keratan sulfate, maintaining transparency. It cannot regenerate and heals with scarring.
4. Dua’s layer or Pre-Descemet's membrane is the toughest.
5. Descemet’s membrane extends anteriorly to Schwalbe’s line and possesses regenerative potential.
6. Endothelium, a metabolically active monolayer, lacks regenerative ability. It maintains deturgescence through active pumps, ensuring transparency with a usual cell density of approximately 3000 cells/mm² measured by specular microscopy.
questions.learning: Bowman's membrane regenerates Bowman's membrane is acellular. Hence, it will not regenerate but heals by scarring when damaged.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman who is on oral contraceptive pills for contraception has forgotten to take her pills on 4 different days in the last 2 weeks. She presents to the primary health center, asking for advice. What would you suggest to her?
options: Take 4 pills now, continue the schedule, use barrier method of contraception
Take 1 pill now, continue the schedule, and use barrier method of contraception
Take 1 pill now, use barrier method, and consider emergency contraception in case of recent intercourse
Discard the pack, start a new pack with alternate method of contraception
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Discard the pack, start a new pack with alternate method of contraception

A woman who has missed 4 oral contraceptive pills in the last two weeks should take one hormonal pill as soon as possible and finish all hormonal pills in the pack as scheduled, throw away the 7 non-hormonal pills in a 28-pill pack and start a new pack the next day.

Missed pills
Management

Missed 1 or 2 pills/ started new pack 1 or 2 days late?

You have two options: take one hormonal pill right away, or take two pills at your usual scheduled time.

The risk of pregnancy is minimal to none.

Missed 3 or more pills in the first or second week/started new pack 3 or more days late?

Take one hormonal pill immediately and then continue taking your pills as scheduled.

Make sure to use a backup method of contraception for the next seven days.

Additionally, if you've had sexual intercourse within the last 72 hours, consider taking emergency contraceptive pills.

Missed 3 or more pills in the third week?

Take one hormonal pill as soon as you can and complete the entire pack of hormonal pills according to the schedule.

Discard the seven non-hormonal pills in a 28-pill pack.

Begin a new pack the following day.

Missed any nonhormonal pills? (last 7 pills in 28-pill pack)

Dispose of any missed non-hormonal pills.

Continue taking your combination oral contraceptives (COCs), one pill each day.

Begin the new pack as you normally would.

If any non-hormonal pills were missed, she can discard the remaining pills. Start the new pack of oral contraceptives and continue taking as usual.

If she vomits within 2 hours of taking a pill, another pill from the pack should be taken as soon as possible. After that, continue taking the pills as scheduled. If the vomiting or diarrhea persists for >2 days, follow the instructions for 1 or 2 missed pills as mentioned above.

The contraceptive method should be discontinued and changed in the following situations:

• Unexplained or prolonged heavy vaginal bleeding that suggests an underlying condition not related to the method
• Starting anticonvulsant medication or treatment with rifampicin
• Migraines
• Non-ambulatory conditions lasting for >1 week like major surgery, leg in a cast, etc. Combined oral contraceptives can be restarted 2 weeks after ambulation.
• Suspected heart or liver disease, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis, stroke, breast cancer, diabetes, or gall bladder disease
questions.learning: Discard the pack, start a new pack with alternate method of contraception A woman who has missed 4 oral contraceptive pills in the last two weeks should take one hormonal pill as soon as possible and finish all hormonal pills in the pack as scheduled,…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Splenic artery is present in which of the structures as given in the image?
questions.explanation: The splenic artery is a major branch of the coeliac trunk and follows a tortuous (curved) course along the superior border of the pancreas before reaching the spleen. In cross-sectional anatomy (CT/MRI or diagrams), it is typically identified as a wavy vessel running posterior to the stomach and along the pancreas, not just within the spleen itself. In the given image, label (4) corresponds to the region along the pancreas where the splenic artery runs. Hence, the artery is “present” in relation to this structure rather than inside the spleen. This makes option (D) correct. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Lesser omentum: Contains vessels like the hepatic artery, not the splenic artery. (B) Coeliac trunk: This is the origin of the splenic artery, not where it is primarily traced. (C) Spleen: Although supplied by the splenic artery, the vessel is identified before entering the spleen, mainly along the pancreas
questions.learning: The splenic artery is a major branch of the coeliac trunk and follows a tortuous (curved) course along the superior border of the pancreas before reaching the spleen.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 10-year-old child presents with throat pain, fever, and ear pain. He is diagnosed with recurrent tonsillitis. Which nerve is responsible for the ear pain in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tympanic branch of glossopharyngeal nerve

The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia from tonsillitis.

The tonsils and tonsillar fossa are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The glossopharyngeal nerve and the styloid process lie in relation to the lower part of the tonsillar fossa. Therefore, any irritation or pain can be referred to the ear along the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal (Jacobson's) nerve.

The image below shows the anatomic relations of the tonsil and tonsillar bed.

The ear receives extensive sensory innervation via four cranial nerves (V, VII, IX, and X) and two spinal segments (C2 and C3).

Referred otalgia transmitted by the glossopharyngeal nerve may be secondary to lesions and/or inflammatory processes of the nasopharynx, palatine tonsil, soft palate, or posterior one-third of the tongue.

Causes of referred otalgia via glossopharyngeal nerve:

• Acute pharyngitis
• Tonsillitis
• Peritonsillitis
• Peritonsillar abscess
• Post-tonsillectomy
• Foreign bodies embedded in the base of the tongue or tonsillar area
• Elongated styloid process

Other options:

Option B: The great auricular nerve provides sensory sensation for the lower two-thirds of the pinna.

Option C: Causes of referred pain via the auriculotemporal nerve which is the branch of the trigeminal nerve include caries tooth, ulcerative lesions of the oral cavity, temporomandibular joint disorders, and sphenopalatine neuralgia.

Option D: Causes of referred pain via the auricular branch of the vagus nerve include malignancy or ulcerative lesion of the vallecula, epiglottis, larynx, and esophagus.
questions.learning: Tympanic branch of glossopharyngeal nerve — The tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) is responsible for referred otalgia from tonsillitis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with a recent onset of difficulty in swallowing. An X-ray reveals an obstructing object, suggestive of foreign body ingestion. Based on the clinical presentation and radiographic findings, what is the most appropriate intervention for managing this condition?
questions.explanation: A two-year-old child presenting with "difficulty swallowing" (dysphagia) and an X-ray showing an obstruction most likely has an esophageal foreign body. The definitive management for removing an object lodged in the esophagus is esophagoscopy, usually performed using a rigid or flexible scope under general anesthesia. This allows for direct visualization and safe removal of the object. Bronchoscopy (Option A) is indicated for foreign bodies in the airway (trachea or bronchi), which would typically present with coughing, wheezing, or respiratory distress rather than just trouble swallowing. Tracheostomy (Option C) is a surgical airway procedure and is not used for foreign body removal unless there is an absolute upper airway obstruction. Heimlich's maneuver (Option D) is an emergency first-aid step for acute, total airway choking and is not used for objects that have already been diagnosed as lodged in the esophagus via X-ray. Therefore, esophagoscopy is the correct clinical intervention
questions.learning: A two-year-old child presenting with "difficulty swallowing" (dysphagia) and an X-ray showing an obstruction most likely has an esophageal foreign body.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A group of 20 students in a hostel had fried rice as dinner. 6 hours later, they all experienced severe vomiting. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bacillus cereus

The most likely causative organism in the given scenario is bacillus cereus. Eating contaminated fried rice can trigger symptoms of food poisoning within 30 minutes to 6 hours.

Food poisoning after consumption of fried rice or Chinese street food is strongly suggestive of Bacillus cereus (Serotypes 1, 3, 5). Two mechanisms of action have been described for the enterotoxin of B.cereus, one involving stimulation of the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) system and the other independent of it.

Food poisoning after eating food contaminated with B. cereus is of two types:

Bacillus cereus

Emetic type

Incubation period

Vomiting, abdominal cramps

The emetic type of Bacillus cereus often contaminates improperly cooked fried rice, as its heat-resistant spores can withstand boiling. If cooked rice is not refrigerated, the spores can germinate and release toxins.

The mainstay of treatment is adequate hydration.

Other Options:

Option B: Enterotoxigenic E.coli is endemic in developing countries of the tropics, seen in all age groups. Its severity varies from mild watery diarrhea to a fatal disease indistinguishable from cholera. It has an incubation period of >16 hours.

Option C: Shiga toxin acts by inactivating the 60s ribosomal subunit thereby inhibiting protein synthesis. Shigella dysenteriae causes acute onset of symptoms(fever, abdominal cramps) with dysentery and tenesmus.

Option D:  Staphylococcus causes nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea 2-6 hrs after the consumption of contaminated food. The common sources of infection are foods that are not cooked after handling. These include sliced meats, puddings, pastries, and sandwiches. Patients present with nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and diarrhea.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following dimorphic fungi is most commonly responsible for subcutaneous mycosis?
questions.explanation: Dimorphic fungi are those that can exist as both molds (at room temperature) and yeasts (at body temperature). Among the options, Sporothrix schenckii is the classic cause of a subcutaneous mycosis known as "Rose Gardener's disease." The infection typically follows traumatic inoculation of the fungus from soil or vegetation (like rose thorns) into the skin. It presents with a primary nodule that ulcerates, followed by a series of secondary nodules tracking along the draining lymphatic vessels (sporotrichoid spread). Histoplasma capsulatum (Option A), Blastomyces dermatitidis (Option C), and Penicilliosis marneffei (Option D) are all dimorphic fungi, but they are primarily associated with systemic (deep) mycoses that start in the lungs rather than primary subcutaneous infection. Sporotrichosis is diagnosed by identifying "cigar-shaped" budding yeasts in tissue or culture. Treatment typically involve oral itraconazole or, historically, potassium iodide. Understanding these fungal niches is essential for diagnosing skin lesions based on the patient's occupational and environmental exposures

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about male sexual development?
options: At eight weeks the embryo is bipotent.
Wolffian duct develops into epidymis and vas deferens on either side of the body.
Mullerian inhibiting substance inhibits mullerian duct.
Dihydrotestosterone leads to the development of secondary sexual characters and external genitalia.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. At eight weeks the embryo is bipotent.

The embryo is bipotent till seven weeks of gestation, not eight.

At the seventh week, the embryo contains both male and female primordial genital ducts. In the case of a female fetus, uterine tubes and the uterus develops from the Mullerian duct. In case of a male fetus, the wolffian duct system on each side develops into the epididymis and vas deferens.

Testosterone is secreted by the Leydig cells of the fetal testis and MIS (Mullerian inhibiting substance) is secreted by the Sertoli cells. MIS is an amino acid that belongs to the family of transforming growth factor β (TGF-β). MIS causes apoptosis of the Mullerian ducts on the side on which it is secreted.

Dihydrotestosterone, a metabolite of testosterone is responsible for the formation of male external genitalia and male secondary sex characteristics. Development of the vas deferens, epididymis, and other structures from the wolffian ducts is due to the action of testosterone.
questions.learning: At eight weeks the embryo is bipotent. The embryo is bipotent till seven weeks of gestation, not eight.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Cardiolipin can be found in which of the following locations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inner mitochondrial membrane

Cardiolipin is the phospholipid found only in the mitochondria, in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

It is essential for the following:

* Optimal function of numerous mitochondrial enzymes that are involved in mitochondrial energy metabolism.

* Maintenance of the structure of the mitochondrial membrane.

Clinical correlation:

Decreased cardiolipin or alteration in its metabolism results in mitochondrial dysfunction seen in Barth syndrome (cardioskeletal myopathy) which is characterized by an enlarged and weakened heart (dilated cardiomyopathy ), weakness in muscles used for movement (skeletal myopathy), recurrent infections due to small numbers of white blood cells (neutropenia), and short stature.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to Vitamin D deficiency: 1. Vitamin D deficiency is common in northern latitudes. 2. Vitamin D deficiency is more likely to develop in people with dark skin. 3. Exposure to UV light is advisable in patients with Vitamin D deficiency. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Vitamin D deficiency is common worldwide and results from inadequate sunlight exposure, reduced cutaneous synthesis, poor dietary intake, malabsorption, or impaired metabolism. Individuals living in higher (northern) latitudes, those with dark skin, and people with limited sun exposure are at increased risk. Management includes vitamin D supplementation along with adequate exposure to sunlight (UVB radiation).

Why is D correct?

• 1. Vitamin D deficiency is common in northern latitudes✅: Reduced UVB exposure limits cutaneous vitamin D synthesis.
• 2. Vitamin D deficiency is more likely in people with dark skin✅: Increased melanin reduces UVB-mediated vitamin D production.
• 3. Exposure to UV light is advisable in patients with Vitamin D deficiency✅: Regular sunlight (UVB) exposure enhances endogenous vitamin D synthesis and complements supplementation.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Vitamin D deficiency is common worldwide and results from inadequate sunlight exposure, reduced cutaneous synthesis, poor dietary intake, malabsorption, or impaired metabolism.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which physiological adaptation does not happen at high altitudes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Respiratory acidosis

The physiological adaptation that does not happen at high altitudes is respiratory acidosis. Respiratory alkalosis is the physiological adaptation seen at high altitudes due to hyperventilation. It is a method of acclimatization. Compensatory mechanisms that are carried out to increase altitude tolerance are called acclimatization.

Following are the physiological changes that occur during acclimatization:

• Hyperventilation leads to respiratory alkalosis and shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left (and shifts to right after aclimitization).
• Increased erythropoietin secretion, leading to an increase in circulating red blood cells
• Increased number of mitochondria
• Increased myoglobin to facilitate the movement of O2 into the tissues.
• Increased tissue cytochrome oxidase
• Increased sympathetic tone
• Renal suppression of carbonic anhydrase and excretion of dilute alkaline urine brings the pH of the blood to normal.
• Decreased maximal exercise capacity (by ~1% for every 100 meters gained above 1500 meters)

Other options:

Option A- In response to the high altitude hypoxia, pulmonary vasoconstriction occurs due to which blood flow is distributed where it is most effective, leading to distribution of blood flow to the pulmonary areas in proportion to their alveolar O2 pressures.

Option B- Polycythemia - Erythropoietin secretion increases on the ascent to high altitude which results in polycythemia

Option D- Hypoxia - Total barometric pressure decreases as altitude increases, resulting in decreased Po2 (partial pressure of oxygen) leading to hypoxic hypoxia.
questions.learning: Respiratory acidosis — The physiological adaptation that does not happen at high altitudes is respiratory acidosis. Respiratory alkalosis is the physiological adaptation seen at high altitudes due to hyperventilation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with episodic upper gastrointestinal bleeding, right hypochondrial pain, and progressive jaundice for 3 days. He had undergone percutaneous liver biopsy 10 days ago. On examination, he is mildly icteric and hemodynamically stable. Ultrasound abdomen reveals echogenic contents within the gallbladder lumen and dilated intrahepatic bile ducts, without gallstones. What is the most appropriate next investigation to establish the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CT angiography of hepatic artery

A patient presenting with the triad of upper GI bleeding, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice following a hepatic intervention (e.g., percutaneous liver biopsy) most likely has hemobilia, classically due to an arteriobiliary fistula or hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm. Ultrasound findings of echogenic material within the gallbladder (blood clots) with dilated intrahepatic bile ducts (biliary obstruction from clot) support this diagnosis in the absence of gallstones.

The most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis and identify the bleeding source is CT angiography of the hepatic artery, as it can demonstrate contrast extravasation, pseudoaneurysm, or arterio-biliary fistula, and guides definitive management (angiographic embolization). Endoscopy may show blood at the ampulla but does not localize the vascular lesion; MRCP outlines biliary anatomy but does not reliably identify active vascular bleeding; ERCP is primarily therapeutic (clot extraction/stenting) after diagnosis is established.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following are done in Breast Conservation Surgery?

1. Wide local excision
2. Axillary node dissection
3. Frozen section (biopsy) to be done during surgery
4. Post-operative radiotherapy optional
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3

Wide local excision, axillary node dissection, and frozen section (biopsy) during surgery are done as a part of Breast Conservation Surgery (BCS). All patients with BCS must receive radiotherapy (Statement 4) and are together known as Breast Conservation Therapy (BCT).

Breast conservation surgery involves removing the tumor with a 1mm margin of normal breast tissue. Removal of primary breast cancer is also called lumpectomy/ tylectomy/ partial mastectomy/ wide local excision (Statement 1). Histological examination via intraoperative frozen section (Statement 3) is done to examine for positive margins. Patients with positive margins should have a revision of margins known as ‘cavity shave’. Assessment of regional lymph nodes is done via a separate incision in the axilla (Statement 2).

Absolute contraindications of BCT:

• 1st trimester of pregnancy (may be done for some 2nd and many 3rd trimester patients who can receive radiation after delivery)
• Persistently positive margin (2 microscopy shows positive margins)
• Multicentric lumps
• Diffuse microcalcification
•

Extensive ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)

•

Inflammatory breast cancer

Relative contraindications of BCT:

• Active SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus), scleroderma
• Large lump-to-breast ratio (>5 cm size lump)
• Known or suspected genetic predisposition to breast cancer (i.e., BRCA1, BRCA2), Li-Fraumeni syndrome (p53 mutation)
• Multifocal disease
• Prior radiation therapy to the chest wall or breast
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 Wide local excision, axillary node dissection, and frozen section (biopsy) during surgery are done as a part of Breast Conservation Surgery (BCS).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an orexigenic hormone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ghrelin

Ghrelin is an orexigenic hormone that increases appetite.

Ghrelin is produced by the oxyntic gland area of the stomach and is primarily involved in the central control of food intake. It is also secreted by the pancreas and adrenal glands.

Functions

* Increases appetite/food intake (orexigenic)

* It stimulates growth hormone secretion by directly acting on the anterior pituitary

* It increases gastric acid secretion and gastrointestinal motility to prepare the body for food intake

* It regulates the distribution and rate of use of energy

* It suppresses the action of leptin and increases the production of neuropeptide Y. It also causes lipolysis

Ghrelin levels increase during fasting, peaking just before food intake begins or when the subject is expecting a meal. The levels fall within 1 hour of the start of feeding.

Melanocyte-stimulating hormone, cholecystokinin, and leptin are anorexigenic and they decrease the appetite.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) includes which of the following? 1. Asymptomatic neurocognitive disorder 2. Minor neurocognitive disorder 3. HIV-associated dementia Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) is a spectrum of cognitive impairment caused by HIV infection of the CNS. According to the Frascati criteria, HAND includes:

• Asymptomatic Neurocognitive Impairment (ANI)
• Mild Neurocognitive Disorder (MND) (previously called minor neurocognitive disorder)
• HIV-Associated Dementia (HAD)

Why are the other statements correct?

• 1. Asymptomatic neurocognitive disorder ✔️: Included in HAND.
• 2. Minor (Mild) neurocognitive disorder ✔️: Included in HAND.
• 3. HIV-associated dementia ✔️: Most severe form of HAND.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with dysphagia, halitosis, and recurrent regurgitation of food. Imaging shows pneumonia affecting a single lobe. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), halitosis (bad breath), and regurgitation of undigested food is classic for Zenker's diverticulum, which is a type of Pulsion diverticula. This outpocketing of the mucosa occurs at the Pharyngoesophageal junction (Killian's dehiscence) due to elevated pressure during swallowing. The pooling of food in the pouch leads to bad breath and nocturnal regurgitation, which puts the patient at high risk for aspiration and subsequent pneumonia. Achalasia cardia (Option B) involves the lower sphincter and presents with more distal dysphagia. CA Esophagus (Option C) would typically involve significant weight loss and an irregular stricture on imaging. GERD (Option D) involves acid reflux, not undigested food regurgitation. Diagnosis of Zenker's is confirmed with a barium swallow, showing a posterior pouch. Management involves surgical or endoscopic diverticulotomy. Clinicians must be extremely cautious during endoscopy to avoid accidental perforation of the thin-walled pouch
questions.learning: The clinical triad of dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), halitosis (bad breath), and regurgitation of undigested food is classic for Zenker's diverticulum, which is a type of Pulsion diverticula.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl presents with severe headache, photophobia and high fever of 101°F. On examination, papilledema and nuchal rigidity was present. Kernig's and Brudzinski signs were positive. CSF examination shows reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes with the predominance of neutrophils. Gram staining of the CSF is shown below. Causative organism is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neisseria meningitidis

History and physical examination findings are suggestive of bacterial meningitis. The given image shows intracellular gram-negative diplococci which is  Neisseria meningitidis.

Fever, convulsions, and signs of meningeal irritation (nuchal rigidity, Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's signs) in a child, with CSF showing reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes levels is a typical presentation of bacterial meningitis.

Pathogenesis & clinical features:

* The organism enters the body through the nasopharynx by attaching to the epithelial cells with the help of pili. From nasopharynx, they enter the bloodstream producing bacteremia, and the symptoms may resemble upper respiratory tract infection.

* Fulminant meningococcemia is the severe form, where the patient presents with high-grade fever and hemorrhagic rash. There is thrombosis of several small blood vessels in various organs with perivascular infiltration and petechial haemorrhages.

* Some patients with fulminant meningococcemia may also develop disseminated intravascular coagulation, and circulatory collapse, a condition known as Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome.

* All patients admitted to the hospital with meningitis should be placed on standard precautions.

* Droplet precautions are recommended for patients with Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) meningitis until they have received 24 hours of effective therapy.

* Chemoprophylaxis is indicated for the household and close contacts. The preferred antibiotics are rifampin, ciprofloxacin, and ceftriaxone.

Option a: Haemophilus influenzae type B is a gram-negative bacillus. In CSF, long bacillary filamentous forms predominate. H. influenzae b grows on chocolate agar (which supplies necessary nutrients from lysed red blood cells) or as satellite colonies surrounding β-hemolytic colonies of S. aureus on blood agar.

Option c: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a gram-positive, capsulated, flame-shaped or lanceolate-shaped diplococcus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a screening test for DM out of 1000 population, 90 were positive. However, a gold standard test for DM was done of which 100 were positive. Calculate the sensitivity of the screening test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 90/100

The screening test only identified 90 people as positive for diabetes, while the gold standard test identified 100 people. This means that out of the 100 confirmed, 90 have been identified as truly positive by the screening test and 10 are falsely negative. Therefore,

• True positive = 90
• False negative = 100-90= 10
• Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) =90/(90+10) = 90/100 = 90%

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following drugs can cause granulomatous liver injury? 1. Carbamazepine 2. Allopurinol 3. Diltiazem 4. Acetaminophen Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Granulomatous hepatitis is a rare form of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) characterized by hepatic granuloma formation. Common offending drugs include carbamazepine, allopurinol, diltiazem, sulfonamides, phenytoin, and quinidine.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Carbamazepine ✔️ – Recognized cause of granulomatous hepatitis.
• 2. Allopurinol ✔️ – Can cause hypersensitivity syndrome with granulomatous liver injury.
• 3. Diltiazem ✔️ – An established cause of granulomatous hepatitis.
• 4. Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) ❌ – Causes dose-dependent centrilobular (zone 3) hepatic necrosis, not granulomatous hepatitis.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Granulomatous hepatitis is a rare form of drug-induced liver injury (DILI) characterized by hepatic granuloma formation. Common offending drugs include carbamazepine, allopurinol, diltiazem, sulfonamides, phenytoin, and quinidine.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: ERCP is least useful in the diagnosis of _____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute pancreatitis without choledocholithiaisis

ERCP is least useful in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis without choledocholithiasis.

ERCP stands for Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangio-Pancreatography. It involves the use of a side-viewing endoscope which is passed through the pylorus of the stomach into the second part of the duodenum to visualise the papilla. This is then cannulated, and dye is injected into the pancreatic or bile duct to visualise the pancreatic or biliary tree. It can be therapeutic or diagnostic. It is the best diagnostic modality for viewing the distal biliary tree, but MRCP is preferred as the diagnostic modality unless a therapeutic intervention is also needed.

Indications of ERCP:

• Choledocholithiasis
• Acute cholangitis
• Biliary stricture, biliary leak
• Pancreatic duct stricture, pancreatic stones
• Extrahepatic biliary strictures related to primary sclerosing cholangitis
• Endoscopic therapy for some patients with sphincter of Oddi dysfunction
• Biliary or pancreatic ductal system tissue sampling
• Balloon dilatation of the duodenal papilla or ductal strictures
• Sphincterotomy

The most common therapeutic indication for ERCP is the relief of biliary obstruction due to gallstone disease and benign or malignant biliary strictures.

Contraindications of ERCP include patients who cannot tolerate anesthesia, patients with type 3 sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, luminal gastrointestinal obstruction (examination limited to an area proximal to the level of obstruction and untreated hemostatic disorder (high risk of bleeding).

Complications of ERCP include duodenal perforation, hemorrhage, pancreatitis and sepsis.

Other options:

Option A: ERCP can help in ruling out the etiology in cases of recurrent pancreatitis.

Option B: ERCP can act as both diagnostic and therapeutic in cases of unexplained jaundice.

Option C: ERCP can be useful in case of a periampullary mass to take a tissue biopsy and cytology.
questions.learning: Acute pancreatitis without choledocholithiaisis ERCP is least useful in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis without choledocholithiasis. ERCP stands for Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangio-Pancreatography.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Following an earthquake, the building codes were changed to earthquake-resistant buildings. Which of the following step of disaster management does this fall under?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Disaster mitigation

The measures that are taken to prevent disasters from causing emergencies or to lessen the likely effects of emergencies are part of disaster mitigation.

Disaster mitigation measures aim to reduce the vulnerability of the system. It complements disaster preparedness and response activities and includes measures taken to lessen the likely effects of emergencies. Some of these measures are:

• Flood mitigation
• Land-use planning
• Improved building codes
• Reduction and protection of vulnerable populations or structures.

Other options:

Option A - Disaster response includes activities such as rescue and first aid, field care, triage and tagging that form a part of the emergency care needed in the first few hours after a disaster.

Option B - Disaster reconstruction is a part of the recovery phase after a disaster.

Option C - Disaster rehabilitation refers to measures that lead to the restoration of pre-disaster conditions. These measures include water supply restoration, food safety, basic sanitation, personal hygiene, and vector control.

The disaster management cycle is given below:
questions.learning: Disaster mitigation — The measures that are taken to prevent disasters from causing emergencies or to lessen the likely effects of emergencies are part of disaster mitigation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A lady comes with a reddish firm nodule on her chest which hasn't grown in size. Its histolopathological image is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hemangioma

The given clinical scenario of a woman with reddish firm nodule on her chest and histology showing multiple dilated vascular structures with a single layer of epithelial cells is suggestive of a hemangioma.

Hemangioma is a benign tumor caused by the abnormal growth of blood vessels. Types of hemangioma are capillary hemangioma (most common), juvenile/ strawberry hemangioma, cavernous hemangioma and pyogenic hemangioma.

Indications for immediate treatment are complications such as ulceration or those pertaining to the location of the mass (e.g. visual issues due to a large hemangioma over the eyelid).

Treatment options include:

• Beta-blockers - oral propranolol
• Steroids - intralesional triamcinolone, topical clobetasol, systemic steroids
• Interferon alfa-2a and vincristine - for steroid-resistant lesions
• Local resection with cutting cautery or carbon dioxide laser

The given image shows a flat to elevated, irregular, pinkish-red mass over the skin of the abdomen suggestive of a strawberry hemangioma.

The given image shows a capillary hemangioma in a child
questions.learning: Hemangioma — The given clinical scenario of a woman with reddish firm nodule on her chest and histology showing multiple dilated vascular structures with a single layer of epithelial cells is suggestive of a hemangioma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the fifth stage of the demographic cycle?
options: Birth rate falls below death rate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Birth rate falls below death rate

In stage 5 of the demographic cycle, the birth rate falls below the death rate.

In this stage, the death rate attains a low stable rate while the birth rate keeps declining. Thus, the curve of the birth rate will cross the curve of the death rate in a graph of the demographic cycle and falls further below.

The demographic gap is negative and the population is declining. So, this stage is known as the declining stage.

Pearl PF0983: Demographic Process and Cycle

* Demographic process

* Fertility

* Mortality

* Marriage

* Migration

* Social Mobility

* Demographic cycle

* Stage 1 : High stationary

* High birth rate and high death rate render the population stationary.

* Narrow demographic gap.

* Stage 2 : Early expanding

* Death rate declines and birth rate remains unchanged

* Demographic gap starts increasing and then becomes maximum

* Stage 3 : Late expanding

* Death rate decline further and birth rate falls

* India is in this stage, currently

* Demographic gap starts declining

* Stage 4 : Low stationary

* Low birth rate and low death rate renders the population stationary

* Narrow demographic gap

* Stage 5 : Declining

* Population begins to decline as birth rate is lower than death rate

* Demographic gap is negative
questions.learning: Birth rate falls below death rate — In stage 5 of the demographic cycle, the birth rate falls below the death rate. In this stage, the death rate attains a low stable rate while the birth rate keeps declining.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the instrument shown below in image?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a Veress needle, a specialized instrument used in laparoscopic surgery to create a pneumoperitoneum (insufflating the abdomen with gas). It features a spring-loaded, blunt inner stylet that retracts when it meets resistance (like the fascia or peritoneum) and pops forward once it enters the empty abdominal cavity to protect the underlying viscera from injury. A Hasson cannula (Option B) is used for "open" laparoscopy, which involves a direct incision rather than a needle. Small and large bore cannulas (Options A and C) are more general surgical tools for drainage or access. The Veress needle is the cornerstone of the "closed" technique for gaining laparoscopic access. Proper technique, including checking for a "negative" aspiration and observing low initial insufflation pressures, is mandatory to ensure safe entry and avoid major vascular or bowel injuries. Correct identification of this instrument is a high-yield clinical task in surgical board exams
questions.learning: The image depicts a Veress needle, a specialized instrument used in laparoscopic surgery to create a pneumoperitoneum (insufflating the abdomen with gas).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the mechanism responsible for the release of secretions from the gland seen in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Holocrine

The gland depicted in the image is a sebaceous gland, which releases its secretions through the holocrine mechanism.

Identification features of sebaceous gland:

• Lobular structure with clusters of cells.
• Foamy cytoplasm due to lipid content.
• Holocrine secretion with disintegrated cells.
• Found near hair follicles in the dermis.

Sebaceous gland cells synthesize and accumulate lipid-rich sebum within their cytoplasm.

Holocrine secretions are produced in the cytoplasm of the cell and released by the rupture of the plasma membrane, which destroys the cell and results in the secretion of the product into the lumen.

Examples of holocrine glands are

• Sebaceous glands of the skin and
• Meibomian glands of the eyelid

Other options:

Option A: Apocrine: involves partial loss of the apical portion of the cell (e.g., mammary glands).

Option B: Merocrine: involves secretion via exocytosis (e.g. sweat glands).

Option C: Eccrine glands are a type of sweat gland responsible for thermoregulation through the secretion of sweat. They use the merocrine mechanism for secretion.
questions.learning: Holocrine — The gland depicted in the image is a sebaceous gland, which releases its secretions through the holocrine mechanism. Identification features of sebaceous gland: • Lobular structure with clusters of cells. • Foamy cytoplasm due to lipid content.…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A mother with her preterm newborn is worried as the newborn hasn't passed the meconium till now. What is the maximum time to wait for meconium to pass in this infant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 48 hours

Meconium is normally evacuated within 6 hours of birth( or earlier), but it can be delayed up to 24-48 hours and the maximum time to wait in a pre-term infant is 48 hours, however, in a term infant, it is 24 hours.

Meconium found in the intestine of a neonate consists of succus entericus (bile salts, bile acids, and debris from the intestinal mucosa).

Meconium ileus occurs in the first 24-48 hours of life when meconium becomes inspissated and obstructs the distal ileum causing abdominal distension and emesis. Abdominal radiographs show dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels and, frequently, a collection of granular, “ground-glass” material in the lower central abdomen.

Meconium ileus may also be seen with pancreatic atresia or pancreatic duct stenosis.

Radiological image shows contrast enema in a newborn infant with abdominal distention and failure to pass meconium. Several air-fluid levels in the small bowel are visible on the upright lateral view.
questions.learning: 48 hours Meconium is normally evacuated within 6 hours of birth( or earlier), but it can be delayed up to 24-48 hours and the maximum time to wait in a pre-term infant is 48 hours, however, in a term infant, it is 24 hours.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding High-Quality CPR?
options: Chest compression to Rescue breath ratio is 30:2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Depth of compression must be 3-4cm

High-quality adult CPR requires compression depth of at least 5 cm (about 2 inches) to generate adequate cardiac output. Recommended rate is 100–120/min with complete chest recoil between compressions.

| Parameter | Recommended Value

| --------- | -----------------

| Compression rate | 100–120/min

| Compression depth | 5–6 cm (2–2.4 inches)

| Compression : ventilation | 30 : 2

| Chest recoil | Must be complete

| Interruptions | <10 seconds

During chest recoil: Negative intrathoracic pressure develops

This allows:

• Venous blood to return to the heart
• Cardiac chambers to refill

If recoil is incomplete:

• Cardiac output decreases
• Coronary perfusion falls

The standard compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2 for single rescuer CPR.

Thus, a depth of 3–4 cm is inadequate, making option D incorrect.
questions.learning: Depth of compression must be 3-4cm High-quality adult CPR requires compression depth of at least 5 cm (about 2 inches) to generate adequate cardiac output.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old P2L2 woman presents with complaints of a mass descending through the vagina and wishes to retain her fertility. She underwent an abdominal sling procedure with mesh placement. Which is the correct site of attachment of the mesh?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sacral Promontory

In abdominal sling procedures such as sacral colpopexy, which is used to treat pelvic organ prolapse while preserving fertility, the mesh is typically attached to the sacral promontory. This site provides strong support for the prolapsed vaginal apex and allows for a durable suspension without significant compromise to the patient's fertility.

Various surgeries were performed for the management of uterovaginal prolapse:

• Anterior colporrhaphy: This is done for cystocele or cystourethrocele.
• Posterior colporrhaphy/ colpoperineorrhaphy: This is done for posterior defects like rectocele or rectal defects with perineal laxity.
• Le Forte's repair: This is preferred only in elderly women with advanced prolapse, or those unfit for surgery. Women wanting an active sexual life are poor candidates for this procedure as it creates an adhesive area in the midline.
• Abdominal sling surgeries: Young women desirous of retaining menstrual and reproductive functions are ideal candidates. These surgeries use tapes as slings to prevent organ descent. These include:

• Abdominal wall cervicopexy (modified by Purandare and Mathre) - sling attached to cervix posteriorly near uterosacral ligaments.
• Shirodkar's sling surgery - the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia.
• Khanna's sling surgery - sling fixed to the anterior superior iliac spine, strengthening the Mackenrodt's ligament.

• Fothergill surgery (Manchester operation): An anterior colporrhaphy is combined with amputation of the cervix. The Mackenrodt ligaments are then sutured in front of the cervix followed by a colpoperineorrhaphy. It is suitable for women <40 years desiring reproductive function, but fertility may be reduced.
• Ward-Mayo surgery: This is a combination of vaginal hysterectomy + pelvic floor repair. It is done in women >40 years, not desiring reproductive function.
• Moschowitz surgery: This is performed for enterocele repair where the pouch of Douglas is obliterated.

Management of Vault prolapse:

• If the patient is fit for abdominal surgery: Transabdominal sacral colpopexy, i.e., suspending the vault to the sacral promontory extraperitoneally. It is best suited for younger women since coital difficulty following vaginal surgery is avoided
• If the patient is not fit for abdominal surgery: Right Transvaginal sacrospinous colpopexy. It is usually preferred in obese and elderly women, who are not fit for abdominal surgery.
• Colpocleisis is permissible if sexual activity is not desired
questions.learning: Sacral Promontory — In abdominal sling procedures such as sacral colpopexy, which is used to treat pelvic organ prolapse while preserving fertility, the mesh is typically attached to the sacral promontory.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman, gravida 5 para 0 aborta 4, at 35 weeks’ gestation presents to labor and delivery triage because she has not felt fetal movements for the past 24 hours. She has had poor oral intake due to nausea. A nonstress test shows a baseline fetal heart rate in the 130s with moderate variability, no decelerations, and no accelerations despite vibroacoustic stimulation. Tocometry shows no uterine contractions. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Biophysical profile

A nonstress test (NST) evaluates fetal well-being by assessing fetal heart rate accelerations with fetal movement.

Interpretation:

• Reactive NST: ≥2 accelerations in 20 minutes → reassuring
• Nonreactive NST: No accelerations despite stimulation → requires further evaluation

When an NST is nonreactive but baseline rate and variability are normal, the next step is a Biophysical Profile (BPP).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presented with hematemesis and was found to have splenomegaly, on examination. There was a past history of exchange transfusion in this child for neonatal jaundice. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Portal Vein thrombosis

As the child has a history of neonatal blood transfusion, along with hematemesis and splenomegaly this is a case of portal vein thrombosis.

Neonatal blood transfusion is done via the umbilical vein and as the umbilical vein drains into the portal vein, thrombosis of the portal vein might have occurred leading to portal hypertension.

A child presenting with hematemesis and splenomegaly is presumed to have variceal bleeding unless proved otherwise. Bleeding from esophageal varices is the most common presentation of portal hypertension.

Pre hepatic

* Portal vein thrombosis

* Splenic vein thrombosis

* Splenomegaly

Intrahepatic - This is further classified as

* Presinusoidal -

* Schistosomiasis

* Sarcoidosis

* Primary biliary cholangitis

* Noncirrhotic portal fibrosis (NCPF)

* Sinusoidal - Cirrhosis due to various causes

* ALD and NAFLD

* Viral hepatitis

* Postsinusoidal - sinusoidal obstruction syndrome

Post hepatic

* Budd Chiari syndrome

* Veno-occlusive disease

* Chronic right-sided cardiac congestion

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with chronic diarrhea, cognitive changes, and a photosensitive skin rash, with a diet mainly consisting of maize. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely causing these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits the classic triad of the "3 Ds": Diarrhea, Dermatitis (on sun-exposed areas), and Dementia (cognitive impairment). This is the hallmark of Pellagra, caused by a deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3). The dietary history of a maize-based diet is a significant clinical clue, as maize is deficient in both niacin and its precursor amino acid, tryptophan. Furthermore, the niacin in maize is often chemically bound and unabsorbable unless treated with lime. Vitamin B6 (Option B) and Biotin (Option D) deficiencies cause different skin and neurological issues but not the specific photosensitive rash of pellagra. Ascorbic acid (Option C) deficiency causes scurvy. Pellagra was historically common in populations where corn was the primary staple. Modern management involve niacin supplementation and dietary diversification. Recognizing the link between maize consumption and the "3 Ds" is a fundamental requirement for diagnosing nutritional deficiencies in clinical practice
questions.learning: The patient exhibits the classic triad of the "3 Ds": Diarrhea, Dermatitis (on sun-exposed areas), and Dementia (cognitive impairment). This is the hallmark of Pellagra, caused by a deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which is not a product of heme catabolism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aminolaevulinic acid

During heme catabolism, heme is degraded by the enzyme heme oxygenase to produce biliverdin, ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), and carbon monoxide (CO). Biliverdin is subsequently reduced to bilirubin by biliverdin reductase.

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is not a product of heme breakdown; instead, it is an intermediate in heme synthesis, formed from glycine and succinyl-CoA by ALA synthase in mitochondria.

Therefore, aminolevulinic acid belongs to the heme biosynthesis pathway, not the catabolic pathway, making it the correct answer.
questions.learning: Aminolaevulinic acid During heme catabolism, heme is degraded by the enzyme heme oxygenase to produce biliverdin, ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), and carbon monoxide (CO).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with ptosis and muscle weakness that worsens by evening and improves after rest in the morning. His symptoms show improvement following administration of neostigmine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the production of antibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. This leads to "fatigable" muscle weakness, meaning the weakness worsens with repetitive use or as the day progresses (diurnal variation). Ptosis and diplopia (ocular myasthenia) are the most common presenting symptoms. The hallmark of MG is the clinical improvement of symptoms with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors like neostigmine or edrophonium (Tensilon test). These drugs increase the availability of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, briefly overcoming the receptor blockade. Huntington chorea (Option B) is a genetic disorder presenting with choreiform movements and cognitive decline. Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS, Option C) involves progressive upper and lower motor neuron degeneration, causing permanent, non-fatigable weakness and atrophy. External ophthalmoplegia (Option D) refers to restricted eye movements but is a descriptive term, not a primary diagnosis, and would not respond to neostigmine. Thus, the classic presentation of fatigable ptosis responsive to anticholinesterases confirms Myasthenia Gravis
questions.learning: Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the production of antibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the immortality of cancer cells?
questions.explanation: Telomeres are protective caps at the ends of chromosomes that shorten with each cell division, eventually leading to cellular senescence or death. Telomerase is the enzyme responsible for maintaining telomere length by adding repetitive sequences back onto the chromosome ends. While telomerase activity is low in most adult somatic cells, its overexpression in cancer cells allows them to bypass the normal aging process and divide indefinitely. Topoisomerase (Option B) manages DNA structural tension by inducing strand breaks during replication. Helicase (Option C) unwinds the double helix to allow access for replication machinery. RNA polymerase (Option D) is essential for synthesizing RNA during transcription but does not directly influence the replicative lifespan of the cell. Consequently, the activation of telomerase is the fundamental mechanism that confers "immortality" upon malignant cells, facilitating uncontrolled tumor growth
