questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with a lesion associated with loss of sensation over the posterior surface of the ear. Which anatomical structure is most likely to be involved?
questions.explanation: The Greater Auricular Nerve, a branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3), provides sensory innervation to the posterior surface of the ear, the skin over the parotid gland, and the angle of the mandible. A lesion involving this nerve or its distribution would lead to the loss of sensation described. Regarding the distractors, the Internal Jugular Vein (Option B) and External Jugular Vein (Option C) are major vascular structures involved in venous drainage of the head and neck; they do not possess sensory functions. Similarly, the External Carotid Artery (Option D) is the primary arterial supply to the face and scalp but plays no role in providing cutaneous sensation. Therefore, because the symptom is strictly sensory and localized to the auricular region, the Greater Auricular Nerve is the only structure listed that explains the deficit
questions.learning: The Greater Auricular Nerve, a branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3), provides sensory innervation to the posterior surface of the ear, the skin over the parotid gland, and the angle of the mandible.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A surgeon is about to start a laparoscopic procedure on a patient. The floor nurse asks the surgeon about the identity of the patient, site of the procedure to be performed and any anticipated critical events during the surgery. These questions are a part of the:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. WHO surgical safety checklist

The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist is a standardized checklist developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to improve patient safety and reduce surgical morbidity and mortality. It promotes effective communication among the surgical team and ensures that critical safety steps are not missed before, during, and after surgery.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Universal precautions checklist: Refers to infection control measures (e.g., hand hygiene, PPE, safe handling of sharps), not surgical team communication.
• B. Nurses safety checklist: No standard checklist by this name is used internationally.
• C. MCI patient safety checklist: There is no recognized Medical Council of India (MCI) surgical safety checklist.
questions.learning: WHO surgical safety checklist — The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist is a standardized checklist developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to improve patient safety and reduce surgical morbidity and mortality.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Cryoglobulinemia is associated with _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hepatitis C

Cryoglobulinemia is associated with hepatitis C infection.

Following Hepatitis C infection, there is an aberrant immune response leading to an immune complex formation containing hepatitis C antigens, polyclonal IgG specific to Hepatitis C, and monoclonal IgM rheumatoid factor, which triggers an inflammatory cascade results in Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis.

Cryoglobulins are the immunoglobulins that precipitate at temperatures less than 37°C, the presence of these cryoglobulins in serum leads to Cryoglobulinemia, which is characterized by cutaneous vasculitis, palpable purpura, arthritis, peripheral neuropathy, and glomerulonephritis.

Important conditions associated with cryoglobulinemia are:

• Hepatitis C
• Multiple myeloma
• Connective tissue disorders
• Lymphoproliferative disorders

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which medical procedure has been banned by the Supreme Court of India due to its association with cases of sexual assault involving doctors?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court of India has strictly banned the "two-finger test" (per-vaginal examination to assess "vaginal laxity") in cases of sexual assault. The court ruled that this test has no scientific or medical validity for determining whether a sexual assault occurred or for assessing the "character" or "habitual" nature of a victim's sexual activity. The test is considered a violation of the victim's dignity, privacy, and bodily integrity, effectively re-traumatizing them. Foley's catheter insertion (Option A), colposcopy (Option B), and speculum insertion (Option C) are legitimate medical procedures used for urinary drainage or gynecological diagnosis and have not been banned, provided they are done with informed consent and for proper medical indications. The ban on the two-finger test is a landmark decision in Indian medical jurisprudence, aimed at modernizing the forensic approach to sexual assault and ensuring that survivors are treated with sensitivity and respect during the legal process

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The audiogram given in the image below is seen in ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endolymphatic hydrops

The given image shows an upsloping/ ascending audiogram in which lower frequencies are affected first like in the early stages of Meniere's disease also known as endolymphatic hydrops.

Meniere's disease (endolymphatic hydrops) is an inner ear disorder where the endolymph distends the endolymphatic system.

Meniere's disease is usually unilateral. It is characterized by episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sense of ear fullness.

Pure tone audiometry reveals a sensorineural type of hearing loss with lower frequencies affected first. It shows a rising type of curve. As the disease progresses, middle and higher frequencies get involved, and the audiogram becomes flat or downsloping type.

The illustration given below shows an audiogram seen in different stages of Meniere's disease.

Other options:

Option A: Ototoxicity causes bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Audiometry shows a downsloping audiogram, typically involving frequencies above 8,000 Hz and progresses to lower speech frequencies. Common drugs causing the same include aminoglycoside antibiotics; loop diuretics (not thiazides); antimalarials; cisplatin; and NSAIDs like ibuprofen, salicylates, and indomethacin.

Option B: Presbycusis is a physiological sensorineural hearing loss occurring in individuals above 65 years of age. Audiometry shows a downsloping graph.

Option C: In noise-induced hearing loss, audiometry shows a typical notch at 4000 Hz. As the duration of noise exposure increases, the notch becomes deeper and wider, involving lower and higher frequencies.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A motorcyclist sustains a metacarpal fracture in a road traffic accident and is found to have hypothenar atrophy. Which nerve is likely involved?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve provides the primary motor supply to the intrinsic muscles of the hand, including those of the hypothenar eminence (abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi, and opponens digiti minimi). Hypothenar atrophy is a classic sign of chronic ulnar nerve injury, often occurring at the wrist (Guyon's canal) or the elbow (cubital tunnel). In trauma, the nerve can be damaged during metacarpal fractures or carpal dislocations. The radial nerve (Option A) primarily supplies the extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers; its injury leads to "wrist drop." The median nerve (Option D) supplies the thenar muscles at the base of the thumb; its injury leads to "ape hand" deformity. The musculocutaneous nerve (Option C) supplies the biceps and brachialis in the upper arm and does not have intrinsic hand motor functions. Therefore, atrophy specifically affecting the hypothenar region confirms the involvement of the ulnar nerve
questions.learning: The ulnar nerve provides the primary motor supply to the intrinsic muscles of the hand, including those of the hypothenar eminence (abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi, and opponens digiti minimi).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not considered a grievous hurt?
options: 7 days admission in yellow zone of hospital
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 7 days admission in yellow zone of hospital

Among the options provided, a seven-day admission in the yellow zone of the hospital is not an example of grievous hurt, but any hurt which causes the sufferer to be in severe body pain for 15 days is considered to be an example of grievous hurt.

Grievous hurt (Sec 116 BNS) is inflicted voluntarily on another person and comprises any of the eight kinds (clauses) enumerated below:

Clause 1 — Emasculation.
Clause 2 — Permanent privation of the sight of either eye.
Clause 3 — Permanent privation of the hearing of either ear.
Clause 4 — Privation of any member or joint.
Clause 5 — Destruction or permanent impairment of powers of any member or joint.
Clause 6 — Permanent disfigurement of head or face.
Clause 7 — Fracture or dislocation of bone or tooth.
Clause 8 — Any hurt that endangers life or causes the sufferer to be in severe bodily pain or unable to follow his or her ordinary pursuits for 15 days.

Punishment for grievous hurt :

BNS Section 117(2) - previously, IPC 325: Punishment for voluntarily causing grievous hurt –imprisonment up to seven years and fine.
BNS Section 118(2) - previously, IPC 326: Punishment for voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means—life imprisonment or imprisonment of a minimum of one year, extendable up to ten years, and fine.

Related IPC's:

BNS Section 115(1) - previously, IPC 321: Voluntarily causing hurt.
BNS Section 117(1) - previously, IPC 322: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt.
BNS Section 115(2) - previously, IPC 323: Punishment for voluntarily causing hurt: Imprisonment up to one year, or with a fine up to one thousand rupees or both.
BNS Section 118(1) - previously, IPC 324: Voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons or means (3 years imprisonment) or with fine or both.

questions.text: A 64-year-old man comes to the OPD due to worsening dyspnea on exertion for the past 3 months. The patient has had a nonproductive cough but no chest pain, fever, or chills. He was diagnosed with hypertension several years ago but takes no medications. Physical examination shows bilateral inspiratory crackles as well as dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the right lung base. Chest x-ray reveals a right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following pleuropulmonary changes are most likely present in this patient?
options: Vascular hydrostatic pressure increased, Oncotic pressure increased, lymphatic flow normal
Vascular hydrostatic pressure normal, Oncotic pressure normal, lymphatic flow decreased
Vascular hydrostatic pressure increased, Oncotic pressure normal, lymphatic flow increased
Vascular hydrostatic pressure normal, Oncotic pressure decreased, lymphatic flow increased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vascular hydrostatic pressure increased, Oncotic pressure normal, lymphatic flow increased

Pleural effusion due to congestive heart failure occurs from increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.

• Elevated hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries → transudation of fluid into the pleural space
• Oncotic pressure remains normal
• Lymphatic drainage increases initially to compensate but may eventually be overwhelmed.

Characteristics:

• Produces a transudative pleural effusion
• Commonly seen in heart failure

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Labour induction is not done in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Induction of labor (artificial initiation of contractions) is contraindicated in Central (Type IV) Placenta Previa. In this condition, the placenta completely covers the internal os of the cervix. Attempting a vaginal delivery (via induction) would lead to massive, life-threatening maternal hemorrhage and fetal distress as the cervix dilates. All such cases must be delivered via a planned or emergency cesarean section. Gestational hypertension (Option B), Premature Rupture of Membranes (PROM) (Option C), and certain cases of stable Abruptio placenta (Option D) are actually common indications for induction to ensure the safety of the mother and fetus. Other contraindications for induction include prior classical C-section scars and active genital herpes. Proper selection of patients for induction is critical in obstetric practice to avoid high-risk vaginal delivery attempts where the placental position or structural anomalies make it unsafe
questions.learning: Induction of labor (artificial initiation of contractions) is contraindicated in Central (Type IV) Placenta Previa. In this condition, the placenta completely covers the internal os of the cervix.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient at the orthopedics OPD complains of troubled sleep at night due to numbness and tingling sensation involving his lateral 3 digits. His symptoms are relieved as he lays his arms hanging from the bed. Which among the following options correctly describes his condition along with the test used to assess it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carpal tunnel syndrome, Durkan's test

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of carpal tunnel syndrome and it can be assessed by Durkan's test.

Durkan's test is the most specific test for the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome. In Durkan's test, direct compression of the median nerve is done for about 30 seconds, which elicits paresthesias and pain in cases of carpal tunnel syndrome.

Carpal tunnel syndrome is the most common entrapment mononeuropathy caused by compression of the median nerve as it passes through the fibro-osseous carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. Patients present with pain and paresthesia over the radial 3 and a half digits. There may be a weakness of thumb opposition. In chronic cases, the thenar eminence is wasted. Carpal tunnel syndrome can be associated with rheumatoid arthritis, pregnancy, chronic renal failure, acromegaly, hypothyroidism, and gout. The diagnosis is usually made on clinical grounds but nerve conduction studies can confirm the diagnosis.

Other tests for CTS -

• Phalen's test - Elicited by holding the wrist flexed fully. The appearance of sensory symptoms within 60 seconds implies a positive test.
• Tinel's sign - Sensory symptoms reproduced by percussing over the median nerve imply a positive test.

Guyon’s canal is a fibro-osseous canal, approximately 4 cm long in the adult, on the anteromedial aspect of the wrist under the superficial part of the flexor retinaculum. The ulnar nerve passes in Guyon’s canal along with the ulnar artery and can be compressed here.  Froment's test is used in a suspected ulnar nerve injury.

In Froment's test or Book Test, the patient is asked to grasp a book or a sheet of paper between the thumb and index finger. Due to weakness of the adductor pollicis muscle, adduction of the thumb is lost. When asked to hold a book, the patient tries to hold the book by using the flexor pollicis longus muscle instead of the adductor, this produces flexion at the interphalangeal joint.

The picture below shows Froment's test

Non-surgical Management of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: In mild to moderate cases of carpal tunnel syndrome, non-surgical management options can be explored to alleviate symptoms and improve function. These conservative treatments include:

1.

Wrist splinting: Wearing a wrist splint at night can help maintain the wrist in a neutral position, reducing pressure on the median nerve and providing relief from nocturnal symptoms.

2.

Activity modification: Identifying and modifying activities that exacerbate symptoms can help in managing carpal tunnel syndrome. For example, taking frequent breaks during repetitive tasks or adjusting the workstation ergonomics can be beneficial.

3.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs): Over-the-counter NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, can help manage pain and inflammation associated with carpal tunnel syndrome.

4.

Corticosteroid injections: In some cases, corticosteroid injections into the carpal tunnel may provide temporary relief from symptoms by reducing inflammation and pressure on the median nerve.

5.

Physical and occupational therapy: Therapists can help patients learn exercises to stretch and strengthen the hand and wrist muscles, improving symptoms and function.

If conservative treatments do not provide sufficient relief or the condition worsens, surgical intervention, such as carpal tunnel release surgery, may be considered.
questions.learning: Carpal tunnel syndrome, Durkan's test — The given clinical vignette is suggestive of carpal tunnel syndrome and it can be assessed by Durkan's test. Durkan's test is the most specific test for the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is used to prevent cardiotoxicity induced by daunorubicin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dexrazoxane

Anthracycline (daunorubicin)

↓

Binds iron → forms free radicals

↓

Oxidative damage

↓

Myocardial cell injury

↓

Dilated cardiomyopathy

Daunorubicin causes dose-dependent anthracycline cardiotoxicity via free radical–mediated myocardial injury. Dexrazoxane is an iron-chelating agent that reduces reactive oxygen species formation in cardiac tissue. It is used prophylactically to protect against anthracycline-induced cardiomyopathy. Cardiac protection is its key clinical role.

| Toxicity | Drug

| -------- | ----

| Anthracycline cardiotoxicity | Dexrazoxane

| Cisplatin nephrotoxicity | Amifostine

| Hemorrhagic cystitis (cyclophosphamide) | Mesna

| Methotrexate toxicity | Leucovorin

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: For an ICU patient who already has an endotracheal tube in place and now requires a tracheostomy, which type of tracheostomy tube would be most appropriate to select?
questions.explanation: In an Intensive Care Unit (ICU) setting, patients requiring a tracheostomy often need continued mechanical ventilation or have a high risk of aspiration. The cuffed tracheostomy tube (Option B) is the standard selection for these patients. The inflated cuff provides a seal against the tracheal wall, ensuring that the volume delivered by the ventilator reaches the lungs and protecting the airway from oropharyngeal secretions (aspiration). Uncuffed tubes (Option A) are typically used in pediatric patients or for long-term management in stable patients who can breathe spontaneously and have good airway protection. Metallic tubes (Option C) are used for chronic airway maintenance in stable outpatients; they lack cuffs and are not compatible with modern ICU ventilators. Re-inserting an endotracheal tube (Option D) is not a solution when a tracheostomy is indicated for long-term airway management. Therefore, the cuffed tracheostomy tube is the most appropriate ICU choice
questions.learning: In an Intensive Care Unit (ICU) setting, patients requiring a tracheostomy often need continued mechanical ventilation or have a high risk of aspiration.

questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with a posterior cortical lesion is unable to perceive more than one object at a time, has difficulty accurately reaching for objects under visual guidance, and shows impaired voluntary eye movements despite normal ocular motility. This constellation of findings is best described as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Balint syndrome

Balint syndrome results from bilateral parieto-occipital (posterior cortical) lesions and is characterized by a classic triad:

1. Simultanagnosia: Inability to perceive more than one object at a time
2. Optic ataxia: Difficulty reaching for objects using visual guidance
3. Oculomotor (ocular) apraxia: Impaired voluntary eye movements despite normal ocular motility

Exam differentiation:

• Gerstmann syndrome: Dominant parietal lesion → acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, L–R disorientation
• Anton syndrome: Cortical blindness with denial of blindness
• Visual agnosia: Cannot recognize objects but vision intact; no optic ataxia or gaze apraxia

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the condition known as when a gallstone becomes impacted in the cystic duct, causes dilation of the common hepatic duct, compresses the common bile duct, and leads to obstructive jaundice?
questions.explanation: The scenario describes Mirizzi's syndrome (Option D), a rare complication of chronic gallstone disease . It occurs when a large gallstone becomes impacted in the cystic duct or the neck of the gallbladder (Hartmann’s pouch). This impacted stone causes significant extrinsic compression or secondary inflammation of the adjacent common hepatic duct (CHD), leading to biliary obstruction and obstructive jaundice. Acute cholecystitis (Option A) involves inflammation of the gallbladder but does not typically cause dilation of the CHD or CBD unless a stone has migrated into the CBD (choledocholithiasis). Porcelain gallbladder (Option B) refers to calcification of the gallbladder wall. Cholesterolosis (Option C) is an accumulation of cholesterol within the gallbladder mucosa ("strawberry gallbladder"). Mirizzi's syndrome is a surgical challenge because the intense inflammation can lead to a cholecystobiliary fistula. Therefore, extrinsic compression of the bile duct by a cystic duct stone is the defining feature of Mirizzi's syndrome

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which hormone is found in the contraceptive shown below in the image?
questions.explanation: The image shows "Today" vaginal contraceptive sponges, which are a form of barrier and chemical contraception. These sponges are impregnated with a spermicide, and the active ingredient used in this specific brand is Nonoxynol-9 (Option A). Nonoxynol-9 is a surfactant that works by disrupting the cell membrane of the sperm, thereby immobilizing or killing them before they can enter the cervix. It is the most widely used spermicide worldwide. Octoxynol-8 (Option B) and Menfegol (Option C) are also surfactants used in some older spermicidal preparations but are not the primary ingredient in the "Today" sponge. Levonorgestrel (Option D) is a synthetic progestogen used in hormonal contraceptives like pills, IUDs, or emergency contraception, but it is not a chemical spermicide. Therefore, Nonoxynol-9 is the definitive component of this vaginal contraceptive device

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following is the most important haematological condition to be ruled out while investigating a case of puberty menorrhagia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coagulation disorder

Puberty menorrhagia (adolescent heavy menstrual bleeding) is most commonly due to anovulatory cycles caused by an immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. However, the most important hematological condition that must be ruled out is an underlying coagulation disorder, especially von Willebrand disease (vWD), the commonest inherited bleeding disorder.

Why not the other options?

• A. Anaemia: A consequence of heavy bleeding, not the underlying hematological disorder to be ruled out.
• C. G-6PD deficiency: Causes hemolytic anemia, not menorrhagia.
• D. Leukemia: Can cause bleeding due to thrombocytopenia but is much less common than coagulation disorders.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: From the given image, which option corresponds to type III choledochal cyst?
questions.explanation: The Todani classification is used to categorize bile duct cysts. According to the provided diagram , the Type III choledochal cyst, also known as a choledochocele, is represented by the image labeled D. A Type III cyst is characterized by a focal dilation specifically of the intraduodenal segment of the common bile duct. Type I (Option B/A) involves fusiform dilation of the extrahepatic duct. Type II (Option A/B) is a saccular diverticulum. Type IV (Option D/C) involves multiple cysts in both the intrahepatic and extrahepatic systems. Because the image marked "D" specifically illustrates the cystic dilation within the wall of the duodenum at the Ampulla of Vater, it corresponds exactly to the definition of a Type III cyst. Accurate classification is essential because the surgical management (ranging from endoscopic sphincterotomy to duct excision) varies significantly depending on the cyst's anatomical type

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a subcentre area with a crude birth rate (CBR) of 20, what would be the expected number of antenatal care (ANC) registrations by the village health nurse (VHN) in a year?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 60

• According to the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) laid down by the Government of India, a subcentre is to serve a population of 5000 in plains.
• In this scenario, the CBR is 20.
• Probable number of pregnancies (Y) = Birth rate x population of the area / 1000 = 20 x 5000/1000 = 100.
• But, we add a correction factor of 10% to adjust for pregnancy wastage in the form of abortions or stillbirths.
• Thus, total number of expected pregnancies= Y + 10% of Y= 110
• As all the pregnancies are not registered, and at any given time an ANM should have atleast half the expected pregnancies registered with her, the number of ANC registrations is taken as 50% of the expected pregnancies.
• Therefore, Total ANC registrations = total number of expected pregnancies/2 = 55
• Hence, the closest answer is 60.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young female comes to the emergency department after ingesting 10 tablets of Phenobarbital. Which of the following components of the ETC is inhibited by this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complex I to Q

Phenobarbital is a barbiturate that inhibits complex I to Q of the electron transport chain.

Complex I of the electron transport chain is NADH-Q oxidoreductase. It oxidizes NADH and reduces coenzyme Q. Phenobarbital inhibits complex I to Q so that the electrons will not be able to be transferred from NADH to coenzyme Q, which is the first step in the electron transport chain. As a result, the rate of oxygen consumption will decrease.

The electron transport chain (ETC) represents the final pathway through which electrons, originating from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fatty acids, and amino acids, are channeled toward a final reaction with oxygen to produce water and ATP. The ETC complexes are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

The oxidation of compounds by ETC complexes leads to the release of free energy. This is used to pump H+ to the intermembrane space. This results in the formation of a proton motive force that is used for the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP. Thus, oxidation is coupled with phosphorylation to generate ATP. NADH generates 2.5 ATP and FADH2 generates 1.5 ATP.

The table below summarizes the inhibitors of the electron transport chain.

Complexes of ETC
Inhibitors

Complex I:

NADH-Q oxidoreductase

Piericidin A, phenobarbital, rotenone

Complex II:

Succinate-Q reductase

TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate

Complex III:

Q- Cyt c oxidoreductase

BAL (British anti-lewisite), antimycin A

Complex IV:

Cyt c oxidase

Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide

Complex V:

ATP Synthase

Atractyloside, oligomycin
questions.learning: Complex I to Q Phenobarbital is a barbiturate that inhibits complex I to Q of the electron transport chain. Complex I of the electron transport chain is NADH-Q oxidoreductase.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 48-year-old male with a 15-year history of alcohol use disorder presents with abdominal distension and fatigue. On examination, he has a distended abdomen with a fluid thrill, mild jaundice, and dilated superficial veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae). LFTs show elevated bilirubin, low albumin, and raised INR. An abdominal ultrasound with Doppler is performed. Which of the following ultrasound findings is the most specific for portal hypertension?
options: Portal vein diameter >13 mm on grey-scale ultrasound
Splenomegaly with splenic vein diameter >10 mm
Free fluid in the hepatorenal pouch and pelvis
A patent tubular structure in the falciform ligament with hepatofugal flow on Doppler
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A patent tubular structure in the falciform ligament with hepatofugal flow on Doppler

This describes a recanalized paraumbilical vein (umbilical vein recanalisation) — the most specific sonographic sign of portal hypertension.

The umbilical vein normally closes at birth and becomes the ligamentum teres. When portal pressure rises significantly, this vessel reopens to shunt blood from the left portal vein → paraumbilical vein → umbilical region → systemic veins. On Doppler, flow is hepatofugal (away from the liver), confirming portosystemic shunting. This is a direct pathophysiological consequence of raised portal pressure and does not occur in any other condition — making it highly specific.

Why the other options lack specificity:

| Finding | Seen in Portal HTN? | Problem with Specificity

| ------- | ------------------- | ------------------------

| Portal vein >13 mm (A) | Yes | Varies with respiration, body habitus, meals; absent in \~30% of confirmed cases

| Splenomegaly (B) | Yes | Also seen in haematological malignancy, infections, infiltrative disorders

| Ascites (C) | Yes | Also seen in CCF, hypoalbuminaemia, nephrotic syndrome, peritoneal malignancy

| Recanalized umbilical vein (D) | Yes | Unique to portal hypertension — pathognomonic

Doppler findings in portal hypertension to know:

• Hepatofugal flow in the portal vein — reversal of normal direction; indicates severe portal hypertension
• Recanalized paraumbilical vein — most specific sign
• Reduced portal vein velocity (<16 cm/s) — sensitive but non-specific
• Spontaneous splenorenal or gastrorenal collaterals — seen in advanced disease

High-yield pearl: The clinical correlate of a recanalized umbilical vein on ultrasound is caput medusae on examination — both represent the same portosystemic collateral pathway made visible by different means. Caput medusae radiates from the umbilicus; a Cruveilhier–Baumgarten murmur (venous hum at the umbilicus) may also be audible.
questions.learning: A patent tubular structure in the falciform ligament with hepatofugal flow on Doppler This describes a recanalized paraumbilical vein (umbilical vein recanalisation) — the most specific sonographic sign of portal hypertension.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In a clinical evaluation, a patient reports deriving sexual gratification from inflicting physical injury on their partner, leading to cuts and burns. What term most accurately describes this behavior?
questions.explanation: The behavior described is a paraphilic disorder known as Sexual Sadism (Option C). It involves deriving sexual excitement and pleasure from the infliction of physical or psychological suffering, pain, or humiliation on another person. Masochism (Option D) is the opposite, where an individual derives pleasure from receiving pain or humiliation. Voyeurism (Option A) involves sexual arousal from observing unsuspecting people who are naked or engaging in sexual activity. Fetishism (Option B) involves sexual arousal from non-living objects or specific non-genital body parts. Because the patient's arousal is specifically linked to the active causing of harm (cuts and burns) to a partner, it fits the definitive clinical definition of sadism. This behavior can be part of a consensual relationship or can cross into criminal assault depending on the context and consent
questions.learning: The behavior described is a paraphilic disorder known as Sexual Sadism (Option C). It involves deriving sexual excitement and pleasure from the infliction of physical or psychological suffering, pain, or humiliation on another person.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 48-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus undergoes an exercise treadmill test for evaluation of intermittent chest discomfort. He has no ECG changes during testing. During peak exercise, his heart rate increases from 70/min to 132/min, and his mean arterial pressure rises from 95 mm Hg to 112 mm Hg. Which of the following hemodynamic changes is most likely to occur during peak exercise compared to rest?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased total systemic vascular resistance

During dynamic exercise, several coordinated cardiovascular changes occur:

• ↑ Cardiac output (↑ HR + ↑ stroke volume)
• ↑ Systolic blood pressure
• ↓ Total systemic vascular resistance (TSVR) due to vasodilation in active skeletal muscles
• Blood flow is redistributed to muscles and skin

Despite increased cardiac output, TSVR falls because metabolic vasodilation predominates.

Why not other options?

A. Decreased cardiac output → Opposite; CO increases during exercise

B. Increased LVEDP → May remain normal or slightly increase, not a key change

C. Increased pulmonary artery pressure → May increase slightly, but not the primary expected change

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What does this image below indicate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Choledochal cyst

The given MRCP image showing saccular dilatation of the common bile duct suggests a diagnosis of type I choledochal cyst.

Todani classification:

• Type I- saccular dilatation of the whole (Ia) or a segment (Ib) of the common bile duct (CBD)
• Type II- diverticulum from the CBD
• Type III- choledochocele that opens into the duodenum
• Type IV- multiple cysts (both intrahepatic and extrahepatic)
• Type V- multiple cysts that are only intrahepatic (Caroli's disease)

The diagnosis is made initially with a right upper quadrant ultrasound, following which a confirmatory MRCP can be carried out to help in pre-operative planning.

Treatment is usually surgical with a Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy with radical resection of all the biliary tissue. There is a risk of malignant transformation in long-standing disease, so surgical removal is usually recommended.

Other options:

Option B: Gall bladder carcinoma would show abnormal growths or masses in the gall bladder rather than cystic dilations of the bile ducts.

Option C: Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignancy of the bile ducts and would present as irregular masses or bile duct strictures rather than cystic structures.

Option D: Choledocholithiasis refers to the presence of stones in the bile duct, which would appear as filling defects within the bile ducts rather than cystic dilations.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The first line of treatment for glaucoma in adults is?
questions.explanation: In modern ophthalmology, Prostaglandin (PG) analogues (such as latanoprost, bimatoprost, or travoprost) are considered the first-line medical treatment for primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension in adults. They are highly effective at lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) by increasing the uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor. Their advantages include once-daily dosing and a relatively mild systemic side-effect profile compared to other agents. Atropine (Option B) is a cycloplegic that can actually worsen angle-closure glaucoma. Acetazolamide (Option C) is a potent carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used for acute pressure spikes but is not preferred for long-term first-line therapy due to systemic side effects. Pilocarpine (Option D) is a miotic drug that was once first-line but is now rarely used due to frequent side effects like brow ache and blurred vision. Beta-blockers (like timolol) are often the second-line or alternative first-line choice. Consistently maintaining low IOP is critical to prevent progressive optic nerve damage and permanent vision loss
questions.learning: In modern ophthalmology, Prostaglandin (PG) analogues (such as latanoprost, bimatoprost, or travoprost) are considered the first-line medical treatment for primary open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension in adults.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Given below is an electron microscopy image of a cell. Identify the cell.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hairy cell

The given electron microscopic image shows a hairy cell.

Hairy cell leukemia is so-called because of the appearance of the leukemic cells, which have fine hair-like projections that are best recognized under the phase-contrast microscope.

Hairy cell leukemia is a distinctive B cell neoplasm, that predominantly affects middle-aged males. The markers expressed in hairy cell leukemia include the usual B-cell markers- CD-19 and 20, and specific markers such as CD 11c, CD 25, CD103, and annexin A1.

On peripheral blood smear, hairy cells have round or reniform nuclei and moderate amounts of pale blue cytoplasm with thread or bleb-like extension. In the bone marrow, these cells are usually trapped in a mesh of reticulin fibers and so it is difficult to aspirate and hence termed a dry tap.

Patients commonly present with massive splenomegaly due to infiltration of the leukemic cells. Pancytopenia due to marrow involvement can also be seen. There can be atypical monocytopenia due to which these patients experience an increased incidence of atypical mycobacterial infections. These tumors respond well to chemotherapy and BRAF (B-type Raf proto-oncogene) inhibitors and they have an excellent prognosis.

The classic hairy cells can be seen in the slide is shown below:

Other options:

Option A: Target cells have a centrally located disk of hemoglobin surrounded by an area of pallor. There is an outer rim of hemoglobin adjacent to the cell membrane giving the cell the appearance of a target. Conditions in which target cells appear are thalassemia, hepatic disease with jaundice, hemoglobin C disorders, and postsplenectomy state.

Option C: Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disorder with a deficiency of acid-β-glucosidase. It has an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. It leads to the accumulation of glucosylceramide in the reticuloendothelial system. The features of this disease include growth retardation, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, anemia, and Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the distal femur. Histology shows the presence of Gaucher cells, a characteristic wrinkled-paper appearance resulting from the presence of intracytoplasmic substrate inclusions. The intelligence of the child is normal.

Option D: Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene, which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Voltage gated calcium channel present on T-tubule is?
questions.explanation: In skeletal muscle, the excitation-contraction coupling process relies on the transmission of action potentials down the T-tubules. The specific voltage-gated L-type calcium channel located on the T-tubule membrane is the Dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR). When an action potential reaches the DHPR, it undergoes a conformational change that mechanically triggers the opening of the Ryanodine receptor (RyR) (Option D), which is the calcium-release channel located on the adjacent terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The SERCA pump (Option A) is an ATP-dependent pump responsible for sequestering calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum to initiate relaxation. The troponin-myosin complex (Option B) represents the contractile proteins where calcium eventually binds to initiate cross-bridge cycling. Understanding the DHPR-RyR interaction is essential for comprehending muscle physiology and pathologies such as malignant hyperthermia, where defective RyR channels lead to uncontrolled calcium release and hypermetabolic crises when exposed to certain anesthetic agents
questions.learning: In skeletal muscle, the excitation-contraction coupling process relies on the transmission of action potentials down the T-tubules. The specific voltage-gated L-type calcium channel located on the T-tubule membrane is the Dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR).

Iron requirement can be fulfilled in a single dose is true regarding Isomaltoside 1000.

Iron isomaltose 1000 is a new IV iron formulation that can supply a complete replacement dose in a short, single visit. It is used in adult patients with an intolerance to oral iron or for patients with CKD not requiring hemodialysis.

Option D: Isomaltoside 1000 can be given with erythropoietin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plexiform neurofibromatosis

The given image showing thickening of tissues in the temporal and orbital regions with coarse overlying skin suggests a diagnosis of plexiform neurofibroma.

Plexiform neurofibroma represents an uncommon variant (30%) of neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1). Plexiform neurofibromas are usually evident at birth and result from a diffuse thickening of nerve trunks and surrounding tissues that are usually located in the orbital or temporal region of the face. The skin overlying it may be coarse and associated with hyperpigmentation.

Plexiform neurofibromas may produce an overgrowth of an extremity and a deformity of the corresponding bone.

NF1 is clinically diagnosed when any 2 of the following 7 features are present:

• Six or more café-au-lait macules >5mm in prepubertal and >15mm in postpubertal
• Axillary or inguinal freckling
• Two or more iris lisch nodules
• Two or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma
• A distinctive osseous lesion such as sphenoid dysplasia or cortical thinning of long bones with or without pseudoarthrosis.
• Optic gliomas
• A first-degree relative with NF-1

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man with a history of construction work presents with progressive shortness of breath and a chronic cough. High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest shows nodular opacities with a ground-glass appearance. Which condition is most likely associated with these radiological findings?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a construction worker presenting with progressive dyspnea and cough suggests an occupational lung disease. On HRCT, the finding of multiple small, discrete nodular opacities—which may show a ground-glass appearance in early stages—is highly characteristic of Silicosis. These nodules typically predominate in the upper lobes and may eventually coalesce into large masses (Progressive Massive Fibrosis). Asbestosis (Option A) primarily involves the lower lobes and is characterized by pleural plaques and a pattern of interstitial fibrosis rather than discrete nodules. Anthracosis (Option C) refers to coal worker's pneumoconiosis, which has similar nodular patterns but a different occupational exposure. Bagassosis (Option D) is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by moldy sugarcane dust and typically shows ill-defined centrilobular nodules rather than the distinct nodular fibrotic pattern of silicosis. Therefore, given the construction history and the HRCT nodularity, silicosis is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with progressively worsening dysphagia for both solids and liquids. Esophageal manometry shows absent or uncoordinated peristalsis and elevated resting pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical and physiological profile provided is diagnostic for Achalasia Cardia. Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by the hallmark manometric triad: aperistalsis (absent contractions), failure of the LES to relax, and elevated resting LES pressure. Clinically, it presents with progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids from the onset, which distinguishes it from esophageal cancer (Option B), where dysphagia typically starts with solids and progresses to liquids. Stomach cancer (Option A) and GERD (Option C) do not produce these specific manometric findings. Barium swallow in achalasia characteristically shows a "bird's beak" appearance due to the persistent narrowing at the GE junction. Management options include pneumatic balloon dilation, botulinum toxin injections, or definitive surgical Heller's myotomy (often performed laparoscopically with a partial fundoplication). While more common in younger adults, achalasia can certainly occur in the elderly and must be differentiated from "pseudoachalasia" caused by a tumor at the cardia

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 17-year-old tall male presents to OPD for a routine checkup. He has long limbs, arachnodactyly, and hypermobile joints. 2D echocardiography revealed mitral valve stenosis, and an eye check-up revealed subluxation of the lens. Workup showed the defects are due to an abnormal FBN1 gene mutation. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Marfan Syndrome

The above clinical scenario of a 17-year-old tall male with long limbs, arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints, and 2D echocardiography revealed mitral valve stenosis and subluxation of the lens with an abnormal Fibrillin 1 gene mutation/ FBN1 gene mutation is highly suggestive of Marfan's syndrome.

It is a clinical diagnosis based on skeletal, cardiovascular, and ocular manifestations. Ghent criteria are used for diagnosing Marfan syndrome.  The main features are tall stature, ectopia lentis, and aortic root dilatation.

Skeletal manifestations:

* Tall stature and long limbs

* Pectus carinatum or pectus excavatum

* Long and slender fingers (arachnodactyly), contracture of fingers (camptodactyly)

* Scoliosis

Cardiovascular manifestations:

* Thickened atrioventricular valves, valvular prolapse (mitral regurgitation)

* Aortic valve dysfunction due to an aortic root aneurysm

* Aortic dissection and rupture due to cystic medial necrosis of the aorta

Ocular manifestations:

* Ectopia lentis with upward and outward displacement of the lenses due to weakening of the ciliary zonules

* Myopia with blurred vision

* Retinal detachments

* Early cataracts and glaucoma

The images below show two important signs seen in Marfan's syndrome:

* Image A shows a positive wrist sign - the ability to join the thumb and fifth finger around the wrist

* Image B shows a positive thumb sign - the thumb tip extends from the palm in a closed fist.

Other options:

Option A: Homocystinuria caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an accumulation of homocysteine in the blood and a clinical syndrome of intellectual disability, subluxated ocular lenses, long and slender extremities, arachnodactyly, and arterial and venous thrombi with megaloblastic anemia.

The image below shows lens subluxation (infero-nasal quad).

Option B: High Myopia usually presents with diplopia, ectopic lens, secondary cataract, or glaucoma with retinal detachment.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 13-year-old girl presents with a history of four meningitis episodes over the past four years. CSF cytology shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, and she is diagnosed with Mollaret’s meningitis. Which pathogen is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Mollaret's meningitis, also known as benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis, is a rare condition characterized by at least three self-limiting episodes of aseptic meningitis. The most common and definitive causative agent responsible for this syndrome is the Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), specifically HSV-2 (Option C) . The virus remains latent in the sensory ganglia and periodically reactivates, causing the recurrent lymphocytic pleocytosis in the CSF described. Measles (Option A), Mumps (Option B), and Rubella (Option D) viruses can cause acute viral meningitis or encephalitis but are not classically associated with the specific pattern of benign, multiple recurrences seen in Mollaret's syndrome . During an acute episode, CSF may also show large, friable endothelial cells known as "Mollaret cells." Because HSV is the pathognomonic pathogen for this specific neurological presentation, it is the most likely diagnosis. Management focuses on antiviral therapy and symptomatic relief during flares
questions.learning: Mollaret's meningitis, also known as benign recurrent lymphocytic meningitis, is a rare condition characterized by at least three self-limiting episodes of aseptic meningitis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study to determine the association between maternal smoking during pregnancy and low birth weight is being carried out. It involves obtaining smoking histories from pregnant women during their antenatal visits and then subsequently assessing the birth weight of their babies soon after delivery. What type of study is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prosprective Cohort

The study of choice is a prospective cohort study.

A prospective cohort study is a study in which the outcome has not yet occurred at the time that the investigations begin. They begin in the present and continue into the future.

This study is a prospective cohort study because the subjects (pregnant women) were categorized on the basis of exposure or lack of exposure to a risk factor -smoking during pregnancy. They were followed to determine if the outcome- the low birth weight of the babies occurred or not.

The design of a prospective cohort is shown below.

A retrospective cohort study is when both the exposure and outcome have occurred before the investigations and study is undertaken. An example would be if the charts in a hospital from the previous year were reviewed, and mothers classified as smokers or nonsmokers based on records. The records are then followed through time and then the birth weight of the children in both groups are compared. It is also called a historical cohort study, a prospective study in retrospect, or a non-concurrent prospective study.

In a case-control study of the same, low birth weight infants would be selected as the cases and normal birth weight babies as the controls. The frequency of maternal smoking would then be compared in the two groups.

In cross-sectional studies, exposure and outcome are measured at the same point in time.

Pearl PF0220: Cohort Study

* A cohort study progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occured but not disease.

* It is also known as forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study.

* Design of a Cohort Study

* Types

* Prospective cohort studies (concurrent cohort studies)

* Retrospective cohort studies (historical cohort study)

* Combination cohort studies

* Steps

* Selection of study subjects

* Obtaining data on exposure

* Selection of comparison groups

* Follow-up

* Analysis in terms of incidence rates and estimation of risk

* Advantages and disadvantages

Advantages

Disadvantages

Incidence can be calculated.

Several possible outcomes related to exposure can be studied at same time.

Provides direct estimate of relative risk

Calculation of dose-response ratio

Minimization of certain biases

Cannot be used for uncommon diseases

Uses a large population

Takes a long time to complete

Many common administrative problems

Attrition is high.

Selection of subjects is difficult.

Dynamism of diagnostics is difficult to incorporate.

Tend to be expensive.

Tends to alter behaviour of subjects: Hawthorne effect.

Ethical problems

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What does the provided population pyramid indicate, with the exception of?
questions.explanation: The population pyramid shown features a broad base that rapidly tapers toward a narrow apex. This "expansive" shape indicates high birth rates and high death rates. Such pyramids are characteristic of developing countries (Option A) where there is a "more young population" (Option C) and the total population is rapidly increasing (Option D). In contrast, developed countries (Option B) typically have a "constrictive" or "stationary" pyramid with a narrower base (low birth rates) and a more vertical shape, representing an aging population and low growth. Because the visual data clearly represents a young, growing, high-fertility demographic typical of less developed regions, the "developed countries" label is the incorrect description and thus the correct "except" choice for this question

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following helminthic infections, that is commonly transmitted by soil, is characterized by the egg in stool as shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trichuris trichiura

The given image shows the egg of Trichuris trichiura (whipworm).

The characteristic features of whipworm eggs are:

• Barrel-shaped in the middle
• Projecting colourless mucus plug at each pole
• Contains an unsegmented ovum.
• Floast in the saturated salt solution.
• It has a triple shell. The outermost layer is stained brown.

Humans acquire infection by swallowing embryonated eggs in contaminated food or water.  The eggs hatch in the small intestine, and the larvae produced pass into the cecum. The larvae become mature adults in 2-3 months. Adult females pass immature un-embryonated eggs in the stool. Thus, diagnosis of whipworm infection is done by microscopic identification of the eggs in a stool specimen.

Most infections are asymptomatic. Moderate whipworm infection (20 adult worms or less), the worms are confined to the caecum and ascending colon. The symptoms include epigastric and lower abdominal pain, diarrhoea (rarely bloody), vomiting, flatulence and distention, weight loss, and increased blood and iron loss. In heavy infections of 200 adult worms or more - trichuriasis dysentery syndrome -, the worms are in the distal colon and rectum. The symptoms include bloody diarrhoea with profuse mucus, abdominal pain, tenesmus, weight loss leading to cachexia, severe anemia, and rectal prolapse. On examination, clubbing may be present. Blood investigations may show moderate eosinophilia.

Chronic infection leads to growth retardation and nutritional deficiencies. Around 0.005 ml of blood is lost per day per worm. In heavy infections, as much as 4 to 5 ml can be lost per day per worm. Treatment is mebendazole or albendazole.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: All lung carcinomas for diagnosis requires CECT thorax but MRI is useful in which of the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pancoast tumor

MRI is useful in Pancoast tumor because of the associated soft tissue infiltration, extent of which can be best visualised using an MRI

Pancoast syndrome/superior sulcus tumor results from a local extension of a tumor growing in the apex of the lung, with the involvement of C8, T1, and T2 nerve roots.

It presents with pain that radiates to the ulnar distribution of the arm, often with the destruction of the 1st and 2nd ribs. Patients with the central or endobronchial growth of the primary tumor may present with a cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, or post-obstructive pneumonitis.

Regional spread can cause

• Tracheal obstruction,
• Esophageal compression with dysphagia
• Recurrent laryngeal paralysis with hoarseness
• Phrenic nerve palsy with the elevation of the hemidiaphragm and dyspnea
• Sympathetic nerve paralysis with Horner’s syndrome (enophthalmos, ptosis, miosis, and anhydrosis).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old male patient presents with a bulky scrotal swelling. On evaluation, malignancy is suspected. Orchidectomy is done and the gross section is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seminoma

The given cut section of testicular mass is homogenous, grey-white, and does not show haemorrhage or necrosis suggesting a diagnosis of seminoma.

Seminoma is the most common testicular tumour. In about 15% of cases, serum HCG levels are raised as these seminomas contain syncytiotrophoblasts. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels are also measured to assess tumour burden. They are bulky, homogenous, pale, and well-circumscribed masses that do not show any haemorrhage or necrosis, as shown in the image below.

Microscopically, sheets of uniform tumour cells divided into poorly demarcated lobules by fibrous septa are seen. Each cell is large, and round, and has a distinct cell membrane, abundant clear cytoplasm, and a large central nucleus with a few nucleoli.

Therapy depends on the stage of the tumour. Seminoma has the best prognosis. Most cases of seminoma stages I and II can be cured by orchidectomy with or without chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

Other options:

Option B, C: Yolk sac tumour and endodermal sinus tumour  will not present with a homogenous appearance on gross examination.

Option D: Teratoma has origins from ectodermal, mesodermal and endodermal germ cell layers. The gross cut section will have tissues from this origin.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient presents with clinical features including non-caseating granulomas and a characteristic saddle nose deformity. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Wegener's granulomatosis (now known as Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis) is a small-vessel vasculitis that characteristically affects the upper and lower respiratory tracts and the kidneys. The combination of non-caseating granulomas on biopsy and a saddle nose deformity (resulting from the destruction of the nasal septal cartilage) is a classic clinical presentation. While Syphilis (Option D) and Leprosy (Option B) can also cause saddle nose deformity through bone and cartilage destruction, their pathology involves endarteritis obliterans or specific neuro-cutaneous features rather than non-caseating granulomatous vasculitis. Tuberculosis (TB) (Option A) is characterized by caseating granulomas and primarily affects the lungs or bones, rarely presenting with primary saddle nose deformity in this manner. Diagnosis of Wegener's is supported by the presence of c-ANCA antibodies. Management requires aggressive immunosuppression with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide. Early recognition is vital to prevent permanent facial disfigurement and life-threatening pulmonary or renal failure. This specific anatomical-histological pairing is a favorite topic in both ENT and pathology exams
questions.learning: Wegener's granulomatosis (now known as Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis) is a small-vessel vasculitis that characteristically affects the upper and lower respiratory tracts and the kidneys.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the primary protein that binds to thyroxine?
questions.explanation: Thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) are poorly soluble in water and must be transported through the bloodstream bound to carrier proteins to regulate their availability to tissues. Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) is the primary and most specific transport protein for these hormones. It possesses a high affinity for thyroid hormones and is responsible for carrying the vast majority of T4 in circulation. Follistatin (Option A) is unrelated to thyroid transport; it primarily binds and inhibits activins. Transthyretin (Option B), or prealbumin, binds a much smaller fraction of T4 and serves a secondary role, mainly within the cerebrospinal fluid. Transferrin (Option D) is specifically dedicated to the transport of iron in the blood and has no role in thyroid hormone metabolism. Therefore, TBG remains the most significant systemic carrier of thyroxine, ensuring its stability and controlled delivery to target organs throughout the body
questions.learning: Thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) are poorly soluble in water and must be transported through the bloodstream bound to carrier proteins to regulate their availability to tissues.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Identify which one is inaccurately describing lithium's characteristics or management guidelines:
options: Lithium is teratogenic if given to pregnant females
Lithium toxicity is exacerbated with thiazide diuretics
Lithium can decrease thyroid hormone level
Hemodialysis is not useful in lithium overdose
questions.explanation: Statement D is incorrect because hemodialysis is, in fact, highly effective and the definitive treatment for severe lithium toxicity. Lithium is a small, water-soluble ion, has negligible protein binding, and a low volume of distribution, making it readily removable by hemodialysis. Indications for dialysis include severe neurologic symptoms, acute lithium levels ≥4.0 mEq/L, or ≥2.5 mEq/L with symptoms or renal impairment. Statement A is correct: lithium is teratogenic, particularly associated with Ebstein’s anomaly when used during pregnancy. Statement B is correct: thiazide diuretics increase lithium toxicity by reducing renal lithium clearance through enhanced proximal tubular reabsorption. Statement C is correct: chronic lithium therapy can cause hypothyroidism by inhibiting thyroid hormone synthesis and release. Because lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (0.6–1.2 mEq/L), regular monitoring and prompt recognition of toxicity are essential. Understanding lithium’s interactions and management principles is critical, as it remains a cornerstone therapy for bipolar disorder

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent self-mutilation, finger-biting, behavioral disturbances, and hyperuricemia. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies is the most likely cause if this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HGPRT

Lesch–Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) deficiency, a key enzyme in the purine salvage pathway. Failure to salvage hypoxanthine and guanine leads to excess uric acid production, resulting in hyperuricemia, while the hallmark clinical feature is self-mutilating behavior (lip and finger biting) accompanied by neurological dysfunction.

Why not the other options?

• B. Sphingomyelinase deficiency: Causes Niemann–Pick disease, characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, neurodegeneration, foam cells, and a cherry-red macula.
• C. Glucocerebrosidase deficiency: Causes Gaucher disease, presenting with hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, cytopenias, and Gaucher cells with “crumpled tissue paper” cytoplasm.
• D. α-Galactosidase A deficiency: Causes Fabry disease, an X-linked disorder characterized by angiokeratomas, acroparesthesias, hypohidrosis, and progressive renal and cardiac involvement.
questions.learning: HGPRT Lesch–Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) deficiency, a key enzyme in the purine salvage pathway.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following spermicides is used in the contraceptive product "TODAY"?
questions.explanation: The contraceptive product "TODAY" is a vaginal sponge that acts as both a mechanical barrier and a chemical contraceptive. It contains the spermicide Nonoxynol-9 (Option C). Nonoxynol-9 is a surfactant that disrupts the cell membrane of the sperm, rendering them immobile and incapable of fertilization. NET-EN (Option A) and DMPA (Option B) are progestogen-only injectable contraceptives (norethisterone enanthate and depot medroxyprogesterone acetate). Norethisterone (Option D) is a common progestin used in oral birth control pills and HRT . Nonoxynol-9 is the most widely used spermicide globally and is also found in many contraceptive gels, foams, and pre-lubricated condoms. While effective as a spermicide, it does not provide protection against STIs and can occasionally cause vaginal irritation. Thus, for the "TODAY" vaginal sponge, Nonoxynol-9 is the active chemical agent
questions.learning: The contraceptive product "TODAY" is a vaginal sponge that acts as both a mechanical barrier and a chemical contraceptive. It contains the spermicide Nonoxynol-9 (Option C).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following factors causes a rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?
questions.explanation: A rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve indicates reduced oxygen affinity, which facilitates oxygen unloading to tissues. This occurs via the Bohr effect, where an increase in leads to increased carbonic acid formation, lowering the pH. Other factors causing a rightward shift include increased temperature, increased hydrogen ions (lower pH), and increased 2,3-BPG. An increase in (Option B) promotes oxygen binding and does not cause a rightward shift. A decrease in (Option C) leads to a higher pH and a leftward shift, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen. Similarly, a decrease in temperature (Option D) stabilizes the oxygen-binding state, shifting the curve to the left. Therefore, increased is the primary physiological driver among these options for enhancing oxygen delivery to metabolically active tissues
questions.learning: A rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve indicates reduced oxygen affinity, which facilitates oxygen unloading to tissues. This occurs via the Bohr effect, where an increase in leads to increased carbonic acid formation, lowering the pH.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A patient was brought to casualty with seizures. He had multiple episodes and was taking herbal medicines for the same. He was conscious in between the episodes. During the episodes, he had arching of his back. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Strychnine

The given clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of strychnine poisoning.

Strychnine poisoning occurs if a person ingests crushed seeds of Strychnos nux vomica. If swallowed uncrushed, the seeds of nux vomica have no poisonous action. The fatal dose is 15-30 mg of strychnine or one crushed seed.

Strychnine is a competitive antagonist of glycine at the postganglionic receptors in the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord. This leads to increased activity in the motor neurons.

Patients typically present with

• Convulsions are clonic initially but eventually become tonic.
• Risus sardonicus results from the contraction of the jaws and facial muscles in which the corners of the mouth are drawn back.
• The convulsions are most marked in anti-gravity muscles so that the body typically arches in hyperextension, the posture known as opisthotonus.
• If the spasm involves the abdominal muscles, the body bends forward (emprosthotonos), or to the side (pleurosthotonus).
• If death is preceded by a severe convulsion, as in strychnine poisoning, it causes an increase in the body temperature known as postmortem caloricity.

The first step in the management of strychnine poisoning is to control convulsions with benzodiazepines or barbiturates to control seizures, and the patients should be placed in a dark room to avoid triggering further convulsions. Activated charcoal can be used to adsorb unabsorbed poison after a thorough stomach wash. Acidification of urine can be done to increase the excretion of strychnine.

Other options:

Option B: Ricinus poisoning leads to symptoms such as the burning of the oral mucosa, salivation, nausea, vomiting, severe abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea. It may also cause drowsiness, convulsions, delirium, and death.

Option C: Nerium poisoning presents with headache, dizziness, respiratory difficulty, and nausea. Ingestion causes difficulty in swallowing and articulation, abdominal pain, vomiting, profuse frothy salivation, and diarrhea. Blood pressure falls, fibrillation, AV block, coma, respiratory paralysis, and death can occur due to cardiac failure.

Option D: Datura poisoning presents with

• Dry hot skin (Temperature rises up to 42°C, a scarlet rash may also be appreciated)
• Dilatation of pupils along with loss of accommodation
• Diplopia
• Dryness of the mouth and throat, unquenchable thirst
• Dysphagia
• Dilatation of cutaneous blood vessels
• Dysarthria (Difficulty in talking)
• Drunken gait
• Delirium
• Drowsiness
• Death due to respiratory or cardiac failure
questions.learning: Strychnine — The given clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of strychnine poisoning. Strychnine poisoning occurs if a person ingests crushed seeds of Strychnos nux vomica.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 1-month-old baby is diagnosed with ventricular septal defect (VSD) and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). The VSD is caused by _________?
options: Improper fusion of both the membranous and muscular portions of the interventricular septum
Improper fusion of the membranous portion of the interventricular septum
Improper development of the muscular portion of the interventricular septum
Improper fusion of the endocardial cushions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Improper fusion of both the membranous and muscular portions of the interventricular septum

A ventricular septal defect (VSD) arises due to incomplete formation or fusion of the membranous and muscular portions of the interventricular septum during embryonic development.

The muscular septum develops from the ventricular floor and grows upward, while the membranous septum forms from the endocardial cushions and conotruncal ridges. Fusion of these components is critical for separating the right and left ventricles. Failure in the growth, alignment, or fusion of these structures can result in a defect, leading to an abnormal connection between the ventricles.

The embryological formation of the interventricular septum begins around the 4th week of gestation. The muscular septum grows upward toward the endocardial cushions, while the neural crest-derived conotruncal ridges spiral and fuse to form the aorticopulmonary septum. The membranous portion is formed by the fusion of the conotruncal septum with the endocardial cushions and the muscular septum.

Defects in the membranous portion are the most common cause of VSD, but malformations in the muscular septum or misalignment of the conotruncal ridges can also contribute. These defects result in abnormal blood flow between the ventricles, which can lead to complications such as heart failure or pulmonary hypertension if left untreated.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which specific cells are responsible for producing and secreting renin?
questions.explanation: Renin is a proteolytic enzyme that plays a fundamental role in the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), which regulates blood pressure and fluid balance. It is synthesized and secreted by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells (Option C). These specialized smooth muscle cells are located primarily in the walls of the afferent arterioles as they enter the glomerulus. JG cells function as baroreceptors that release renin in response to decreased blood pressure or sympathetic stimulation. The macula densa (Option B) consists of specialized tubular cells that sense sodium chloride levels in the distal tubule and signal the JG cells to release renin, but they do not secrete it themselves. Standard tubular cells (Option A) are involved in reabsorption and secretion but not renin production. Therefore, the JG cells are the definitive source of renin, which eventually leads to the formation of Angiotensin II and systemic vasoconstriction
questions.learning: Renin is a proteolytic enzyme that plays a fundamental role in the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS), which regulates blood pressure and fluid balance.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The patient presented with alcoholic gait, and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus) after RTA. Which lobe of the cerebellum is likely affected?

RTA - Road Traffic Accident
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flocculonodular Lobe

The flocculonodular lobe is involved in this patient with an alcoholic gait and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus) following an RTA.

The cerebellum has three parts based on function.

• Vestibulocerebellum (or flocculonodular lobe): The oldest part of the cerebellum which contains nodulus in the vermis and the flanking flocculus. It has vestibular connections and is concerned with equilibrium and gait.  Loss of it can cause disturbance of equilibrium and postural movements, especially during rapid movements.

• Spinocerebellum: The region that receives proprioceptive input from the body as well as a copy of the “motor plan” from the motor cortex. By comparing the plan with performance, it smooths and coordinates movements that are ongoing. The superior vermis is a part of the spinocerebellum. Loss of it can cause problems with coordination.
• Cerebrocerebellum: They are the newest from a phylogenetic point of view, reaching their greatest development in humans. They interact with the motor cortex in planning and programming movements.

Other options:

Option B: The Dentate nucleus(largest) is one of the 4 deep cerebellar nuclei others being, Emoliform, Globose, and Fastigial nuclei. These receive input from climbing fibers and are the only motor output from the cerebellar cortex.

Option C: Anterior lobe is a part of the Paleo/Spinocerebellum responsible for the coordination of movement and regulation of muscle tone whose lesion results in hypotonia.

Option D: Interposed nuclei / Nucleus interpositus is the term used to describe the cerebellar nuclei, Emboliform, and Globose.
questions.learning: Flocculonodular Lobe — The flocculonodular lobe is involved in this patient with an alcoholic gait and abnormal eye movements (nystagmus) following an RTA.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Hematology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 41-year-old woman with a long history of menorrhagia comes to the physician due to a low hemoglobin level identified on routine laboratory evaluation. She is diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia and started on oral ferrous sulfate. Which of the following cells secrete a substance that controls iron storage and release by other cells involved in iron homeostasis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hepatic parenchymal cells

Hepcidin, the master regulator of iron homeostasis, is produced by hepatic parenchymal cells (hepatocytes) and controls iron storage and release. Key actions of hepcidin:

• Inhibits ferroportin → decreases iron export
• ↓ Iron release from macrophages
• ↓ Iron absorption from enterocytes
• ↓ Iron release from liver stores

Clinical relevance:

• ↑ Hepcidin → anemia of chronic disease (iron trapped in stores)
• ↓ Hepcidin → iron overload (e.g., hemochromatosis)
• In iron deficiency → hepcidin levels fall to increase absorption
questions.learning: Hepatic parenchymal cells Hepcidin, the master regulator of iron homeostasis, is produced by hepatic parenchymal cells (hepatocytes) and controls iron storage and release.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In children with GBS, all are true except?
options: Areflexia of the affected limb is a mandatory diagnostic criteria
Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases
Intravenous immunoglobulin is the first line of management
Albuminocytological dissociation in CSF is characteristic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases

Plasmapheresis is preferred in refractory cases of GBS.

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy characterized by weakness, areflexia, and sensory symptoms. It often follows an infection, vaccination, or other immune trigger. The autoimmune mechanism attacks the peripheral nervous system, leading to demyelination or axonal damage.

Mandatory diagnostic criteria for GBS:

• Progressive, symmetric muscle weakness of more than one limb: Weakness evolves over a period of hours to weeks. Typically starts in the legs and ascends (ascending paralysis).

• Areflexia or hyporeflexia: Deep tendon reflexes are reduced or absent in affected limbs. Reflex loss is a hallmark clinical feature.

Symptoms:

• Progressive weakness, starting in the legs and moving upwards (ascending paralysis).
• Areflexia (loss of reflexes) or hyporeflexia in the affected limbs. (Option A)
• Sensory symptoms like tingling or numbness may occur but are less prominent.
• Autonomic dysfunction, such as fluctuations in heart rate or blood pressure, in severe cases.

CSF Findings:

• Albuminocytological dissociation: High protein levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with normal or low white blood cell counts. (Option D)

Treatment:

• Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG): First-line therapy. (Option C)
• Plasmapheresis (plasma exchange): in severe or refractory cases. (Option B)
• Supportive care for respiratory or autonomic complications.
questions.learning: Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases Plasmapheresis is preferred in refractory cases of GBS. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy characterized by weakness, areflexia, and sensory symptoms.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The world's only licensed malaria vaccine, MOSQUIRIX (RTS,S), is prepared from which component of Plasmodium falciparum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Circumsporozoite protein

RTS,S (brand name MOSQUIRIX) is a recombinant protein-based vaccine that targets the circumsporozoite protein (CSP) of Plasmodium falciparum, the protein found on the surface of the sporozoite — the pre-erythrocytic stage injected by the Anopheles mosquito during a bite.

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Vaccine name | RTS,S / MOSQUIRIX

| Target antigen | Circumsporozoite protein (CSP) of P. falciparum

| Carrier/adjuvant | Fused with Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) + AS01 adjuvant

| Status | First licensed malaria vaccine

| Efficacy | \~26–50% (partial protection, wanes over time)

| Stage targeted | Pre-erythrocytic (sporozoite stage) — prevents hepatocyte invasion

Why each distractor is wrong:

• A. Gametocytic protein — Gametocyte-stage antigens are the target of transmission-blocking vaccine candidates (e.g., Pfs25), not RTS,S.
• B. Polysaccharide sheath — Plasmodium has no polysaccharide capsule/sheath; this is a feature of certain bacteria (e.g., pneumococcus), not protozoa.
• D. Lipoprotein envelope — Malaria parasites don't have a lipoprotein envelope in the way enveloped viruses do; this is a distractor with no real basis in Plasmodium biology.

Exam Pearl: Remember "CSP for Circumsporozoite" — RTS,S works by inducing antibodies + CD4+ T-cell response against CSP, blocking sporozoites from invading hepatocytes. A newer vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, also targets CSP but with higher efficacy (\~70-80%) and was WHO-recommended after RTS,S — good to remember for newer-pattern questions, since INICET/NEET PG increasingly tests recent WHO vaccine recommendations.
