questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presented with excessive fatiguability towards the end of the day that improved with rest. He also gives a history of ptosis and difficulty in speech and swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

This patient has symptoms of fatiguability that worsen with repetitive movements but resolve after rest, along with oculobulbar symptoms such as ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia. From the given clinical picture, myasthenia gravis is the most likely diagnosis.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles.

It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness.

Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age.

Clinical features of myasthenia gravis:

• Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or during late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical
• Cranial muscles particularly the lids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course - diplopia, ptosis
• Facial weakness - snarling expression on smiling
• Weakness in chewing
• Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of palate and tongue
• Difficulty in swallowing
• Deep tendon reflexes are intact
• Myasthenic crisis - acute exacerbation of muscle weakness especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse.

Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, neuromyelitis optics, and systemic lupus erythematosus.

Diagnosis:

• Ice-pack test - application of ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases activity of acetylcholinesterase, this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increase transmission)
• Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies
• Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response.
• Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test - improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission.

Treatment:

• Anticholinesterase drugs - Pyridostigmine
• Thymectomy
• Immunosuppression therapy with glucocorticoids, azathioprine, tacrolimus, rituximab, etc.
• Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin

Other options:

Option B:

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder affecting the presynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction. It is due to the autoantibodies against the P/Q-type calcium channels at the motor nerve terminal which results in the impaired release of Ach from the presynaptic nerve terminal.

Patients present with proximal muscle weakness of the lower limbs, ptosis, and diplopia. However, symptoms might improve after brief exercise. Deep tendon reflexes are absent or reduced. They also experience autonomic dysfunction and present with dry mouth and impotence. It is most commonly associated with small cell lung cancer.

Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows an incremental response at higher rates.

Treatment involves plasmapheresis, immunotherapy, and drugs such as 3,4-diaminopyridine (3,4-DAP) and pyridostigmine.

Option C:

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is X-linked muscular dystrophy due to mutations in the dystrophin gene. It most commonly affects boys in their childhood.

Patients initially present with proximal muscle weakness predominantly of the lower limbs. Calf muscle hypertrophy is a cardinal feature. Other features include mental retardation, cardiac failure, and myoglobinuria.

Elevated serum creatinine kinase levels and genetic testing are diagnostic of DMD.

Option D:

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that most commonly presents with arthralgia with early morning stiffness. It predominantly occurs in middle-aged women. Other important features of SLE include malar rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, pleuritis, pericarditis, and lupus nephritis.

Anti-nuclear antibodies, Anti-dsDNA antibodies, anti-Smith antibodies are positive in SLE.
questions.learning: Myasthenia gravis — This patient has symptoms of fatiguability that worsen with repetitive movements but resolve after rest, along with oculobulbar symptoms such as ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Inquest in a case of custodial death is handled by _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Executive magistrate

An inquest in a case of custodial death is handled by the Executive Magistrate.

Magistrate inquest (Section 196 BNSS) is an inquest conducted by a district magistrate, subdivisional magistrate, and magistrate of the first-class rank or any other magistrate as empowered by the state government, such as collector, deputy collector or Tehsildar (executive magistrate).

It is conducted in cases of:

* Death under police custody

* Death due to police firing

* Death in prison, reformatories, borstal schools

* Dowry death

* Death in a psychiatric hospital

* Exhumation

* Death or disappearance of any person, or rape of a woman who is under the custody of police or any other person authorized by the court.

In the above-mentioned scenarios, a Magistrate can conduct the inquest independently or in addition to the police inquest.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In the given image, the tendon marked by the arrow is?
questions.explanation: The tendon indicated in the image lies on the radial (lateral/thumb) side of the anterior wrist, which corresponds to the flexor carpi radialis (FCR). This tendon becomes prominent when the wrist is flexed, especially during a clenched fist. The flexor carpi radialis originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and inserts into the bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals. Functionally, it is responsible for flexion and abduction of the wrist. Due to its position, the FCR tendon is located just lateral to the palmaris longus, which lies more centrally. In the image, the marked tendon is clearly not in the midline, ruling out palmaris longus, and instead is positioned toward the radial side, confirming it as flexor carpi radialis. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Palmaris longus → Midline tendon 2. Flexor carpi ulnaris → Ulnar (medial) side 3. Flexor digitorum superficialis → Deep tendon
questions.learning: The tendon indicated in the image lies on the radial (lateral/thumb) side of the anterior wrist, which corresponds to the flexor carpi radialis (FCR).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with breathing difficulties since birth, but respiratory effort improves when the baby cries. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this pattern of symptom improvement?
questions.explanation: Newborns are obligate nasal breathers. The classic clinical hallmark of bilateral choanal atresia is cyclical cyanosis and respiratory distress that is immediately relieved when the baby cries. Choanal atresia is a congenital obstruction of the posterior nasal apertures (choanae). When the baby is quiet and attempting to breathe through the nose, the obstruction causes distress; however, when the baby cries, they breathe through their mouth, bypassing the nasal obstruction and allowing for normal oxygenation. Atrophic rhinitis (Option A), Acute rhinosinusitis (Option B), and Allergic rhinitis (Option C) are inflammatory conditions seen in older children and adults, not as immediate neonatal respiratory emergencies. Diagnosis is suspected when a catheter cannot be passed through the nose into the pharynx and is confirmed via CT scan. Immediate management involves the use of an oral airway (McGovern nipple) to facilitate mouth breathing until surgical correction can be performed
questions.learning: Newborns are obligate nasal breathers. The classic clinical hallmark of bilateral choanal atresia is cyclical cyanosis and respiratory distress that is immediately relieved when the baby cries.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following agents is not commonly used in the management of bronchial asthma?
questions.explanation: Cholinergic drugs (parasympathomimetics) are not used in asthma because they stimulate muscarinic receptors, leading to bronchoconstriction and increased mucus secretion, which would severely worsen an asthma attack. Instead, anticholinergic drugs like Ipratropium are used to cause bronchodilation. Phosphodiesterase inhibitors (Option A), such as Theophylline, increase cAMP levels to relax bronchial smooth muscle. Steroids (Option B), such as Fluticasone or Prednisolone, are essential for reducing the underlying airway inflammation. Beta-agonists (Option C), like Salbutamol (SABA) or Salmeterol (LABA), are the mainstay for rapid relief and long-term control by stimulating beta-2 receptors to cause bronchodilation. Asthma management focuses on relaxing airway smooth muscle and suppressing immune-mediated inflammation. Because cholinergic stimulation is a primary physiological trigger for airway narrowing, these drugs are strictly avoided in asthmatic patients. Thus, Cholinergic drugs are the correct answer as they are contraindicated rather than utilized in asthma management
questions.learning: Cholinergic drugs (parasympathomimetics) are not used in asthma because they stimulate muscarinic receptors, leading to bronchoconstriction and increased mucus secretion, which would severely worsen an asthma attack.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Bubo is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: A bubo is a painful, markedly swollen lymph node, typically in the groin or axilla. It is a characteristic feature of Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV), a sexually transmitted infection caused by specific serotypes (L1, L2, L3) of Chlamydia trachomatis. In LGV, the buboes are often divided by the inguinal ligament, creating the pathognomonic "Groove sign." Herpes simplex (Option B) causes multiple painful superficial ulcers and mild lymphadenopathy, not massive buboes. Primary syphilis (Option C) presents with a painless chancre and painless, rubbery lymph nodes. Donovanosis (Option D) presents with painless, "beefy-red" ulcers and pseudo-buboes (granulomatous swelling in the groin), rather than true lymph node involvement. Buboes are also the hallmark of the bubonic plague. Identifying the nature of the inguinal swelling is essential for differentiating STIs and initiating correct antimicrobial therapy, such as doxycycline for LGV
questions.learning: A bubo is a painful, markedly swollen lymph node, typically in the groin or axilla. It is a characteristic feature of Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV), a sexually transmitted infection caused by specific serotypes (L1, L2, L3) of Chlamydia trachomatis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient was brought to the emergency with a history of consumption of 8 tablets of digoxin. On examination, he was unstable and his heart rate was 56 bpm. ECG showed a 3rd-degree heart block. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Antibody against digoxin

Administration of digibind (antibody against digoxin) is the next step in managing this patient. An unstable patient with bradycardia and 3rd-degree heart block following digoxin toxicity should be treated with digibind.

Digibind is a nonimmunogenic antibody used to treat cardiotoxicity due to digoxin. It is nonimmunogenic because it lacks the Fc fragment.

Digoxin is the cardiac glycoside used to treat heart failure and control ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation/flutter.

It inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase, a membrane-bound transporter to increase intracellular sodium. As a result, there is less expulsion of calcium from the cell by the sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX). Increased calcium inside the myocyte leads to an increase in cardiac contractility.

The most common cardiac manifestations of digitalis toxicity are ventricular tachycardia, partial to complete A-V block, severe bradycardia, and atrial fibrillation/flutter.

Factors that increase the risk of digoxin toxicity are:

• Hypokalemia
• Drugs that decrease digoxin elimination (inhibitors of P-glycoprotein) like quinidine
• Renal/hepatic failure
• Thyrotoxicosis

Option B: Lidocaine is commonly used as a local anesthetic. It has anti-arrhythmic properties and is used to suppress ventricular tachycardia caused by digitalis toxicity.

Option C: DC cardioversion is used for tachyarrythmias when pharmacologic treatment fails. It is not used in bradyarrhythmias.

Option D: Phenytoin is an antiepileptic used for the treatment of generalized tonic-clonic seizures and partial seizures. It can also be used for the treatment of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia due to QT prolongation.
questions.learning: Antibody against digoxin Administration of digibind (antibody against digoxin) is the next step in managing this patient. An unstable patient with bradycardia and 3rd-degree heart block following digoxin toxicity should be treated with digibind.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which among the following aids in supination and pronation of the forearm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pivot joint

Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot joints (synovial) and are involved in pronation and supination movements of the forearm.

Pearl PF1691: Types of Synovial Joints

Classification of Synovial Joints

Type
Articular surfaces
Movement
Examples

1. Plane
Almost flat
Minimal sliding movements
Intercarpal, intermetacarpal, carpometacarpal (except first), intertarsal, intermetatarsal, tarsometatarsal, joints between articular processes of vertebrae, cricothyroid joint, cricoarytenoid joint, superior tibiofibular, interchondral joint (5-9 ribs), costovertebral, costotransverse, acromioclavicular, chondrosternal (except first) joints

2. Hinge
Pulley shaped
Uniaxial - flexion & extension
Elbow, ankle, interphalangeal joints

3. Pivot
Central pivot (peg) surrounded by osteoligamentous ring
Uniaxial - rotation (supination and pronation)
Superior and inferior radioulnar joints, median atlantoaxial joint

4. Condylar (bicondylar)
2 convex condyles articulate with concave or flat surfaces on the other side
Biaxial - but predominantly one axis movement (flexion & extension) with limited rotation
Knee joint, temporomandibular joint

5. Ellipsoid
Oval convex surface fitting into an elliptical concavity
Biaxial - flexion & extension, abduction & adduction, circumduction
Radiocarpal (wrist), metacarpophalangeal joints

6. Saddle
Each articular surface has a concave and convex region fitting the convex and concave regions of the other surface
Biaxial - mainly 2 axis, flexion & extension,  abduction & adduction; very limited coupled axial rotation (conjunct rotation)
First carpometacarpal joint (of thumb), calcaneocuboid joints, incudomalleolar joint, sternoclavicular joint

7. Ball & Socket
Globular head fitting into a cup-shaped socket
Multiaxial - flexion & extension, abduction & adduction, circumduction, and rotation
Shoulder, hip, talocalcaneonavicular, incudostapedial joint
questions.learning: Pivot joint Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot joints (synovial) and are involved in pronation and supination movements of the forearm.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with gradual progressive hearing loss. On examination, he has difficulty perceiving high frequency sounds, but other findings are normal. Which structure is primarily affected in this condition?
options: Inner hair cell of basal turn
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inner hair cell of basal turn

High-frequency hearing loss in elderly patients (presbycusis) primarily involves damage to the inner hair cells at the basal turn of the cochlea.

• Base (basal turn) → detects high-frequency sounds
• Apex → detects low-frequency sounds

Pathophysiology:

• Age-related degeneration of hair cells (especially inner hair cells)
• Most pronounced at the basal turn → early loss of high-frequency hearing

Why other options are incorrect:

• Stria vascularis: Affects endolymph production (metabolic hearing loss)
• Tectorial membrane: Structural role, not primary site here
• Outer hair cells: Amplify sound, but inner hair cells are primary sensory receptors

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following is a high-level disinfectant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutaraldehyde

Glutaraldehyde is an example of a high-level disinfectant.

High-level disinfectant- This is a chemical that kills all microbial pathogens except a large number of spores. It may have some activity against a smaller number of spores if the contact time is increased. Eg- Glutaraldehyde, hydrogen peroxide.

Intermediate level disinfectant: A chemical that kills all microbial pathogens including mycobacteria and non enveloped viruses except spores. Eg- Alcohol, iodophors.

Low-level disinfectants:They kill only vegetative bacteria, fungi, and lipid enveloped viruses, e.g Benzalkonium chloride
questions.learning: Glutaraldehyde Glutaraldehyde is an example of a high-level disinfectant. High-level disinfectant- This is a chemical that kills all microbial pathogens except a large number of spores.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Simultaneous infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis D virus (HDV) followed by full recovery is associated with appearance of:
options: Low titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgM type
Low titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgA type
High titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgM type
High titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgG type
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgG type

In simultaneous HBV–HDV coinfection, most patients recover completely and clear both viruses. After recovery, anti-HDV IgM disappears, while anti-HDV IgG antibodies appear and persist, indicating past infection and immunity.

Why not the other options?

• A. Low titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgM type: IgM is a marker of acute infection and disappears after recovery.
• B. Low titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgA type: IgA antibodies are not used in the serological diagnosis of HDV.
• C. High titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgM type: Suggest ongoing acute or active infection, not recovery.
questions.learning: High titres of anti-HDV antibody, IgG type — In simultaneous HBV–HDV coinfection, most patients recover completely and clear both viruses. After recovery, anti-HDV IgM disappears, while anti-HDV IgG antibodies appear and persist, indicating past infection…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Based on the spirometry tracing shown, which respiratory parameter or volume is represented by the point labeled F?
questions.explanation: The spirometry diagram illustrates the various lung volumes and capacities. Point F spans from the peak of maximal inspiration to the trough of maximal expiration. This represents the Vital Capacity (VC), which is the total volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximal inhalation. VC is the sum of the Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV), Tidal Volume (TV), and Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV). Total lung capacity (Option B) would include the Residual Volume (RV) and is usually labeled G or H in such diagrams. Expiratory reserve volume (Option C) is only the volume below tidal expiration (labeled C). Inspiratory capacity (Option D) is the sum of TV and IRV (labeled E). VC is a vital clinical parameter used to assess ventilatory function and monitor progress in chronic lung diseases or neuromuscular disorders affecting breathing. It varies based on age, height, and sex, and a significant decrease can indicate restrictive lung disease or severe obstructive pathology
questions.learning: The spirometry diagram illustrates the various lung volumes and capacities. Point F spans from the peak of maximal inspiration to the trough of maximal expiration.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with pain and redness in the right eye after sustaining an injury while welding. On examination, the finding shown in the image below is noted. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes a classic corneal foreign body, a common occupational injury among welders and metalworkers. The accompanying image shows a metallic fragment embedded in the superficial corneal layers. The immediate management involves the removal of the foreign body to prevent infection and promote healing. This is typically performed at the slit lamp using a sterile 26-gauge needle or a specialized ophthalmic burr after applying topical anesthesia. If a "rust ring" has formed around the metallic site, as is common with iron-based fragments, it must also be carefully debrided. Steroids (Option A) are generally avoided initially as they can delay epithelial healing and mask infection. Surgical exploration (Option B) is reserved for suspected globe perforations, which are not indicated by this superficial presentation. Keratoplasty (Option C), or corneal transplant, is a radical procedure for end-stage corneal disease and is not an initial treatment for a foreign body. Following removal, a topical antibiotic ointment and sometimes a patch or bandage contact lens are prescribed
questions.learning: The clinical scenario describes a classic corneal foreign body, a common occupational injury among welders and metalworkers. The accompanying image shows a metallic fragment embedded in the superficial corneal layers.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to dermatology with an itchy rash. Examination reveals flat- topped, polygonal, purplish papules with fine white lines, predominantly on the inner wrists, forearms, and lower back. He also reports oral discomfort and white, lacy patches inside his cheeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided clinical description is pathognomonic for Lichen Planus (Option C) . Lichen planus is defined by the "6 Ps": Purple, Pruritic (itchy), Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped), Papules, and Plaques. The "fine white lines" on the surface are known as Wickham striae. Its characteristic distribution on flexor surfaces like the inner wrists and forearms is typical. Furthermore, the presence of white, lacy patches in the mouth (buccal mucosa) confirms oral lichen planus. Psoriasis (Option A) presents with thick plaques and silvery scales on extensor surfaces (elbows/knees). Eczema (Option B) involves poorly defined, itchy, red patches. Tinea corporis (Option D) is a fungal infection characterized by ring-shaped (annular) lesions with central clearing. Because the patient’s symptoms perfectly match the color, shape, and systemic distribution (oral/cutaneous) of the 6 Ps, Lichen Planus is the definitive diagnosis. It is often associated with Hepatitis C infection
questions.learning: The provided clinical description is pathognomonic for Lichen Planus (Option C) . Lichen planus is defined by the "6 Ps": Purple, Pruritic (itchy), Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped), Papules, and Plaques.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young patient presents with hepatosplenomegaly and prominent cheekbones. Peripheral blood smear findings show anemia, and the Mentzer index is less than 13. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms—splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and facial bone changes (prominent cheekbones or "chipmunk facies")—are classic for Beta-thalassemia major. These skeletal changes result from massive erythroid hyperplasia and expansion of the bone marrow in response to severe chronic anemia. The Mentzer index is a critical diagnostic tool used to differentiate between causes of microcytic anemia. It is calculated as the MCV divided by the RBC count. A Mentzer index of less than 13 (Option C) strongly favors Thalassemia, as the RBC count is often high relative to the very low MCV. Iron-deficiency anemia (Option B) typically shows a Mentzer index greater than 13. Megaloblastic and pernicious anemias (Options A and D) are macrocytic conditions with an elevated MCV. Therefore, the combination of specific physical stigmata and a low Mentzer index identifies Thalassemia as the diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms—splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and facial bone changes (prominent cheekbones or "chipmunk facies")—are classic for Beta-thalassemia major.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient presents with a recently developed fixed false belief in which a close family member, though identical in appearance, is perceived as an imposter. This delusion is causing marked distress and disruption in family interactions. This phenomenon is characteristic of a specific neuropsychiatric syndrome seen in certain forms of cognitive decline. In which type of dementia is this belief—where a familiar person is thought to be replaced by a look- alike—most commonly encountered?
questions.explanation: The belief that a familiar person has been replaced by a look-alike imposter is a specific delusion known as Capgras syndrome (or Capgras delusion). While it can occur in several psychiatric and neurological disorders, it is most commonly observed and highly characteristic of Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB). DLB is defined by its core features: fluctuating cognition, vivid visual hallucinations, and spontaneous motor features of parkinsonism. Capgras syndrome is thought to result from a disconnection between the brain's facial recognition system and its emotional appraisal system. Frontotemporal dementia (Option B) primarily presents with personality changes or language deficits. Vascular dementia (Option D) follows a "step-wise" decline related to cerebrovascular events. Embolism (Option A) is a cause of stroke but not a type of dementia. Recognizing Capgras syndrome in an elderly patient with cognitive decline is a vital clinical clue for differentiating DLB from Alzheimer's disease. Management involves the cautious use of atypical antipsychotics or cholinesterase inhibitors
questions.learning: The belief that a familiar person has been replaced by a look-alike imposter is a specific delusion known as Capgras syndrome (or Capgras delusion). While it can occur in several psychiatric and neurological disorders, it is most commonly observed and…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 70-year-old individual with a history of presbyopia suddenly finds they can read fine print, such as a newspaper, without using glasses. What is the most likely diagnosis explaining this change in vision?
questions.explanation: The phenomenon where an elderly patient suddenly regains the ability to read without glasses is colloquially known as "second sight." This is most commonly caused by nuclear sclerosis, a type of age-related cataract. As the lens nucleus becomes more dense and dehydrated, its refractive index increases. This "index myopia" shifts the patient's overall refraction toward nearsightedness. For a presbyopic patient who previously required plus-powered reading glasses, this new myopic shift compensates for their loss of accommodation, allowing them to focus on near objects again without assistance. Index hypermetropia (Option B) would worsen the ability to see near objects. "Regression of presbyopia" (Option C) is a misnomer, as the physiological hardening of the lens that causes presbyopia is irreversible; the change is refractive, not accommodative. While the improved near vision is a temporary convenience, it usually signals the progression of a cataract that will eventually blur distant vision significantly. Therefore, index myopia due to nuclear cataract is the correct clinical diagnosis for this specific visual change
questions.learning: The phenomenon where an elderly patient suddenly regains the ability to read without glasses is colloquially known as "second sight." This is most commonly caused by nuclear sclerosis, a type of age-related cataract.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young woman presents to the ENT OPD with sudden-onset unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo following an acute otitis media episode two weeks ago. Initially, the Rinne and fistula tests were positive, but she had declined treatment. She now reports worsened hearing in the affected ear, and the fistula test is negative. What is the most likely result of the Rinne test in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The patient’s initial symptoms (vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss) following ASOM, combined with a positive fistula test, indicated a labyrinthine fistula. However, the subsequent "worsened hearing loss" and the "negative fistula test" suggest that the inner ear has now completely failed, resulting in total sensorineural hearing loss (dead ear). In a dead ear, the Rinne test on the affected side will yield a false negative result. This occurs because when the tuning fork is placed on the mastoid bone (bone conduction), the sound is transmitted through the skull and heard by the healthy contralateral ear. Since the patient "hears" the sound by bone but cannot hear it by air conduction in the dead ear, it appears as if . Option A (True positive) occurs in normal hearing. Option B (True negative) occurs in conductive hearing loss ( with a functioning cochlea). Option C is not a standard clinical interpretation of the Rinne test. Therefore, the "crossover" of sound to the good ear is the defining mechanism of a false negative Rinne
questions.learning: The patient’s initial symptoms (vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss) following ASOM, combined with a positive fistula test, indicated a labyrinthine fistula.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the structure given in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incus

The structure given in the image is the incus.

It is one of the three ossicles that are in the middle ear cavity i.e, malleus, incus, and stapes. Ossicles conduct sound energy from the tympanic membrane to the oval window and then to the inner ear fluid.

Incus is shaped like an anvil. It has a body, a short process, and a long process. It has a saddle-shaped articular facet on its anterior surface that articulates with the malleus. The long process descends vertically and ends as a rounded lenticular process.

Incus has a single nutrient vessel within the long process and no collateral circulation. Thus, it is more susceptible to aseptic necrosis following a middle ear infection.

The malleus (option A) is the largest ossicle and is shaped like a mallet. The parts of the malleus are the head, neck, handle (manubrium), and anterior and lateral processes. The head and neck lie in the attic. The tympanic membrane is connected to the handle of the malleus.

The stapes (option C) has a head, neck, footplate, and anterior and posterior crura. The annular ligament holds the footplate of stapes in the oval window.

The joints between the ear ossicles are synovial joints. A saddle-shaped joint is present between the incus and malleus. Incus and stapes articulate via a ball and socket joint.

Option D- The vomer is a small bone in the posteroinferior part of the nasal septum. Along with perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, and the septal cartilage, it forms the nasal septum.
questions.learning: Incus — The structure given in the image is the incus. It is one of the three ossicles that are in the middle ear cavity i.e, malleus, incus, and stapes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Revised Which of the following is not an indication for cesarean section?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Previous history of macrosomia

Previous history of macrosomia is not an indication of a cesarean section(CS).

Cesarean is needed even with a dead fetus when vaginal delivery is not possible.
The following are the absolute indication:

* Central placenta previa (Option C)

* Contracted pelvis or cephalopelvic disproportion (absolute)(Option A)

* Pelvic mass causing an obstruction (cervical or broad ligament fibroid)

* Advanced carcinoma cervix (Option D)

* Vaginal atresia or stenosis

Relative indications for cesarean section are those where vaginal delivery may be possible but risks to the mother and/or baby are high. They are as follows:

* Nonreassuring FHR

* Dystocia- It may be due to a relatively large fetus (passenger), small pelvis (passage), or inefficient uterine contractions (power)

* Antepartum hemorrhage: Placenta previa and abruptio placenta

* Malpresentation: Breech, shoulder (transverse lie), brow

* Previous cesarean delivery-a) When primary CS was due to recurrent indication (contracted pelvis), (b) Previous two CS,(c) Features of scar dehiscence, (d) Previous classical CS

* Cephalopelvic disproportion (relative)

* Failure to progress in labor

* Hypertensive disorders: Severe pre-eclampsia, eclampsia— uncontrolled fits even with antiseizure therapy.
questions.learning: Previous history of macrosomia Previous history of macrosomia is not an indication of a cesarean section(CS). Cesarean is needed even with a dead fetus when vaginal delivery is not possible.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An adolescent male patient presents to you with exercise intolerance. He gives a history of developing cramps on exertion. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies could be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myophosphorylase

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of McArdle disease, which results due to a deficiency of the enzyme myophosphorylase (muscle glycogen phosphorylase).

McArdle disease, also known as type V glycogen storage disorder, is an autosomal recessive condition. It typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation.

Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. A second wind phenomenon, where the symptoms subside after a short period of rest, can also be seen. Myoglobinuria secondary to rhabdomyolysis leads to the passage of burgundy-colored urine in some patients.

Rarely, it can present during infancy as hypotonia, muscle weakness, and respiratory complications. It is generally fatal.

Muscle biopsy to measure glycogen content is the standard diagnosis. Avoiding strenuous exercise prevents symptoms. Glucose administration before exercise can improve tolerance. Vitamin B6 is also recommended.

Other options:

Option B - Hexokinase is a glycolytic enzyme. Its deficiency leads to hemolytic anemia. Splenomegaly may be another presenting feature.

Option C - Glucose-6-phosphatase is an enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis. Its deficiency leads to von Gierke disease also known as type I glycogen storage disease.

Option D - Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency results in type VI glycogen storage disease, also known as Hers disease.
questions.learning: Myophosphorylase — The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of McArdle disease, which results due to a deficiency of the enzyme myophosphorylase (muscle glycogen phosphorylase).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Infiltration of the small-intestine mucosa with ‘foamy’ macrophages, which stain positive with Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) reagent, is a characteristic feature of which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Whipple’s disease

Whipple’s disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei, a gram-positive actinomycete. The organism accumulates within macrophages in the lamina propria of the small intestine, producing characteristic foamy macrophages that stain strongly PAS-positive.

Why not the other options?

• A. Radiation enteropathy: Causes mucosal atrophy, ulceration, fibrosis, vascular injury, and telangiectasia after radiation exposure.
• B. Coeliac disease: Shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes; PAS-positive foamy macrophages are absent.
• C. Tropical sprue: Causes villous atrophy and malabsorption, but does not show PAS-positive macrophages.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 33 Weeks multigravida woman presents with epigastric pain, headache, visual symptoms, and proteinuria - 3+. The next step of management would be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MgSO4 IV

The given clinical scenario of a 33 weeks pregnant woman with epigastric pain, headache, visual symptoms, and proteinuria 3+ indicates severe preeclampsia. The next step of management would be iv administration of MgSO4 for the prevention of seizures.

Preeclampsia can be classified as severe if any of the following are present:

• BP ≥160/110
• Headache
• Visual disturbance
• Upper abdominal pain
• Elevated creatinine, oliguria
• Thrombocytopenia (<1,00,000 cells per mm3)
• Pulmonary edema
• Marked elevation in serum transaminases
• Fetal growth restriction

Dexamethasone (option B) is also given in severe preeclampsia <34 weeks for fetal lung maturity. But the administration of MgSO4 before corticosteroids would be the next best step for the prevention of seizures.

Immediate delivery (options A and C) is not indicated in this case as the patient doesn't have any contraindication for conservative management. Conservative management is contraindicated in the following cases:

• Persistent symptoms, refractory to treatment or severe hypertension
• Eclampsia, pulmonary edema, HELLP syndrome
• Significant renal dysfunction or coagulopathy
• Placental abruption
• Nonreassuring fetal status
• Fetal demise
• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
• Stroke, myocardial infarction

MgSO4 regimens for management of eclampsia and severe preeclampsia:

Regimen
Loading Dose
Maintenance Dose

Intramuscular (Pritchard)
4g (20% solution) IV over 3-5 minute
followed by 10g (5O%), deep IM
(5 gm in each buttock)
5g (5O%) IM 4 hourly in the alternate buttocks

Intravenous (Zuspan or Sibal)
4g IV slow over 15-20 minute
1-2g/h IV infusion

Magnesium sulfate is discontinued either 24 hours after delivery or 24 hours after the onset of convulsions (whichever is later).
questions.learning: MgSO4 IV — The given clinical scenario of a 33 weeks pregnant woman with epigastric pain, headache, visual symptoms, and proteinuria 3+ indicates severe preeclampsia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: New A patient presents with abdominal pain and distension. An X ray was taken which showed dilated bowel loops as given in the image below. Identify the segment involved.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Jejenum

The given clinical scenario and X-ray suggest intestinal obstruction with involvement of the jejunum. The obstructed bowel loops are central in location and show valvulae connivente (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel). The presence of valvulae connivente with gas bubbles trapped between them gives a string of beads/ ladder effect. Radiological features of bowel obstruction

* Small bowel - The involved dilated segments are straight and mostly centrally located.

* Jejunum - It is characterized by the presence of valvulae conniventes with gas bubbles trapped between them. This gives a string of beads/ ladder effect.

* Ileum - The distal ileal obstruction is usually featureless.

* Caecum - A rounded gas shadow in the right iliac fossa is suggestive of caecal obstruction.

* Large bowel - The presence of haustrations is a feature of large bowel obstruction. Haustral folds are not regular. They are not present in the caecum and do not traverse the whole diameter of the bowel.
questions.learning: Jejenum — The given clinical scenario and X-ray suggest intestinal obstruction with involvement of the jejunum. The obstructed bowel loops are central in location and show valvulae connivente (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is presented with a staggering gait and nystagmus after a road traffic accident. Which lobe of cerebellum is affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Flocculonodular

Staggering gait with nystagmus indicates involvement of the vestibulocerebellum.

The flocculonodular lobe controls balance, posture, and eye movements via vestibular connections.

Lesions cause truncal ataxia, vertigo, and nystagmus with a positive Romberg sign.

Anterior lobe causes limb ataxia, and vermis affects axial posture without prominent eye signs.

| Structure | Function | Lesion Feature

| --------- | -------- | --------------

| Flocculonodular | Balance + eye movement | ⭐ Ataxia + nystagmus

| Anterior lobe | Posture | Gait disturbance

| Posterior lobe | Fine movement | Limb ataxia

| Vermis | Trunk control | Truncal instability
questions.learning: Flocculonodular Staggering gait with nystagmus indicates involvement of the vestibulocerebellum. The flocculonodular lobe controls balance, posture, and eye movements via vestibular connections.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: When performing diagnostic paracentesis in a patient with ascites using the midline approach, which needle gauge is commonly used for aspiration of the fluid?
questions.explanation: Paracentesis is a procedure used to sample or drain ascitic fluid from the peritoneal cavity. For a "diagnostic" paracentesis, where only a small amount of fluid (typically 20–50 ml) is needed for laboratory analysis (e.g., cell count, albumin, culture), a smaller needle is preferred to minimize trauma and the risk of a persistent leak or hematoma. A 22-gauge needle is typically used for this purpose. Larger bore needles, such as 14-gauge (Option A) or 16-gauge (Option B), are reserved for "therapeutic" paracentesis, where several liters of fluid are drained quickly to relieve symptoms of tension. A 17-gauge needle (Option C) is also unnecessarily large for simple diagnostics. The midline approach, usually 2 cm below the umbilicus along the linea alba, is chosen because it is relatively avascular. Using a fine-gauge needle ensures the procedure is safe and well-tolerated by the patient, while still allowing for the aspiration of fluid for essential diagnostic testing

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with pain abdomen, diarrhea, and a stepladder pattern of fever for the past five days. He also complains of a headache and malaise. Which of the following is the best screening test to perform now if typhoid is suspected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blood culture

The best test to screen a symptomatic patient for typhoid in the first week is blood culture.

Enteric fever (typhoid fever) is caused by Salmonella species. The patient presents with stepladder pyrexia (fever), abdominal pain, diarrhoea, headache, and malaise.

Diagnosis of enteric fever:

*

Blood culture: It is more sensitive during 1st week than in the subsequent weeks. It rapidly becomes negative on treatment with antibiotics.

* Antibody testing: WIDAL test to detect rising titers of H and O agglutinins against salmonella typhi and paratyphi. Agglutinins appear by the end of the first week and rise steadily up to the 3rd or 4th week, after which they disappear.

*

Stool culture: It yields positive results from the 3rd week onwards.

*

Urine culture: Results may be positive after the 2nd week.

*

Bone marrow culture remains positive for 5 days even after the start of antibiotics and is the most sensitive test in the first week. The culture of duodenal aspirate may yield positive results when bone marrow culture is inconclusive.

Empirical treatment of typhoid fever includes management with ceftriaxone 2g/day intravenously for 10-14 days along with azithromycin  1g/day for 5 days. Other antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin, chloramphenicol, and amoxicillin should be considered in resistant cases.
questions.learning: Blood culture — The best test to screen a symptomatic patient for typhoid in the first week is blood culture. Enteric fever (typhoid fever) is caused by Salmonella species.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient comes with long-standing non-pitting edema in the legs. What is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymphedema

Lymphedema is the most probable cause of long-standing non-pitting edema in the limbs.

Lymphedema is the abnormal accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the interstitial spaces of the tissues.

Lymphedema can be primary or secondary.

Primary lymphedema includes:

• Lymphedema congenita (0-2 years): more common in males, involves multiple limbs, face, and genitalia. It can be familial or sporadic. The familial type is called Nonne Milroy syndrome.
• Lymphedema praecox (2-35 years): more common in females, the most common type of primary lymphedema with a peak incidence in puberty. It can be familial or sporadic. The familial type is called Meig's disease.
• Lymphedema tarda (>35 years): Rare and uncommon.

Secondary lymphedema is more common than primary and is the most common cause of lymphedema overall. Causes include lymph node dissection (axillary or inguinal), post-mastectomy, postoperative radiotherapy, obesity, varicose vein surgery, and trauma.

Complications of lymphedema include infections, skin changes, recurent cellulitis, non-healing ulcers, and lymphangiosarcoma.

Treatment mostly includes patient education and nonsurgical interventions, which include limb elevation, and external compressive garments. When the above methods fail, surgery can be considered.
questions.learning: Lymphedema Lymphedema is the most probable cause of long-standing non-pitting edema in the limbs. Lymphedema is the abnormal accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the interstitial spaces of the tissues.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The AKIN and RIFLE criteria are used for the classification and assessment of which clinical condition?
questions.explanation: The RIFLE (Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss of kidney function, and End-stage kidney disease) and AKIN (Acute Kidney Injury Network) criteria are internationally recognized systems used to standardize the definition and severity of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI). These systems categorize AKI based on changes in serum creatinine levels and urine output over specific timeframes. Chronic kidney failure (Option B) is classified using the GFR-based stages (G1–G5) from the KDIGO guidelines. Acute glomerulonephritis (Option C) and Nephrotic syndrome (Option D) are clinical diagnoses based on biopsy findings or specific urinary protein and sediment patterns, rather than these generic injury scales. Standardizing AKI classification helps clinicians predict patient prognosis, determine the need for renal replacement therapy, and compare clinical research outcomes. The more recent KDIGO criteria have largely integrated both RIFLE and AKIN into a unified staging system
questions.learning: The RIFLE (Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss of kidney function, and End-stage kidney disease) and AKIN (Acute Kidney Injury Network) criteria are internationally recognized systems used to standardize the definition and severity of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is the most common bone to be fractured in children?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Distal forearm bones

The most common bones to be fractured in children are the distal forearm bones.

The distal radius is the most commonly fractured bone in childhood. It is more commonly fractured than the clavicle.

The clavicle is most commonly fractured during birth.
questions.learning: Distal forearm bones — The most common bones to be fractured in children are the distal forearm bones. The distal radius is the most commonly fractured bone in childhood.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: After undergoing vasectomy, how many ejaculations and months are required for a man to become sterile?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 20 ejaculations and 3 months

After vasectomy, sperm already present in the reproductive tract must be cleared before sterility is achieved.

Traditionally, men are advised to use another contraceptive method until:

• At least 20 ejaculations, and
• Approximately 3 months have passed.

Semen analysis should be performed to confirm azoospermia (or acceptable rare non-motile sperm) before discontinuing contraception.

Therefore, the correct answer is C. 20 ejaculations and 3 months.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the ideal pressure exerted by the method of dressing for a non-healing leg ulcer shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 110-130 mmHg

The pressure used in vacuum-assisted closure for wound healing is around –125 mmHg. That lies in the range of 110-130 mmHg

Applying negative pressure appears to hasten debridement and the formation of granulation tissue in chronic wounds and ulcers.

It acts by decreasing edema, by removing interstitial fluid, and as a result, helps in decreasing bacterial counts and cell proliferation increases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During subclavian vein catheterization, a patient develops a sudden drop in oxygen saturation. Chest examination reveals increased resonance in the upper right lung. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Subclavian venous catheterization is a high-risk procedure due to the proximity of the lung apex (pleura). A sudden drop in oxygen saturation during the procedure is a major warning sign. The clinical finding of "increased resonance" (hyperresonance) on percussion in the upper right lung indicates an air-filled space where lung tissue should be. This is pathognomonic for an iatrogenic pneumothorax (Option B) caused by the needle accidentally puncturing the lung. Arterial puncture (Option A) would cause local hematoma but not immediate hyperresonance or oxygen drops. Cardiac tamponade (Option C) presents with distant heart sounds and low BP (Beck's triad). Chylothorax (Option D), or lymph leakage, would cause dullness on percussion due to fluid accumulation rather than hyperresonance. Therefore, the combination of acute respiratory distress and hyperresonance identifies pneumothorax as the definitive procedural complication. Immediate management includes stopping the procedure and considering a chest tube or needle decompression
questions.learning: Subclavian venous catheterization is a high-risk procedure due to the proximity of the lung apex (pleura). A sudden drop in oxygen saturation during the procedure is a major warning sign.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A professor underwent a left parotidectomy. Post surgery she complains of left lower lip paralysis. Which structure is involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facial nerve- Cervical branch

Lower lip paralysis is caused by damage to the cervical branch of the facial nerve.

The cervical branch of the facial nerve is responsible for innervating the platysma muscle, which is one of the muscles involved in the movements of the lower lip. Damage to this nerve can potentially lead to paralysis of the lower lip.

The facial nerve is the motor nerve of the face. Its five terminal branches emerge from the parotid gland and diverge to supply the various facial muscles as follows :

• Temporal — frontalis, auricular muscles, orbicularis oculi
• Zygomatic — orbicularis oculi (lower eyelid part)
• Buccal — muscles of the cheek and upper lip
• Marginal mandibular — muscles of the lower lip
• Cervical — platysma
questions.learning: Facial nerve- Cervical branch Lower lip paralysis is caused by damage to the cervical branch of the facial nerve. The cervical branch of the facial nerve is responsible for innervating the platysma muscle, which is one of the muscles involved in the…

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person was found dead in the bushes with his hands tied. On examination of the body, there was cyanosis, petechial hemorrhages, abrasions, and bruises around the mouth and lips. There was associated facial congestion and edema. What is the least likely cause of death here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Suicide

The least likely cause of death in this person is suicide

The presence of cyanosis, petechial haemorrhages, abrasions, bruises around the mouth and lips, facial congestion, and edema suggests a form of asphyxia or smothering. As the victim's hands are tied and there are signs of asphyxia and smothering, these findings are more consistent with homicide being the cause of death rather than self-inflicted suicide.

Classic signs of asphyxia

* Petechial haemorrhages

* Congestion and edema

* Cyanosis

* Engorgement of the right side of the heart and abnormal fluidity of blood

Note: The coexistence of these findings, in themselves, does not prove that death resulted from mechanical asphyxia. All these phenomena are non-specific and are in no way peculiar to this mode of death. They are of no value in proving that death resulted from mechanical asphyxia.

Smothering: It is defined as a form of asphyxia that is caused by closing the external respiratory orifices either by the hand or by other means or blocking up the cavities of the nose and mouth by the introduction of a foreign substance.

They can be either :

* Accidental smothering

* Suicidal smothering

* Homicidal smothering

Accidental Smothering :

* Most fatal smotherings are accidental

* An epileptic or intoxicated person may smother himself accidentally by burying his face in a pillow that is impervious to air.

* A person may accidentally fall into a large quantity of semisolid or finely divided material so that his mouth and nose are covered by the substance.

* Children may be suffocated accidentally while playing with plastic bags

* Smothering from plastic bags may occur due to the addictive habit of "glue-sniffing"

Suicide by Smothering :

* Suicidal smothering by hand is impossible

* Suicide is possible by burying the face in a mattress or lying against the bed clothing to obstruct the nose and the mouth. It is usually seen in mental patients or prisoners.

* Suicidal smothering can occur by tying a polythene bag over the head as well.

Homicidal Smothering :

* It is a simple and convenient method of asphyxial homicide that is extremely difficult to prove as it may not leave any evidence.

* The mouth and nose are closed by a hand or cloth, or the face may be pressed into a pillow (gentle homicide).

Petechial hemorrhages are rarely seen. Bruising of the inner surface of the lips may be seen if greater force is applied during smothering. At times, mucus and squamous respiratory epithelium from the victim may be found in the smothering material.
questions.learning: Suicide — The least likely cause of death in this person is suicide The presence of cyanosis, petechial haemorrhages, abrasions, bruises around the mouth and lips, facial congestion, and edema suggests a form of asphyxia or smothering.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: E.coli can be grown best in which of the following media?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mac-Conkey agar

E.coli can be grown best in MacConkey agar.

MacConkey agar is used to distinguish lactose fermentators (seen as pink colonies) from non-lactose fermentators(seen as colourless or pale). It is selective and differential media.

MacConkey agar is Selective because bile salts and dyes inhibit Gram-positive organisms and Gram-negative cocci. It is Differential because the pH indicator turns pink-red when the lactose is fermented.

Contents of MacConkey agar: Mnemonic: PLANT

P – Peptone

L – Lactose

A – Agar

N – Neutral red

T– Sodium Taurocholate

MacConkey agar showing LF and NLF

Other options:

Option A: Chocolate agar is used for Hemophillus influenza.

Option B: Thyer-Martin agar is used for Nesseria.

Option C: SDA agar is used for fungal culture.
questions.learning: Mac-Conkey agar E.coli can be grown best in MacConkey agar. MacConkey agar is used to distinguish lactose fermentators (seen as pink colonies) from non-lactose fermentators(seen as colourless or pale).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with the complaint of blurring of vision. On examination, you note that there are aqueous flares with numerous keratic precipitates. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iridocyclitis

The features of aqueous flares and keratic precipitates indicate a diagnosis of Fuch's heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHI).

Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a chronic, non-granulomatous anterior uveitis, that is usually unilateral. It is normally seen in middle-aged people who may complain of symptoms such as blurring of vision and persistent floaters.

Heterochromia iridis (the affected eye is hypochromic/hyperchromic) is noted in FHI. Rubeosis iridis and posterior subcapsular cataract are also fairly common findings.

On examination, stellate keratic precipitates known as endothelial dusting are seen. Tiny crystals (Russell bodies) and iris nodules (Koeppe nodules)  may also be found on the iris surface. Iris atrophy which appears as a smooth-looking iris can also be seen.

Long-term monitoring is indicated to detect glaucoma and other complications.

The below image shows an example of heterochromia iridis (the left eye is hypochromic when compared to the right eye).

Other options:

(a) Intermediate uveitis: Intermediate uveitis primarily involves inflammation in the vitreous humor, which is the jelly-like substance in the middle of the eye. It is less likely to present with aqueous flares and keratic precipitates, making it an incorrect option.

(c) Posterior uveitis: Posterior uveitis involves inflammation in the posterior segment of the eye, including the choroid and retina. Aqueous flares and keratic precipitates are less likely to be observed in posterior uveitis, making it an incorrect option.

(d) Toxoplasma uveitis: Toxoplasma uveitis is a specific type of uveitis caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. While it may involve the anterior or posterior segment of the eye, the presence of aqueous flares and keratic precipitates is not specific to Toxoplasma uveitis alone.

questions.learning: Iridocyclitis — The features of aqueous flares and keratic precipitates indicate a diagnosis of Fuch's heterochromic iridocyclitis (FHI). Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is a chronic, non-granulomatous anterior uveitis, that is usually unilateral.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A primi presented to the hospital in active labor and was found to be HIV positive. She is not on any antiretroviral therapy. According to the NACO guidelines, what is the minimum prophylactic antiretroviral therapy to be started in the neonate after birth?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nevirapine + zidovudine 6 weeks

A baby born to an HIV-positive mother who is not on ART is classified as a high-risk infant. The recommended minimum ARV prophylaxis is syrup nevirapine + syrup zidovudine from birth to 6 weeks. For exclusively breastfed infants, this is extended till 12 weeks.

According to the National AIDS Control Organization (NACO), antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be given to all pregnant women, including during labor hours and breastfeeding. They are started on a triple-drug ART. ART should be given irrespective of the CD4 count, and clinical stage and should be continued lifelong.

Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) is recommended for all HIV-exposed infants. At 6 months of age, these infants should be offered complementary foods along with breast milk.

Infants should receive ARV prophylaxis. A single drug or dual drug regimen is followed depending on the risk of transmission which can be low or high risk.

* Low-risk infants are those born to mothers with a low viral load which is detected after 32 weeks of pregnancy till delivery.

* High-risk infants are those born to HIV-positive mothers, not on ART, with viral load not estimated beyond 32 weeks, maternal viral load not suppressed after 32 weeks, or mothers newly diagnosed with HIV within 6 weeks of delivery.

HIV Risk
ARV prophylaxis
Duration

Low-risk infants
Syrup nevirapine or zidovudine

Birth to 6 weeks of age irrespective of feeding

High-risk infants
Syrup nevirapine + syrup zidovudine

• Exclusive replacement feeding: Birth to 6 weeks
• Exclusive breastfeeding: Birth till 12 weeks
questions.learning: Nevirapine + zidovudine 6 weeks — A baby born to an HIV-positive mother who is not on ART is classified as a high-risk infant. The recommended minimum ARV prophylaxis is syrup nevirapine + syrup zidovudine from birth to 6 weeks.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Tuning fork frequency used for testing is:
questions.explanation: In clinical otology, tuning fork tests such as the Rinne, Weber, and ABC tests are fundamental for distinguishing between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. The most commonly used and medically standard frequency for these bedside tests is 512 Hz. This specific frequency is preferred because it falls within the range of important speech frequencies and provides a good balance between auditory and vibratory (tactile) sensation. A 256 Hz fork (similar to Option C) provides too much bone vibration, which can lead to false-positive results. Higher frequencies like 1024 Hz (Option B) fade too quickly and are harder to hear by bone conduction. While a set of forks is used in research, the 512 Hz fork is the single definitive standard used by clinicians globally. Therefore, 512 Hz is the correct answer for the standard frequency utilized in routine hearing evaluations
questions.learning: In clinical otology, tuning fork tests such as the Rinne, Weber, and ABC tests are fundamental for distinguishing between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a side effect of salbutamol?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypoglycemia

Hypoglycemia is not a side effect of salbutamol. It causes hyperglycemia.

The side effects of salbutamol are due to the stimulation of extrapulmonary β2 receptors. They are more common after oral or intravenous administration. The side effects seen are:

• Muscle tremor
• Tachycardia
• Hypokalemia
• Restlessness
• Hypoxemia
• Increase in free fatty acid, insulin, glucose, pyruvate, and lactate
questions.learning: Hypoglycemia Hypoglycemia is not a side effect of salbutamol. The side effects of salbutamol are due to the stimulation of extrapulmonary β2 receptors.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study, an investigator compares the mean blood pressure values (along with their standard deviations) between two independent groups. Which statistical test is most appropriate to determine whether the difference between the two means is statistically significant?
questions.explanation: The study involves comparing the means of two independent groups with continuous data (blood pressure). The unpaired (independent samples) t-test is the standard parametric test for this purpose. A paired t-test (Option A) is used only for matched pairs or before-and-after measurements within the same group. The chi-square test (Option C) is used to determine associations between categorical variables, not to compare means. ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) (Option D) is used when comparing the means of more than two independent groups. Since the investigator is specifically assessing the difference between exactly two separate, independent sets of mean values, the unpaired t-test is the most appropriate statistical choice
questions.learning: The study involves comparing the means of two independent groups with continuous data (blood pressure). The unpaired (independent samples) t-test is the standard parametric test for this purpose.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An infant is brought to the OPD with a swelling which developed after around 15 hours after birth. The clinical image is given below. What could be the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cephalhematoma

In the given clinical picture, the swelling over the infant's head is likely to be a cephalhematoma.

Cephalohematoma is a collection of blood in between the pericranium and the flat bone (subperiosteal) of the skull, usually unilateral and over a parietal bone. It is never present at birth but gradually develops after 12–24 h. The swelling is limited by the suture lines of the skull as the pericranium is fixed to the margins of the bone.

The arrow mark in the radiographic image below represents cephalohematoma.

Other options:

Subgaleal hematoma occurs between the galea aponeurotica and the periosteum. It is commonly caused by birth trauma, particularly forceps or vacuum-assisted delivery. Subgaleal hematoma can cross suture lines and typically presents as a soft, fluctuant swelling on the scalp.

Caput succedaneum is an edema of the scalp that can cross suture lines. It is usually present at birth or develops shortly after due to pressure on the presenting part of the head during labor. It generally resolves within a few days.

Encephalocele is a neural tube defect that results in a sac-like protrusion of the brain and its meninges through an opening in the skull. It is a congenital condition and is typically diagnosed at birth or via prenatal ultrasound.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Given below is an instrument which is used to measure air humidity. Identify the instrument.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sling psychrometer

The instrument seen in the image is a Sling Psychrometer, It is used to measure the humidity/ moisture content in the air.

Sling Psychrometer has 2 mercury thermometers (wet and dry) in it. The wet bulb is moistened first with distilled water and the instrument is whirled/rotated standing with the back to the sun. The reading is noted twice.

Later the dry bulb is taken up for the reading and the relative air humidity is obtained by use of suitable tables and charts.

Pearl PF1005: Measurement of Air Temperature

* A number of thermometers which employ mercury or alcohol are used for measuring air temperature.

* These thermometers are mounted on a special screen called Stevenson screen as air should have free access to their bulbs and they must be protected from radiant heat.

* The instruments used to measure air temperature are:

* Dry bulb thermometers:

* These are ordinary mercury thermometers mounted on a Stevenson screen at about 1.20 to 1.80 metres above sea level

* Wet bulb thermometers

* These are just like the dry bulb variants but the bulb is kept wet by a muslin cloth that is fed with water from a bottle through a wick.

* Maximum thermometer

* This is a mercury thermometer which has a very fine constriction near the neck of the bulb

* Minimum thermometer

* The liquid in this thermometer is spirit which has a dumb-bell shaped index immersed in it

* Six’s maximum-minimum thermometer

* This thermometer has both mercury and alcohol

* It measures the maximum and minimum air temperatures reached over a period of time

* A mercury-free variant of this thermometer is available

* Globe thermometer:

* It is used for the direct measurement of mean radiant temperature of the surroundings.

* It has a hollow metal bulb (6 inches diameter) which has a matte black paint which absorbs radiant heat. A specially calibrated mercury bulb thermometer is kept inside.

* The difference between the readings of the globe thermometer and the bulb thermometer is the measure of the radiant heat.

* Kata thermometers:

* It is an alcohol thermometer and consists of a wet kata and a dry kata.

* A wet kata reading of 20 and above and a dry kata reading of 6 and above were taken as indices of thermal comfort.

* It was originally used to measure the cooling power of air (air temperature, humidity and air movement) but currently it is used only as an anemometer to measure low air velocities.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person is found dead in a swimming pool. Autopsy reveals water in the stomach and lungs, along with fine mucoid froth at the nose and mouth. What is the most likely mode of death?
questions.explanation: Wet drowning is the mode of death in approximately 90% of drowning cases and occurs when water is actively inhaled into the respiratory tract. This aspiration leads to the washout of pulmonary surfactant, alveolar collapse, and terminal asphyxia. The pathognomonic autopsy findings for wet drowning include copious, persistent mucoid froth at the nostrils and mouth, as well as overdistended, water-logged lungs and water in the stomach from swallowing. Dry drowning (Option A) occurs due to severe reflex laryngospasm that prevents water from entering the lungs; in these cases, the lungs remain dry. Near drowning (Option C) refers to a scenario where the individual survives for at least 24 hours after the event. Cardiac arrest (Option D) is a non-specific terminal event. Thus, the presence of lung water and froth confirms wet drowning
questions.learning: Wet drowning is the mode of death in approximately 90% of drowning cases and occurs when water is actively inhaled into the respiratory tract. This aspiration leads to the washout of pulmonary surfactant, alveolar collapse, and terminal asphyxia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 60-year-old man with chronic congestive cardiac failure (CCF) presents with jugular venous distention, ascites, and bilateral pedal edema. Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) levels. ANP promotes natriuresis by decreasing sodium reabsorption predominantly at which of the following nephron segments?
options: Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Medullary collecting duct

Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) promotes natriuresis primarily by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct.

Why Medullary Collecting Duct Specifically?

The medullary collecting duct (MCD) is the primary site of ANP action because:

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Receptor density | Highest concentration of NPR-A receptors in the entire nephron

| Transport target | Inhibits ENaC (Epithelial Sodium Channels) on luminal side

| Net effect | ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → Na⁺ stays in tubule → osmotic water retention in lumen → natriuresis + diuresis

| Aldosterone antagonism | ANP opposes aldosterone action at this same segment

ANP Actions Across the Nephron

| Site | Action | Significance

| ---- | ------ | ------------

| Medullary Collecting Duct ⭐ | ↓ ENaC → ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Primary natriuretic effect

| Glomerulus | ↑ GFR (dilates afferent, constricts efferent arteriole) | ↑ filtered Na⁺ load

| Proximal tubule | Mild ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption | Minor contribution

| Inner medullary CD | ↓ Urea transporters | Reduces medullary tonicity → impairs concentrating ability

| Adrenal gland | ↓ Aldosterone secretion | Indirect natriuresis

| Vasculature | Vasodilation | ↓ BP, ↓ venous return
questions.learning: Medullary collecting duct Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) promotes natriuresis primarily by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the medullary collecting duct.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which term describes the practice of imposing a specific point of view on people while suppressing independent thinking?
questions.explanation: Propaganda is a communication technique that aims to influence people's attitudes and behaviors by presenting information in a one-sided, often biased manner. In health settings, it involves instilling a specific viewpoint while actively discouraging or inhibiting independent critical thinking. Health Education (Option D), by contrast, is a planned process designed to provide individuals with balanced information and skills to make informed independent choices about their well-being. Health Promotion (Option B) is a broader ecological concept that includes education along with environmental and political changes to give people more control over their health. Health Awareness (Option C) is simply the state of being conscious that a health problem exists. Propaganda relies on repetition and emotional appeals rather than logic. While it can be used for "positive" outcomes like vaccination, its fundamental method—bypassing the individual's rational choice—is distinct from the empowering principles of health education
questions.learning: Propaganda is a communication technique that aims to influence people's attitudes and behaviors by presenting information in a one-sided, often biased manner.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman with a long history of dyspnea, chronic cough with sputum, and wheezing died of respiratory failure following a bout of lobar pneumonia. She was not a smoker or an alcoholic. The lung at autopsy is shown in the image below. Which of the following is most likely to cause the pathological changes shown?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency

The above gross specimen shows emphysematous damage involving enlargement of the entire acinus suggestive of panacinar emphysema. It is caused due to alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency.

In panacinar (panlobular) emphysema, the acini are uniformly enlarged from the level of the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal blind alveoli. It occurs commonly in the lower zones and in the anterior margins of the lung and is most severe at the bases.

The image below shows panacinar emphysema.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 1st pharyngeal arch gives rise to all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Levator veli palatini

Levator veli palatini is not derived from first pharyngeal arch.

All soft palate muscles including levator veli palatini are derived from the 4th pharyngeal arch and are supplied by vagal plexus.

First pharyngeal arch gives rise to:

• Muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, lateral and medial pterygoids)
• Mylohyoid
• Anterior belly of digastric
• Tensor tympani
• Tensor veli palatini and
• Anterior 2⁄3 of tongue.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Identify the mask in the image used for patients with COVID-19 infection.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Non-rebreathing mask

The mask in the image is a non-rebreathing mask (NRBM). It can be used for patients with COVID-19 infection.

A NRBM has a reservoir bag attached to the mask in order to provide additional reservoir volume. In addition, there is a valve attached, which provides a unidirectional flow of gases. Flutter valves on the side ports prevent room air entrainment, while a valve incorporated between the mask and the reservoir bag prevents the entry of the exhaled gases.

NRBM can provide the highest FiO2 of 0.9 to 1.0. without intubation at the fresh gas flow of 12-15 L/min. They are used for preoxygenation before intubation and post-extubation in covid patients.

Other options:

Option A: The venturi mask is a high-flow, fixed-performance device that delivers a specific oxygen concentration to the patient. It is a color-coded device that connects to the oxygen tubing distally and has a nozzle connecting to a mask proximally. Oxygen flows through a central constriction inside the device. Room air enters through surrounding apertures which dilutes the oxygen to the required concentration. The venturi mask is based on Bernoulli's principle.

Option B: Hudson mask is a simple face mask that delivers oxygen without forming a tight seal against the patient's face. There are holes on either side of Hudson's mask. This provides air entrainment, meeting the peak inspiratory flow and venting out the expired gases.

Option C: A nebulizer is used to deliver drugs to the breathing system. It generates an aerosol, producing droplets of varying sizes. It is shown below.
questions.learning: Non-rebreathing mask — The mask in the image is a non-rebreathing mask (NRBM). It can be used for patients with COVID-19 infection.

questions.text:
Match the following weapons with the possible injuries caused by them:

A. Axe
1. Incised wound

B. RTA
2. Tram track bruise

C. Blade
3. Grazed abrasion

D. Lathi
4. Chop wound
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2

The correctly matched sets of the above-mentioned weapons and the possible injuries are as follows:

A. Axe
4. Chop wounds

B. Road traffic accident
3. Graze abrasions

C. Blade
1. Incised wound

D. Lathi
2. Tram track bruise

Mechanism of injury with the above mentioned weapons:

Axe - it is a heavy weapon that may or may not be sharpened. Injury is produced by chopping action of the weapon and it may be in a spectrum of an incised wound to laceration depending upon the sharpness of the blade.

Road traffic accident - rubbing of epidermis tangential to a rough or hard surface gives rise to graze abrasion also called brush burn. It can occur in a road traffic accident after a pedestrian is being hit by a vehicle and the victim is slid/grazed for some distance before he comes to a halt.

Blade - it gives rise to a clean-cut wound which is usually deepest at its starting. Tailing of the wound indicates the direction of injury. Length is the biggest parameter of this type of wound.

Lathi- It is a blunt force injury giving rise to a patterned abrasion with 2 parallel lines and a normal unbruised area on site of impact or stick/lathi. The lathi forces the blood from the site of impact to either side which gives rise to tramline appearance.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In ORS, sodium is given along with glucose to facilitate___?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Co-transport

In ORS, sodium is given along with glucose to facilitate co-transport.

Glucose co transported with sodium is an example of Secondary Active transport.

The glucose-dependent sodium and water absorption is the principle behind replacing glucose and sodium in a 1:1 molar ratio in the WHO oral rehydration solution (ORS). The low osmolarity of the ORS in the lumen as compared to the blood facilitate absorption of fluid and hence the electrolytes due to the solvent drag.

The low-osmolality World Health Organization (WHO) oral rehydration solution (ORS) is now the global standard of care in the management of acute gastroenteritis.

Note:

Types of transport:

* Active transport:

* Primary

* Energy is derived from the transporter itself. Eg Na+ K+ ATPase pump.

* Secondary:

* Energy is derived indirectly. Eg. SGLT – Sodium linked glucose transport

* Passive transport

* Simple:

* No energy is required.

* No carrier molecule is involved.

* Eg. O2 exchange in alveoli.

* Facilitated:

* No energy is required.

* Carrier molecule involved.

* Eg. Glucose transport by GLUT transporters.
