questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: For day care anesthesia, which intravenous induction agent is preferred?
questions.explanation: Propofol (Option B) is the "gold standard" and preferred intravenous induction agent for day care (ambulatory) anesthesia. Its primary advantages include an extremely rapid onset, a very short duration of action due to rapid redistribution, and a smooth, quick recovery profile that allows patients to be discharged sooner. Most importantly, propofol has intrinsic antiemetic properties, which significantly reduces the risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), a common cause of delayed discharge. Ketamine (Option A) can cause emergence delirium and hallucinations. Thiopentone (Option D) has a longer "hangover" effect due to its accumulation in fat tissues. Etomidate (Option C) is preferred for cardiovascular stability but can cause myoclonus and adrenocortical suppression . Because of its "clear-headed" recovery and antiemetic benefit, Propofol is the ideal choice for procedures where rapid recovery and same-day discharge are essential

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with corneal scar has a visual acuity of 6/36, which improves to 6/18 with a pinhole. The most likely reason for this is ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Irregular astigmatism

The given findings suggest that the most likely reason is irregular astigmatism.

In refractive errors up to 3D, there is an improvement with pinhole to 6/6, if the macula is normal. Pinhole prevents the peripheral rays and also reduces the spherical aberration.

However, in this patient, it improved to only 6/18. A thing to note is that the corneal scar mentioned in the case would make the surface highly uneven, indicating irregular astigmatism. So, the best answer is irregular astigmatism.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are essential steps of Fothergill’s operation? 1. Laparoscopic or vaginal ligation 2. Amputation of cervix 3. Plication of Mackenrodt’s ligaments in front of cervix 4. Anterior colporrhaphy Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Fothergill’s operation (Manchester operation) is a uterus-preserving surgery performed for uterine prolapse associated with cervical elongation in women who wish to retain the uterus but have completed childbearing. The operation corrects uterine descent by shortening and repositioning the cardinal (Mackenrodt’s) ligaments and removing the elongated cervix.

• 1. Laparoscopic or vaginal ligation ✗

• This is not a step of Fothergill’s operation.

• 2. Amputation of cervix ✓

• Amputation of the elongated cervix is the hallmark of the procedure.

• 3. Plication of Mackenrodt’s (cardinal) ligaments in front of the cervix ✓

• The cardinal ligaments are shortened and sutured anterior to the cervix to provide uterine support.

• 4. Anterior colporrhaphy ✓

• Anterior colporrhaphy is routinely performed to repair the associated cystocele.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Fothergill’s operation (Manchester operation) is a uterus-preserving surgery performed for uterine prolapse associated with cervical elongation in women who wish to retain the uterus but have completed childbearing.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with renal calculus of > 4 cm of the staghorn type. What is the best management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy

The best management for staghorn renal calculus of >4 cm is percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL).

The initial management of renal stones depends on the stone size and includes conservative management, extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL), and PCNL. PCNL is preferred for stones > 2cm in size and for staghorn calculi, while ESWL is used to treat renal stones of size 0.6 to 1.5 cm. PCNL is indicated in

• Renal stones >2 cm
• Staghorn calculus
• Failed shockwave lithotripsy (SWL) or retrograde intrarenal surgery (RIRS) for renal calculi
• Lower pole renal stones with anatomy that is unfavorable for ESWL

Other options:

Option C: Ureteroscopic removal is attempted for failed SWLs or PCNLs, and is not the first choice in the surgical management of renal stones.

Option D: RIRS is a minimally invasive procedure similar to ureteroscopic removal, where the kidney is accessed using a slim and flexible ureteroscope in a retrograde manner via the ureteric orifice. It is indicated for lower pole renal stones < 2 cm.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The factors that can cause a person to drink water due to stimulation of thirst mechanism is/are ___________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

Dehydration, hemorrhage, and prandial drinking: All three can cause increased thirst resulting in water drinking.
Increased osmolality acts via osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus.

The decreased plasma volume, as in hemorrhage, acts via
1. Renin-angiotensin system
2. Baroreceptors in heart and blood vessels.
The intake of liquids during a meal is known as prandial drinking. The increase is known as learned or habit response but is not understood completely.

The following factors are thought to play a role
1. Increase in plasma osmolality due to food absorption
2. Action on hypothalamus by one or more gastrointestinal hormones
questions.learning: All of the above Dehydration, hemorrhage, and prandial drinking: All three can cause increased thirst resulting in water drinking. Increased osmolality acts via osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus.

questions.text: Identify the type of tympanoplasty shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type 3

The columella tympanoplasty is type 3 as per the Wullstein's classification of tympanoplasty.

While performing this procedure, the diseased ear would have already lost the malleus and incus, and hence the graft is placed over the stapes superstructure. Therefore, it is also called myringostapediopexy.

Type

Type I
Perforation of tympanic membrane which is repaired with a graft (myringoplasty)

Type II
Perforation of tympanic membrane with erosion of malleus. The graft is placed on the incus or remnant of the malleus.

Malleus and incus are absent. The graft is placed directly on the stapes head (myringostapediopexy)

Only the footplate of stapes is present. The graft is placed between the oval and round windows on the stapes footplate

Type V
The stapes footplate is fixed but the round window is functioning. The graft is placed in contact with a new window created on the fenestra in the horizontal semicircular canal

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A female patient presents with a breast abscess. An aspiration was attempted under antibiotic cover which failed to reveal any aspirate. What is the next step in management?
options: Stop antibiotics as no aspirate was collected
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A second attempt at aspiration

In a patient with a breast abscess, the next step after a failed aspiration is to attempt aspiration once again under antibiotic cover.

Incision and drainage is not preferred, as it can potentially interfere with breastfeeding, and delicate structures such as ducts, lobules, and tubules may be injured, possibly leading to a non-healing milk fistula.

A breast abscess is a complication of acute mastitis, which is more common in new mothers at the beginning of lactation (lactational mastitis). Non-lactational mastitis is more common in diabetic, immunosuppressed people and people predisposed by duct ectasia and periareolar infections.

Clinical features of a breast abscess include:

• Fever and malaise
• Localized pain and tenderness
• Redness and swelling of the affected breast
• Positive fluctuation test.

An ultrasonogram of the affected breast is performed to confirm the abscess, and treatment proceeds as follows:

• Analgesics, antipyretics, and breast support for pain and fever relief.
• Aspiration is performed under antibiotic cover, and the pus is cultured. If aspiration proves unsuccessful, it should be reattempted after a few days.
• Incision and drainage should be considered in cases of:

• Mastitis unresponsive to antibiotics for 48 hours.
• Brawny induration.
• Progressive mastitis with persistent fever

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presented with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, and the x-ray showed the following features. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Putty kidney

A patient with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, with the given x-ray showing diffuse alveolar calcification in the right renal region point towards a diagnosis of a putty kidney.

The putty kidney is a characteristic finding of genitourinary tuberculosis (TB), specifically renal TB. The given image shows a homogenous and ground-glass-like calcification of the kidney appearing like putty. It is caused by the dissemination of the organism through the bloodstream and is thus always a secondary TB. There is either reinfection or reactivation of old TB.

Genitourinary TB is a cause of sterile pyuria. Diagnosis is confirmed with a tuberculin test, or at least 3 consecutive early-morning specimens of urine are examined for acid-fast bacilli. They are stained with a Ziehl-Neelsen stain and subsequently cultured.

CT is the most sensitive modality and is the preferred means of visualizing renal calcifications. CT urography is done to assess the various stages of renal TB and its manifestations, which are as follows:

• Early:

• Papillary necrosis

• Progressive:

• Multifocal strictures
• Generalized or focal hydronephrosis
• Mural thickening and enhancement
• Poorly enhancing renal parenchyma

• End-stage:

• Progressive hydronephrosis
• Amorphous dystrophic calcification that involves the entire kidney - putty kidney

Treatment involves short-course therapy with antitubercular drugs like pyrazinamide, isoniazid, and rifampicin. Partial nephrectomy, nephrectomy, or reconstructive surgery is often done.

Option B: Nephrocalcinosis - This condition is characterized by the deposition of calcium in the kidney parenchyma or tubules, often seen in hypercalcemic conditions like hyperparathyroidism. However, it would not explain the clinical presentation of sterile pyuria.

Option C: Staghorn calculi are large kidney stones that fill the renal pelvis and extend into the renal calyces, often caused by urinary tract infections with organisms such as Proteus, Pseudomonas, and Staphylococcus. While these calculi can cause abdominal pain, they usually do not result in sterile pyuria, as they are associated with infection.

The image below shows a staghorn calculus of the left kidney.

Option D: Psoas calcification - This refers to calcification within the psoas muscle and is often seen after acute renal failure and rhabdomyolysis. It is not associated with sterile pyuria and is not the cause of the patient's symptoms.
questions.learning: Putty kidney — A patient with abdominal pain and sterile pyuria, with the given x-ray showing diffuse alveolar calcification in the right renal region point towards a diagnosis of a putty kidney.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man presented with a history of stab injury over the arm. On examination, there was a hematoma present, and radial and ulnar pulses were not felt. A 3.5cm longitudinal tear is noted in the brachial artery. Which among the following is the best treatment option?
options: Primary repair with end to end anastomosis
Repair with great saphenous vein graft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Repair with great saphenous vein graft

In this patient, who has sustained a long tear to the brachial artery due to a stab injury, the best treatment option is to repair it with a great saphenous vein interposition graft harvested from the patient's uninjured leg.

The most desirable graft used is the great saphenous vein . A native vein graft is preferable to a prosthetic graft because:

• Its elastic properties are comparable to that of an artery and enable pulsatile flow
• The diameter is similar to that of an extremity artery
• It is not thrombogenic and has long term patency

Other grafts that can be used are cephalic vein, lesser saphenous vein, and prosthetic conduits. Cephalic vein is not the first choice because it is less muscular than greater saphenous vein, and might also compromise the upper limb venous access in the already injured patient. Both the cephalic and the lesser saphenous veins present problems while harvesting in a trauma patient.

Other options:

Option A: Primary arterial repair with end-to-end anastomosis can be done only if the repair is tension-free. If the length of the injured area is long, vessel injuries cannot be repaired by primary end-to-end anastomoses and instead require an interposition graft.

Option C: Prosthetic grafts are only preferred when there has been a trauma to the native saphenous vein or when there is a size mis-match. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) graft is commonly used.

Option D: Saphenous vein patch is used in the closure of the arteriotomy site during carotid endarterectomies.
questions.learning: Repair with great saphenous vein graft — In this patient, who has sustained a long tear to the brachial artery due to a stab injury, the best treatment option is to repair it with a great saphenous vein interposition graft harvested from the patient's…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient complains of significant eye discomfort while reading printed text or using digital screens, despite having normal visual acuity and an otherwise unremarkable eye examination. The only abnormal finding is a Schirmer’s test result of 5 mm. What is the most appropriate and effective treatment in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of discomfort during visually intensive tasks (like reading or screen use) and a Schirmer's test result of 5mm (normal is mm) are diagnostic of Dry Eye Disease (keratoconjunctivitis sicca). A result of 5mm indicates significant aqueous tear deficiency. The most effective and standard first-line treatment for managing symptoms and protecting the ocular surface is the frequent use of lubricants (Option C), such as artificial tears or gels. Steroids (Option A) are only used for short-term control of severe inflammation and carry risks of glaucoma or cataracts. Antihistamines (Option B) are used for allergic conjunctivitis and can actually worsen dry eyes by reducing tear production. Since the patient has normal visual acuity, prescribed spectacles (Option D) would not address the underlying tear deficiency. Therefore, tear film replacement with lubricants is the most appropriate management
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of discomfort during visually intensive tasks (like reading or screen use) and a Schirmer's test result of 5mm (normal is mm) are diagnostic of Dry Eye Disease (keratoconjunctivitis sicca).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 23-year-old man develops eye pain, redness, and photophobia two days after sustaining an ocular injury from leaves and thorns while gardening. Based on this history and presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fungal keratitis (keratomycosis) must be the primary suspicion in any patient presenting with a corneal ulcer following trauma with "vegetative matter" such as leaves, thorns, or wood. Agricultural workers and gardeners are at the highest risk. The most common organisms are Aspergillus and Fusarium. Clinical signs often include a "dry" looking ulcer with "feathery" margins and satellite lesions. Option A (Simplex keratitis) typically features a dendritic ulcer and is a viral reactivation rather than trauma-induced. Option B (Bacterial keratitis) is more acute and usually follows general trauma, appearing more "suppurative". Option D (Acanthamoeba) is strongly linked to contaminated contact lens solutions or swimming in fresh water. Fungal keratitis is notoriously difficult to treat because antifungal drugs have poor corneal penetration. Diagnosis is confirmed by corneal scrapings showing fungal hyphae on KOH mount. Treatment requires long-term topical antifungals such as Natamycin or Voriconazole
questions.learning: Fungal keratitis (keratomycosis) must be the primary suspicion in any patient presenting with a corneal ulcer following trauma with "vegetative matter" such as leaves, thorns, or wood.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: How does the World Health Organization (WHO) define blindness?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization (WHO) provides a standardized definition for blindness to facilitate global health comparisons and resource allocation. According to these criteria, blindness is defined as a visual acuity (VA) of less than (Snellen) or its equivalent in the better eye with the best possible correction. This means the individual cannot count fingers from a distance of 3 meters. Additionally, a visual field of less than 10 degrees from the point of fixation in the better eye is also classified as blindness. A visual acuity of less than but better than or equal to (Option B) is categorized as "severe visual impairment" rather than blindness. Standardizing this definition is critical for programs like "VISION 2020: The Right to Sight" to monitor the prevalence of avoidable blindness. Properly identifying these thresholds ensures that public health interventions are targeted toward those with the greatest need for rehabilitative or surgical services
questions.learning: The World Health Organization (WHO) provides a standardized definition for blindness to facilitate global health comparisons and resource allocation. According to these criteria, blindness is defined as a visual acuity (VA) of less than (Snellen) or its…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The malignancy associated with Stewart-Treves syndrome is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymphangiosarcoma

Stewart–Treves syndrome is the development of lymphangiosarcoma, a rare but highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor, in the setting of chronic lymphedema. It classically occurs after radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection, although it can develop in any cause of longstanding lymphedema.

Why not other options?

• B. Malignant melanoma: Associated with UV exposure, dysplastic nevi, and genetic syndromes, not chronic lymphedema.
• C. Basal cell carcinoma: Related to chronic sun exposure and fair skin.
• D. Liposarcoma: A malignant tumor of adipose tissue with no association with Stewart–Treves syndrome.
questions.learning: Lymphangiosarcoma Stewart–Treves syndrome is the development of lymphangiosarcoma, a rare but highly aggressive malignant vascular tumor, in the setting of chronic lymphedema.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents to the outpatient department with complaints of hearing loss. On examination, the Rinne test is positive in the left ear and negative in the right ear. Weber’s test shows lateralization to the left ear, and bone conduction is reduced in the right ear but normal in the left ear. How should these findings be interpreted?
options: Sensorineural hearing loss in left ear
Sensorineural hearing loss in right ear
Conductive hearing loss in left ear
Conductive hearing loss in right ear.
questions.explanation: Interpretation of tuning fork tests requires a combined analysis of all results. In this case, a negative Rinne in the right ear suggests either conductive loss or a "false negative" due to profound sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). The bone conduction test is the deciding factor; because it is reduced in the right ear, it confirms sensorineural involvement. In SNHL, the Weber test lateralizes to the better-hearing ear. Since the sound lateralizes to the left, the left ear is the better ear, and the right ear is affected by SNHL. Options C and D (conductive loss) are ruled out because conductive loss would show lateralization to the poorer ear in the Weber test and normal bone conduction. Option A is incorrect as the left ear shows a positive Rinne and normal bone conduction, indicating it is likely the healthy ear. Thus, the clinical cluster confirms SNHL in the right ear
questions.learning: Interpretation of tuning fork tests requires a combined analysis of all results. In this case, a negative Rinne in the right ear suggests either conductive loss or a "false negative" due to profound sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A man with known history of diabetes has come to your clinic. His vision is 6/6. However, on retinal examination, he is classified to have severe NPDR. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Disc neovascularisation

Disc neovascularization is not a feature of nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), and is seen in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

The important findings in severe NPDR are one or more of severe retinal hemorrhages in 4 quadrants, significant venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, and moderate intraretinal microvascular anomalies (microaneurysms) in 1 or more quadrants. This is known as the 4-2-1 rule.
Diabetic retinopathy is used to describe retinal changes seen in diabetic patients. It is classified into the following types:

• Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR).
• Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR).
• Diabetic maculopathy.
• Advanced diabetic eye disease.

Management of diabetic retinopathy includes intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs, intravitreal steroids, laser therapy, and or surgical management.

Surgical management is done in the following cases:

• Tractional diabetic macular edema with NPDR:  pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) with the removal of posterior hyaloid.
• Advanced PDR with dense vitreous hemorrhage/ fibrovascular epiretinal membrane: PPV along with the removal of opaque vitreous gel/ membrane and endophotocoagulation.
• Advanced PDR with tractional retinal detachment: PPV with endophotocoagulation and reattachment of the detached retina by scleral buckling.

Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study classification:

Nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) -

1. Very mild NPDR :
- Microaneurysms only.
- Management - Review in 12 months.

2. Mild NPDR :
- Any or all of : microaneurysms, retinal hemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, up to the level of moderate NPDR. No intraretinal microvascular anomalies (IRMA) or significant beading.
- Management - Medical control of diabetes with follow-up in 9-12 months.

3. Moderate NPDR :
- Severe retinal hemorrhages (about 20 medium-large per quadrant) in 1–3 quadrants or mild IRMA.
- Significant venous beading can be present in no more than 1 quadrant.
- Cotton wool spots commonly present.
- Management - Review in approximately 6 months.

4. Severe NPDR : The 4–2–1 rule; one or more of:
• Severe hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants
• Significant venous beading in 2 or more quadrants
• Moderate IRMA in 1 or more quadrants
• Management - Review in 4 months.

5. Very severe NPDR : The 4–2–1 rule, two or more of the criteria for severe NPDR
• Review in 2–3 months.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)-

1. Mild to moderate PDR :
• New vessels on the disc (NVD) or new vessels elsewhere (NVE), but extent insufficient to meet the high-risk criteria.
• Management- Prompt Pan-retinal photocoagulation is done if type 2 DM in a patient >40 years of age, otherwise defer PRP.

2. High-risk PDR :
• New vessels on the disc (NVD) (about 1/3 disc area).
• Any NVD with vitreous hemorrhage.
• NVE greater than 1/2 disc area with vitreous hemorrhage.
• Management - Prompt pan-retinal photocoagulation.
questions.learning: Disc neovascularisation Disc neovascularization is not a feature of nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), and is seen in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the cause of lactational amenorrhea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased prolactin secretion

The cause of lactational amenorrhea is increased prolactin secretion as a result of the baby sucking at the mother's breast.

Lactational amenorrhea:

* Type of secondary amenorrhea due to the effect of prolactin secretion.

* During lactation, there are pulsatile bursts of prolactin secretion in response to suckling.

* Prolactin suppresses GnRH, LH, and FSH causing lactational amenorrhea.

* Regular lactation with one feed at night delays ovulation and pregnancy for up to 6 months, provided she remains amenorrhoeic.

* After 6 months, lactation has no bearing on ovulation and pregnancy can occur, despite amenorrhoea and might need other forms of contraception.
questions.learning: Increased prolactin secretion — The cause of lactational amenorrhea is increased prolactin secretion as a result of the baby sucking at the mother's breast.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old man was referred to the surgery OPD from the infertility clinic. On inspection, the scrotum appeared as in the image. On palpation, a bag of worms sensation was felt. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Varicocele

The clinical scenario with the given image showing abnormal dilation and enlargement of the scrotal venous pampiniform plexus,  like bag of worms is suggestive of a varicocele.

Varicocele is an abnormal dilatation and enlargement of the scrotal venous plexus draining the testis. Left-sided varicocele is more common. Most varicoceles are idiopathic, obstruction of the testicular vein by a renal tumour or nephrectomy is seen in some cases.

The pathogenesis behind varicocele is due to increased blood flow to the testis leading to higher intratesticular temperatures, which inhibits spermatogenesis and results in low sperm count, motility and morphology. Most varicoceles are asymptomatic. Those symptomatic tend to present in adolescence or early adulthood, with a dragging discomfort that is worse on standing at the end of the day. There may be a cough impulse. Additionally, patients may have infertility.

Grades of varicocele

Grade 1
Varicocele only palpable on Valsalva’s maneuver

Grade 2
Varicocele palpable without Valsalva’s maneuver

Grade 3
Varicocele is seen on inspection of the testis

Often, patients may be asymptomatic and do not require treatment. Treatment of symptomatic and young patients includes surgical ligation of the gonadal vein. It may be achieved through embolectomy or varicocelectomy. Approaches to varicocelectomy are:

* Inguinal ( Ivanisevic method )

* Retroperitoneal (Palomo procedure)

* Natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery through the transvesical route

In older patients, NSAIDs and scrotal support are adequate.

Other options :

Option a: Hydrocele is an accumulation of fluid within the tunica vaginalis. In the case of a primary hydrocoele, as the fluid is collected within a closed sac, a cough impulse is unlikely to be seen. Important positive clinical findings in a hydrocoele are that they are irreducible,  the testes cannot be palpated separately, ability to get above the swelling, and transillumination of the swelling.

Option c : Testicular torsion is the twisting of the spermatic cord and its contents such that the testicular blood supply becomes compromised. It is a surgical emergency and if left untreated, the testes may become gangrenous.

Option d : Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac. It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract.
questions.learning: Varicocele — The clinical scenario with the given image showing abnormal dilation and enlargement of the scrotal venous pampiniform plexus, like bag of worms is suggestive of a varicocele.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child presented to the OPD with a characteristic type of cataract as seen in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Galactosemia

The image shown below shows an oil drop cataract seen in galactosemia. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia which is an autosomal recessive disorder.

Clinical features :

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, convulsions.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.

* Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.

* Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes oil-drop cataract.

* Patients with galactosemia are at an increased risk of developing Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and the Mucic acid test is positive.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.

Diabetes show snow flake cataract, Wilson’s disease shows sunflower cataract and myotonic dystrophy shows Christmas tree cataract.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statement: “The people should seek to preserve their traditional eating patterns and lifestyles associated with low levels of Coronary Heart Disease (CHD).” Which level of prevention is implied in this statement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primordial

Primordial prevention aims to prevent the emergence of risk factors themselves by promoting healthy lifestyles and preventing the development of social, environmental, and behavioral conditions that increase disease risk. It is particularly important for non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as coronary heart disease (CHD), diabetes, and hypertension.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. High-risk approach: Targets individuals already at increased risk (e.g., smokers, hypertensive patients).
• C. Primary prevention: Prevents disease after risk factors have already developed, such as treating hypertension or promoting smoking cessation.
• D. Secondary prevention: Involves early diagnosis and prompt treatment to halt disease progression.
questions.learning: Primordial Primordial prevention aims to prevent the emergence of risk factors themselves by promoting healthy lifestyles and preventing the development of social, environmental, and behavioral conditions that increase disease risk.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with vision loss. On radiological investigation, an aneurysm causing damage to the optic chiasma was noted. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be the artery that is causing the damage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior communicating artery

An aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery is most likely to be causing damage to the optic chiasma, leading to vision loss in this patient.

Circle of Willis is a large arterial anastomosis that unites the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. It lies in the subarachnoid space within the basal cisterns that surround the optic chiasma and infundibulum.

Anterior communicating artery aneurysm:

Anterior communicating artery (Acom) links the right and left anterior cerebral arteries and is directed anterior and superior to the optic chiasma. The aneurysm will protrude in the posterior direction and will impinge upon the optic chiasma from above, leading to loss of vision.

Compression of the optic chiasma (central lesion) by an ACom aneurysm, will lead to bitemporal hemianopia i.e, loss of vision in the left/temporal halves of both visual fields. Nasal fibers of each retina cross through the chiasma at this level and hence, these fibers will be compromised.

In the case of a bilateral peripheral lesion of the optic chiasma, binasal hemianopia will be seen.

Other causes of chiasmal lesions are

• Pituitary adenoma (most common)
• Craniopharyngioma
• Meningioma
• Glioma

Blood supply of optic chiasma: The left and right anterior cerebral arteries, along with the superior hypophyseal artery (branch of the internal carotid artery) form the blood supply of optic chiasma.

The given cadaveric image below is of the vascular structures (Circle of Willis) at the base of the brain.

Investigation: Digital subtraction angiogram is the definitive imaging modality for aneurysms arising from the circle of Willis. Other investigations are CT and MRI.

Other options:

Aneurysms of the anterior choroidal artery (option B) and middle cerebral artery (option C) aneurysms will not compress the optic chiasma as they are anatomically not in close proximity to be able to exert pressure on the chiasma and cause loss of vision.

Despite the anatomical proximity of the anterior cerebral artery (option D) to the optic chiasma, anterior communicating artery (Acom) aneurysm is the commonest intracranial aneurysm.
questions.learning: Anterior communicating artery — An aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery is most likely to be causing damage to the optic chiasma, leading to vision loss in this patient.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: HEADSSS assessment will be used by an intern for which of the following patient groups?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Adolescents

HEADSSS assessment is done in adolescents to determine early symptoms of mental disorders and functional impairment in major life domains such as home and family, school, peers, and community.

These domains are included in the HEADSSS (Home, Education, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/Depression, Safety) Interview Guide. An adolescent’s risk and protective factors are identified during each visit using this assessment. Risk factors increase the likelihood that an adolescent will engage in risky behaviors, whereas protective factors build an adolescent’s resiliency and ability to cope with stress.

Examples of questions in HEADSSS assessment :

Home

• Who lives at home, and where?
• Do you have your own room?
• What are relationships like at home?
• What do parents and relatives do for a living?

Education

• School/grade performance-any recent changes? Any dramatic past changes?
• Any years repeated/classes failed
• Suspension, termination, dropping out?
• Any current or past employment?

Activities

• On own, with peers (what do you do for fun? where? when?)
• Hobbies-other activities?
• History of arrests-acting out-crime?

Drugs

• Use by peers? Use by young person? (include tobacco, alcohol)
• Use by family members?
• Amounts, source, frequency, patterns of use/abuse

Sexuality

• Degree and types of sexual experience and acts? Number of partners?
• Sexually transmitted diseases-knowledge and prevention? Contraception? Frequency of use?
• History of pregnancy/abortion?

Suicide / Depression / Self Image

• Sleep disorders, appetite/eating behavior changes, emotional outbursts and highly impulsive behavior, history of withdrawal/isolation, hopeless/helpless feelings, suicidal ideation
• History of past suicide attempts, depression, psychological counseling

Safety

• Do you ever feel unsafe?
questions.learning: Adolescents HEADSSS assessment is done in adolescents to determine early symptoms of mental disorders and functional impairment in major life domains such as home and family, school, peers, and community.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following may lead to a decrease in GFR?
options: Decrease in bowman capsule oncotic pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decrease in bowman capsule oncotic pressure

A decrease in bowman's capsule oncotic pressure would lead to a decrease in GFR.

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of fluid filtered from the renal glomerular capillaries into the Bowman's capsule per unit time.

The GFR is determined by sum of the hydrostatic and colloid osmotic forces across the glomerular membrane, which gives the net filtration pressure. It is dependant on Glomerular Kf (glomerular ultrafiltration coefficient) also.

Mathematically, it can be expressed as follows:

GFR= Kf [PG + πB -PB- πG]

Forces favoring Filtration

• PG: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure
• πB: Bowman’s capsule oncotic pressure

Forces opposing Filtration

• PB: Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure
• πG: Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure

Factors that can increase the GFR are as follows:

• Increase in glomerular capillary filtration coefficient Kf: This coefficient depends on the hydraulic conductivity and surface area of the glomerular capillaries.
• Decrease in Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure: Conditions with urinary tract obstruction can lead to an increase in this pressure and a fall in GFR.
• Decrease in glomerular colloid osmotic pressure: Accumulation of plasma proteins that are not filtered from the blood contributes to this pressure and an increase reduces the further filtration and GFR. It is directly proportional to the following factors:Arterial plasma colloid osmotic pressure
• Filtration fraction
questions.learning: Decrease in bowman capsule oncotic pressure — A decrease in bowman's capsule oncotic pressure would lead to a decrease in GFR. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of fluid filtered from the renal glomerular capillaries into the Bowman's capsule…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pallor, and jaundice, and investigations show hemolytic anemia with spherocytes on peripheral smear. In which condition is elective splenectomy considered the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is an inherited disorder of the red blood cell membrane, typically due to defects in proteins like ankyrin or spectrin. This results in the formation of rigid, spherical RBCs (spherocytes) that are selectively trapped and destroyed as they pass through the narrow splenic sinusoids. This destruction leads to the classic triad of anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly. Elective splenectomy is the preferred and definitive treatment for symptomatic HS, as it effectively stops the premature destruction of these abnormal cells, thereby resolving the anemia and jaundice. G6PD deficiency (Option A) is an episodic condition managed by avoiding triggers. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (Option B) involves a complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis and is treated with eculizumab. Hairy cell leukemia (Option D) is a malignant lymphoproliferative disorder where splenectomy was historically used but has been replaced by chemotherapy. While splenectomy does not correct the underlying membrane defect in HS, it removes the primary site of cell death, significantly improving the patient's quality of life
questions.learning: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is an inherited disorder of the red blood cell membrane, typically due to defects in proteins like ankyrin or spectrin. This results in the formation of rigid, spherical RBCs (spherocytes) that are selectively trapped and…

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is the causative agent for acne fulminans?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Propionibacterium

Propionibacterium acnes is believed to be responsible for acne fulminans.

Acne fulminans is a severe destructive form of acne. It is predominantly seen in white, adolescent males.

The exact etiopathogenesis of this disease is unknown. However, the presence of elevated testosterone levels and infection by Propionibacterium acnes has been implicated.

The patient clinically presents with sudden onset of multiple ulcerative and hemorrhagic nodules over the face, back, and trunk. In addition, the lesions may be accompanied by various signs and symptoms of systemic inflammation like fever and arthralgia.

The onset of these symptoms is commonly heralded by the presence of mild to moderate acne for 6 months to 2 years. Treatment failure to antimicrobial therapy is seen.

The diagnosis is clinical and the management entails:

* Removal of crusts by soaking the crusts in an emollient oil.

* Applying a potent steroidal/antimicrobial cream over the lesions for 2-3 weeks after the removal of crusts.

* Oral prednisolone(0.5-1 mg/kg) therapy should be started and tapered over 2-3 months.

Systemic symptoms like fever and arthralgia are treated using oral salicylates or oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
questions.learning: Propionibacterium Propionibacterium acnes is believed to be responsible for acne fulminans. Acne fulminans is a severe destructive form of acne.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of these steps is followed first for the management of shoulder dystocia after McRoberts maneuver?
options: Flex the legs over the abdomen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Apply gentle supra pubic pressure

Applying a gentle suprapubic pressure is the first step in the management of shoulder dystocia after the McRoberts maneuver.

Shoulder dystocia drill to better organize emergency management:

* Call for help. Initially, a gentle attempt at traction is made. Drain the bladder if it is distended.

* Episiotomy

* McRoberts maneuver: involves flexing the legs on the abdomen with concurrent suprapubic pressure. This causes straightening of the sacrum relative to the lumbar vertebrae, rotation of the symphysis pubis toward the maternal head, and a decrease in the angle of pelvic inclination. This tends to free the impacted anterior shoulder. It is shown in the image below.

These maneuvers will resolve most cases of shoulder dystocia. If not -

* Delivery of the posterior arm is attempted.

* Woods screw maneuver is applied.

* Rubin maneuver is attempted.

Other techniques generally should be reserved for cases in which all other maneuvers have failed. These include intentional fracture of the anterior clavicle and the Zavanelli maneuver.
questions.learning: Apply gentle supra pubic pressure Applying a gentle suprapubic pressure is the first step in the management of shoulder dystocia after the McRoberts maneuver.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Drug of choice for long-term management of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) to reduce disease activity and flares is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the cornerstone of long-term treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and is recommended for nearly all patients unless contraindicated. Hydroxychloroquine exerts its effect by inhibiting lysosomal antigen processing and Toll-like receptor (TLR-7 and TLR-9) signaling, thereby decreasing autoantigen presentation and cytokine production.

• Hydroxychloroquine is the drug of choice for long-term maintenance therapy in SLE because it:

• Reduces disease flares
• Improves skin and joint manifestations
• Prevents disease progression
• Improves long-term survival
• Lowers thrombotic risk, especially in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies

Why not the other options?

• B. Methotrexate: Used as a steroid-sparing agent for lupus arthritis or skin disease but is not the first-line maintenance drug for all SLE patients.
• C. Cyclophosphamide: Reserved for severe organ-threatening lupus (e.g., lupus nephritis, neuropsychiatric lupus) because of significant toxicity.
• D. Ibuprofen: Provides symptomatic relief of pain and arthritis but does not modify disease activity or prevent flares.
questions.learning: Hydroxychloroquine Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the cornerstone of long-term treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and is recommended for nearly all patients unless contraindicated.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In clinical trials, to ensure reliable and valid results, selection bias—where the sample may not accurately represent the broader population— must be minimized. Which method is primarily used in clinical trial protocols to reduce the risk of selection bias?
questions.explanation: Randomization is the hallmark of a high-quality clinical trial and is the primary method used to eliminate or minimize selection bias. It involves assigning participants to different study groups (e.g., treatment vs. control) purely by chance, ensuring that both known and unknown confounding variables are distributed equally between the groups. This process makes the groups comparable and ensures that any observed differences in outcomes can be attributed to the intervention itself rather than baseline participant characteristics. Selecting the population (Option A) relates to the external validity or generalizability of the study but doesn't fix internal bias between groups. Intervention (Option B) is the treatment being tested. Written informed consent (Option D) is a fundamental ethical requirement to protect patient autonomy but does not impact the statistical validity or the reduction of bias. Therefore, randomization remains the most powerful statistical tool for maintaining the integrity and scientific rigor of a randomized controlled trial (RCT)
questions.learning: Randomization is the hallmark of a high-quality clinical trial and is the primary method used to eliminate or minimize selection bias. It involves assigning participants to different study groups (e.g., treatment vs. control) purely by chance, ensuring…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The instruments shown below are used for which of the following procedures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy

The instruments shown in the image is used to perform percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy.

A standard endoscopy is performed to ensure that there are no contraindications to gastrostomy insertion. The stomach is insufflated with air and direct percutaneous needle puncture made at a point where the stomach abuts the abdominal wall. Lignocaine is infused on withdrawal. A trocar is inserted and a wire is passed into the stomach, which can be caught with a snare. The scope is withdrawn, pulling the wire out through the mouth,at which point it is attached to the gastrostomy tube. The gastrostomy is pulled through into the stomach and out through the track created by the trocar insertion.

The insertion of a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube improves nutritional and functional outcomes in patients who cannot maintain oral nutritional intake. PEG insertion is often a preliminary step in the treatment of complex orofacial malignancies and can also be used to support nutrition in patients with various malignant, degenerative, or inflammatory diseases.

Procedure risks include bleeding, perforation,aspiration risk, dislodgment with peritoneal contamination, wound site infection and granulation.
questions.learning: Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy — The instruments shown in the image is used to perform percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. A standard endoscopy is performed to ensure that there are no contraindications to gastrostomy insertion.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with chest pain and breathlessness that worsen in the supine position and improve on sitting up. On examination, heart sounds are muffled. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits the classic clinical features of Pericardial Effusion: pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that are relieved by sitting forward (positional relief). The hallmark physical finding is muffled (distant) heart sounds due to the fluid surrounding the heart. In severe cases, this can lead to Beck’s triad (muffled sounds, JVP distension, and hypotension) indicating cardiac tamponade. The provided X-ray shows the characteristic "Water-bottle heart" appearance, where the heart shadow is globular and massively enlarged. Tetralogy of Fallot (Option B) would show a "boot-shaped" heart. Transposition of great arteries (Option C) classically shows an "egg-on-a-string" heart . Pulmonary hypertension (Option D) shows enlarged pulmonary arteries but not a globular heart shadow. Diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography, which can visualize the fluid in the pericardial sac. Treatment involves treating the underlying cause or performing pericardiocentesis
questions.learning: The patient exhibits the classic clinical features of Pericardial Effusion: pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea that are relieved by sitting forward (positional relief).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 54-year-old patient receiving chemotherapy with cisplatin develops notable adverse effects. Which side effect is most commonly associated with cisplatin therapy?
questions.explanation: Cisplatin is a potent platinum-based alkylating agent used for various solid tumors, but it has a very high "emetic potential". The most common and immediate side effects of cisplatin are severe GI symptoms, specifically nausea and intractable vomiting. These symptoms are so prevalent that almost all patients require aggressive pre-treatment with anti-emetics like 5-HT3 antagonists (e.g., ondansetron) and dexamethasone. While Neuropathy (Option B, specifically sensory peripheral neuropathy) and Nephrotoxicity (damage to renal tubules) are significant dose-limiting toxicities, they are typically cumulative rather than immediate. Cardiotoxicity (Option C) and Myopathy (Option D) are rare side effects compared to the near-universal GI distress. Clinicians must also vigilantly monitor renal function and hearing (ototoxicity), as cisplatin can cause permanent damage to the hair cells in the cochlea. Aggressive hydration is a standard preventive measure used during administration to minimize the risk of acute kidney injury
questions.learning: Cisplatin is a potent platinum-based alkylating agent used for various solid tumors, but it has a very high "emetic potential". The most common and immediate side effects of cisplatin are severe GI symptoms, specifically nausea and intractable vomiting.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A woman presents at 8 weeks of gestation. Which of the following signs can be elicited at this gestation?

1. Goodell's sign
2. Osiander's sign
3. Internal ballottement
4. Lightening
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1,2

The signs that can be elicited at 8 weeks of gestation are Goodell's sign and Osiander's sign.

Goodell’s sign is a sign of early pregnancy, which describes the marked softening of the cervix in contrast to the non-pregnant state. It is seen as early as the 6th week.

Osiander's sign describes the pulsations felt in the lateral fornix due to increased vascularity. It is seen around 8 weeks of gestation.

Internal ballottement can be elicited between 16–28th weeks of gestation, before which the fetus is too small and after which it is too large to displace. It may not be elicited in cases with scanty liquor amnii, or when the fetus is transversely placed.

Lightening is a sense of relief of the pressure symptoms due to the engagement of the presenting part. It is felt at about 38 weeks of gestation.
questions.learning: 1,2 The signs that can be elicited at 8 weeks of gestation are Goodell's sign and Osiander's sign. Goodell’s sign is a sign of early pregnancy, which describes the marked softening of the cervix in contrast to the non-pregnant state.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the best parameter to assess in case of male infertility
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The morphology of sperms

The morphology of sperms is the best parameter to assess male infertility.
Characterization of normal sperm morphology shows improved correlation with fertilization rates during IVF cycles.

The criteria requires careful analysis of the following:

• The shape and size of the sperm head,
• The relative size of the acrosome in proportion to the head,
• And characteristics of the tail, including length, coiling, or presence of two tails.

Significantly decreased fertilization rates are observed when normal morphology of the sample falls below 4 percent.

Abnormal sperm morphology is termed teratospermia or teratozoospermia. Whereas sperm concentration and progressive motility have value for distinguishing fertile from infertile men, strict sperm morphology (as determined by an individual having extensive training and experience) was the one most discriminating value.

Parameters In Semen Analysis
Reference Limits

Volume
>1.5mL

Count
>15 million/mL

Total motility
> 40%

Morphology
>4% normal forms

WBCs
< 1 million/mL

Round cells
<5 million/mL
questions.learning: The morphology of sperms — The morphology of sperms is the best parameter to assess male infertility. Characterization of normal sperm morphology shows improved correlation with fertilization rates during IVF cycles.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following are true about neonatal cholestasis, except?
options: Biliary atresia is the most common cause of neonatal cholestasis
Kasai procedure should be done within 90 days
HIDA scan is the best investigation for diagnosis
Can be differentiated from other differential diagnoses by biopsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kasai procedure should be done within 90 days

Neonatal cholestasis is defined as conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in early infancy and requires prompt evaluation, with biliary atresia being the most important cause to rule out.

• Early diagnosis is critical because Kasai portoenterostomy is most effective when performed before 6–8 weeks of age (60 days is the usual cut-off)
• HIDA scan helps assess bile flow but is not definitive
• Liver biopsy is a key investigation to differentiate biliary atresia from other causes (e.g., neonatal hepatitis)
questions.learning: Kasai procedure should be done within 90 days Neonatal cholestasis is defined as conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in early infancy and requires prompt evaluation, with biliary atresia being the most important cause to rule out. • Early diagnosis is critical…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What remnant is derived from the structure marked in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nucleus pulposus

The nucleus pulposus is derived from the notochord (marked by the arrow).

The nucleus pulposus is a mucoid, gel-like substance that lies between the centre of the intervertebral disc and its posterior surface. At birth, it is almost completely gelatinous and liquid, but as the individual ages, it becomes less differentiated from the remainder of the intervertebral disc, becoming less hydrated and increasingly fibrous.

The notochord is derived from the epiblast cells. Epiblast cells from the primitive knot region of the primitive streak multiply and pass cranially in the midline between the ectoderm and endoderm. They undergo several stages of rearrangement to form the notochord. During the initial stages of neurulation, the notochord induces overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate.

During vertebral column development, the notochord gradually regresses, with its cells persisting as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.

Rarely, these notochordal remnants may give rise to slow-growing tumors known as chordomas. These malignant bone tumors arise from residual embryonic notochordal tissue and are usually located along the axial midline. It is the most common primary malignancy of the sacrum.

Pearl PF0426: Derivatives of Mesoderm

Mesoderm derivatives

Paraxial mesoderm

• Skeletal muscles of the trunk, limbs, head, and neck
• Extraocular muscles
• Intrinsic muscles of the tongue
• Bones: Vertebrae, ribs
• Dermis of Skin
• Duramater

Intermediate mesoderm

• Urinary system: Kidneys, ureters, trigone of the urinary bladder
• Dorsal part of prostatic urethra (males)
• Gonads: Testes and ovaries
• Genital ducts
• Adrenal cortex

Lateral plate mesoderm

• Bones: Sternum, limb bones
• Serous membranes of body cavities: Pleura, pericardium, peritoneum
• GIT layers: Lamina propria, muscularis mucosae, submucosa, muscularis externa, adventitia
• Blood cells: Microglia, Kupffer cells
• Cardiovascular system
• Lymphatic system
• Laryngeal cartilages

Pearl PF0425: Neural crest derivatives

Neural

Mesenchymal

All ganglions

Connective tissue and bones of the face and skull

All enteric plexus

Dermis of the head and face

Schwann cells and Satellite glial cells

Odontoblasts (Dentine)

Adrenal Medulla

Arachnoid and Piamater

Parafolliular C cells of Thyroid

Conotruncal septum in the heart

Melanoblast/Melanocytes (except Retinal Pigment Epithelium)
questions.learning: Nucleus pulposus — The nucleus pulposus is derived from the notochord (marked by the arrow). The nucleus pulposus is a mucoid, gel-like substance that lies between the centre of the intervertebral disc and its posterior surface.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the following flowchart representing natural history of disease, The duration between point A to B is called as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Screening time

The period between the first possible time of detection (point A) and the first critical point of diagnosis (point B) is called Screening time.

The period between the first possible time of detection (point A) and the usual time of diagnosis (point C) is called lead time.

Pearl PF0975: Lead Time in Screening

Lead time is the advantage gained by screening which is the period between diagnosis by early detection and diagnosis by other means.
questions.learning: Screening time — The period between the first possible time of detection (point A) and the first critical point of diagnosis (point B) is called Screening time.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 38-year-old man falls directly onto the front of his knee while descending stairs. He presents with acute knee pain and swelling and is unable to perform an active straight-leg raise or actively extend the knee. Which of the following injuries is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Patellar tendon rupture

A patellar tendon rupture disrupts the extensor mechanism of the knee, preventing force transmission from the quadriceps muscle to the tibia. As a result, the patient is unable to actively extend the knee or perform a straight-leg raise, which is the key clinical finding.

Patients typically present with:

• Sudden pain after a fall or forceful quadriceps contraction
• Inability to actively extend the knee
• Inability to perform a straight-leg raise
• Patella alta (high-riding patella) on lateral knee X-ray due to loss of distal patellar attachment
• Palpable defect below the patella

Why not the other options?

• A. Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear: Presents with a twisting injury, immediate hemarthrosis, instability ("giving way"), and a positive Lachman or anterior drawer test. Active knee extension is preserved.
• C. Meniscal tear: Causes joint-line tenderness, locking, clicking, and pain with twisting movements, but patients can usually extend the knee unless mechanical locking occurs.
• D. Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear: Commonly results from a dashboard injury or fall onto a flexed knee, causing posterior knee instability and a positive posterior drawer test. The extensor mechanism remains intact.

High-yield pearl

• Loss of active knee extension = Injury to the extensor mechanism.
• Think of:

• Quadriceps tendon rupture → Usually older patients (>40 years); patella baja (low-riding patella).
• Patellar tendon rupture → Usually younger patients (<40 years); patella alta (high-riding patella).

Exam tip:

• A patient who cannot perform a straight-leg raise almost always has a disruption of the quadriceps tendon, patella, or patellar tendon rather than an isolated ligament or meniscal injury.
questions.learning: Patellar tendon rupture — A patellar tendon rupture disrupts the extensor mechanism of the knee, preventing force transmission from the quadriceps muscle to the tibia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure after high grade fever. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diazepam

This is a febrile seizure presenting as a generalized tonic–clonic seizure in a child with high-grade fever. The immediate management is benzodiazepine administration to abort the seizure.

Diazepam (IV/rectal) is the drug of choice for acute control.

↓

↓

Seizure stops

Phenytoin, valproate, and ethosuximide are not used for immediate termination of febrile seizures.

| Drug | Role | Use

| ---- | ---- | ---

| Diazepam | ⭐ First-line | Acute seizure

| Phenytoin | Second-line | Status epilepticus

| Valproate | Maintenance | Chronic seizures

| Ethosuximide | Specific | Absence seizures

Febrile Seizure-

| Feature | Finding

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In judicial hanging, what is the primary cause of death?
questions.explanation: In the context of forensic medicine, "judicial hanging" is distinct from suicidal hanging because it involves a long drop calculated to break the neck. The primary cause of death is the fracture and dislocation of the upper cervical vertebrae (most classically a C2 fracture, known as the "Hangman’s fracture"), which results in the crushing or complete transection of the spinal cord and lower brainstem. This leads to immediate cessation of respiratory and cardiac functions. Vagal inhibition (Option A), cerebral hypoxia (Option C), and asphyxia (Option D) are common causes of death in cases of "typical" or suicidal hanging where there is no significant drop. In those instances, the pressure of the ligature constricts the carotid arteries or the airway. Judicial hanging is designed to ensure a rapid, certain death through mechanical disruption of the central nervous system rather than slow strangulation
questions.learning: In the context of forensic medicine, "judicial hanging" is distinct from suicidal hanging because it involves a long drop calculated to break the neck.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A boy presented with a fever and chills. Rapid test was positive for specific antigen HRP-2. Which of the following species of Plasmodium is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Plasmodium falciparum

The given clinical scenario and the HRP-2 positivity are suggestive of P. falciparum malaria.

Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by the Plasmodium species transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito. It is characterized by many nonspecific symptoms, including but not limited to tachycardia, tachypnea, chills, malaise, fatigue, diaphoresis (sweating), and headache. The fever of malaria is characterized by periodicity depending on the infective Plasmodium species. The fever returns every other day for P. vivax, P. ovale, and P. falciparum, and every three days for P. malariae.

The newer tests include rapid antigen detection tests that employ immunochromatographic methods. The parasite-F test is one of them. This test is based on the detection of histidine-rich protein-2 (HRP-2) which is produced only by the asexual forms of Plasmodium falciparum that are present on the surface of RBCs. The test strip has monoclonal antibodies against the HRP-2 antigen. This test has very high sensitivity and specificity. The disadvantages of the test include that it can detect only Plasmodium falciparum HRP-2 antigen but not the other three species of Plasmodium. Also, the test remains positive until 2 weeks after the cure.

Another diagnostic test of significance is the dual antigen test. This test detects both the parasite lactate dehydrogenase of trophozoites and gametocytes of all the Plasmodium species and HRP-2 produced by P. falciparum simultaneously.
questions.learning: Plasmodium falciparum — The given clinical scenario and the HRP-2 positivity are suggestive of P. falciparum malaria. Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by the Plasmodium species transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the current ideal total fertility rate (TFR) in India?
questions.explanation: In demography, a Total Fertility Rate (TFR) of "2.1" is known as the "replacement level fertility". This is the ideal rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, without migration. Achieving a TFR of 2.1 has been the primary goal of India’s National Population Policy since 2000. A TFR higher than 2.1 (like Options A and B) leads to population growth. A TFR lower than 2.1 (like Option D) eventually leads to a shrinking population. According to recent data (NFHS-5), India has actually achieved a national TFR of 2.0, which is below the replacement level. However, the "ideal" or "target" replacement level remains globally recognized as 2.1. Reaching this target is essential for long-term socio-economic stability and ensuring that the dependency ratio of the country remains balanced as the population ages
questions.learning: In demography, a Total Fertility Rate (TFR) of "2.1" is known as the "replacement level fertility". This is the ideal rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, without migration.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 24-year-old female comes to emergency with complaints of acute abdominal pain. The attending physician wants to get an abdominal X-ray done for the same. What does the “10 day rule” advise regarding x-ray exposure for women of child bearing age refer to?
options: A gap of less than 10 days between 2 successive X rays.
Avoid non urgent X-rays within 10 days post menstruation.
Perform X-rays during the first 10 days of the menstrual cycle.
X-rays should be avoided 10 days before menstruation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Perform X-rays during the first 10 days of the menstrual cycle.

• The “10-day rule” recommends that non-urgent radiological examinations involving ionizing radiation in women of reproductive age should be performed within the first 10 days of the menstrual cycle (counting from the first day of menstruation).
• This timing minimizes the risk of irradiating an unrecognized early pregnancy, as ovulation and potential conception are unlikely during this period.
questions.learning: Perform X-rays during the first 10 days of the menstrual cycle. • The “10-day rule” recommends that non-urgent radiological examinations involving ionizing radiation in women of reproductive age should be performed within the first 10 days of the menstrual…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy has non-blanching rashes on the legs and buttocks as seen in the picture. He also complains of joint pains, abdominal pain, vomiting, and blood in the stool. Lab investigations revealed normal platelet count and urine analysis shows haematuria +++ and proteinuria +. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP)

This clinical scenario describes Henoch Schonlein purpura.

Features of Henoch Schonlein purpura (HSP):

* Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) is a common small vessel vasculitis in childhood.

* It is characterized by a purpuric rash and commonly accompanied by arthritis and abdominal pain.

* About half of the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, which vary from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria to severe, progressive glomerulonephritis: The pathogenesis of HSP nephritis appears to be mediated by the deposition of polymeric immunoglobulin A (IgA) in glomeruli.

* Laboratory studies generally show a mild leukocytosis, a normal platelet count, and occasionally eosinophilia. Serum complement components are normal.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A doctor receives two separate court summons on the same day: one to appear as a witness in a murder trial, and another to provide an expert opinion in a case of medical negligence involving wrong leg amputation. According to legal priority, which case should the doctor attend first?
options: Appearance for providing opinion on negligence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Appearance for murder case

When a doctor receives multiple court summons on the same day, priority is given to criminal cases involving serious offences (e.g., murder) over civil or expert opinion cases.

• Hierarchy of legal priority:

• Criminal cases (especially grave offences like murder) take precedence
• Over civil cases or expert testimony (e.g., medical negligence)

• Reason:

• Criminal cases involve state prosecution and serious offences against society

Doctor’s responsibility:

• Attend the higher-priority court (murder case)
• Inform the other court in advance and request adjournment

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a fish bone impacted in the pyriform sinus. During its removal, an accidental nerve injury occurs. Which nerve is most likely to be damaged in this situation?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN) provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords, the pharynx, and the pyriform sinus. It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane along with the superior laryngeal artery. During procedures in the pyriform sinus, this purely sensory nerve is at high risk of accidental injury due to its close proximity. Damage to this nerve results in the loss of the protective cough reflex in the supraglottic region, significantly predisposing the patient to aspiration. The recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option A) supplies motor innervation to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles but is not typically exposed during pyriform sinus surgery. The glossopharyngeal nerve (Option B) provides sensation to the oropharynx and posterior tongue rather than the pyriform sinus. The external branch (Option D) is located more superficially and provides motor supply to the cricothyroid muscle
questions.learning: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (IBSLN) provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords, the pharynx, and the pyriform sinus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What does the number 9 in the provided diagram on hypertension represent?
questions.explanation: The diagram refers to the "Rule of Halves" in hypertension epidemiology, which highlights the significant gaps in the care continuum. According to this rule: half of the people with hypertension in a community are diagnosed; half of those diagnosed are treated; and half of those treated are adequately treated to reach their target blood pressure. In standard instructional diagrams illustrating these nested proportions, the innermost segment (often labeled with a specific number like 9 in this session) represents the small percentage of the total hypertensive population that is adequately treated and controlled. Option A (diagnosed/untreated) and Option C (inadequately treated) represent larger segments of the population falling out of the "ideal" care path. Option B is an intermediate stage. Public health efforts aim to "break" the rule of halves by improving screening, initiating early treatment, and ensuring adherence to reach therapeutic goals. Improving this final controlled proportion is the most effective way to reduce the population burden of strokes and heart attacks
questions.learning: The diagram refers to the "Rule of Halves" in hypertension epidemiology, which highlights the significant gaps in the care continuum. According to this rule: half of the people with hypertension in a community are diagnosed; half of those diagnosed are…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the principle behind the wound-healing procedure shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Negative pressure wound therapy

The given image shows negative pressure wound therapy using a vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) device to promote healing in chronic wounds.

Principle: An intermittent negative pressure of -125 mmHg hastens debridement and formation of granulation tissue in chronic wounds.

Indications: Chronic wounds (such as diabetic foot ulcers, stage III and IV pressure ulcers), traumatic wounds, flaps and grafts, and dehisced incisions.

Contraindications:

1. Exposed vital structures (organs, blood vessels, or vascular grafts)
2. Preexisting infection
3. Inadequate debridement of devitalized soft tissue or bone increases the risk of infection.
4. The presence of malignancy (Marjolin’s ulcer).
5. An allergic reaction towards the adhesive used to maintain the vacuum seal.

Though not an absolute contraindication, there is no appreciable benefit for ischemic wounds.
questions.learning: Negative pressure wound therapy — The given image shows negative pressure wound therapy using a vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) device to promote healing in chronic wounds.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT typically used for antenatal screening?
questions.explanation: In the context of antenatal screening and diagnosis, we categorize tests by the source of fetal genetic material. While (A), (B), and (C) are standard sources of fetal cells, peripheral lymphocytes from the mother are not used because they belong to the mother, not the fetus. Why (D) is the Correct Answer: Antenatal screening for genetic disorders (like Down Syndrome) requires fetal DNA. While modern Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT) uses maternal blood, it analyzes cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) floating in the plasma, not the mother's own peripheral lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are part of the maternal immune system and do not carry the fetal genetic blueprint. Why the other options are used: (A) Cord blood: Obtained via cordocentesis (after 18 weeks), it provides rapid fetal karyotyping and is used to screen for fetal anemia or infections. (B) Amniotic fluid: Obtained via amniocentesis (15–20 weeks), it contains shed fetal cells (amniocytes) used for definitive chromosomal analysis. (C) Chorionic villi: Obtained via CVS (10–13 weeks), these placental tissues share the same genetic makeup as the fetus and are excellent for early screening of metabolic or genetic defects
questions.learning: In the context of antenatal screening and diagnosis, we categorize tests by the source of fetal genetic material. While (A), (B), and (C) are standard sources of fetal cells, peripheral lymphocytes from the mother are not used because they belong to the…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In relation to which wall of the orbit is the canaliculi that opens into the lacrimal sac present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medial wall

The canaliculi that open into the lacrimal sac are present in relation to the medial wall of the orbit.

Anatomy

The lacrimal drainage system consists of the following structures:

* The puncta are openings on the lid margin.

* Each canaliculus (superior and inferior) has two parts:

* Vertical (2 mm)

* Horizontal (8 mm)

* The superior and inferior canaliculi usually unite to form the common canaliculus, which opens into the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac.

* A small flap of mucosa (Rosenmüller valve) overhangs the junction of the common canaliculus and the lacrimal sac and prevents the reflux of tears into the canaliculi.

* The lacrimal sac is 10–12 mm long and lies in the lacrimal fossa. The lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla separate the lacrimal sac from the middle meatus of the nasal cavity.

* The nasolacrimal duct is 12–18 mm long and is directed downwards, backward, and laterally.

* Inferior meatus: Nasolacrimal duct, guarded by the valve of Hasner

* Middle meatus: Frontal sinus, maxillary sinus, anterior ethmoidal sinus. All these together form the osteo-meatal complex or Picadle’s circle.

* Superior meatus: Posterior ethmoidal sinus

* Sphenoethmoidal recess: Sphenoid sinus

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In the context of solid organ transplantation, which transplanted organ has the highest rate of rejection?
questions.explanation: In the field of solid organ transplantation, the small intestine is associated with the highest incidence of rejection among all listed organs. This is primarily because the intestine is an "immunologically active" organ containing a large amount of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) and a high density of donor immune cells (Graft-versus-Host risk). Furthermore, the constant exposure to a diverse luminal microbiome increases the risk of infection and inflammation, which triggers the recipient's immune system. Lungs (Option A) also have a high rejection rate compared to the heart or kidneys, but the intestine remains the most challenging. The Kidney (Option C) and Heart (Option D) have relatively lower rates of acute rejection due to established immunosuppression protocols and the lower load of lymphoid tissue. Because of this high risk, intestinal transplant recipients require extremely high doses of immunosuppressive drugs and vigilant monitoring via frequent endoscopic biopsies to detect early signs of rejection
