questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs has dual activity against hepatitis B and HIV both?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tenofovir

Tenofovir is an acyclic nucleotide analog used in the treatment of hepatitis B and HIV.

The preferred first-line regimen for managing HIV-1 and hepatitis B co-infection is tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir.

Tenofovir is an acyclic nucleotide analog that is used as first-line therapy for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B and lamivudine-resistant chronic hepatitis B. It is also a potent antiretroviral agent used in the treatment of HIV infection.

In patients with hepatitis B, tenofovir is more potent at suppressing HBV DNA and is active against both wild-type and lamivudine-resistant HBV. It is given as an oral once-daily dose of 300 mg for 48 weeks. Tenofovir therapy provides histologic improvement, reduction in fibrosis score, and regression of cirrhosis in patients. Side effects include acute renal failure and low blood phosphate levels.

Tenofovir, an Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) is used to treat HIV by inhibiting the reverse transcriptase enzyme. It converts to tenofovir diphosphate in cells, competing with dATP to incorporate into viral DNA. This causes chain termination due to the absence of a 3'-hydroxyl group, halting viral DNA synthesis and reducing replication.

Other options :

Option B: Nevirapine is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). Nevirapine PLUS twice-daily zidovudine is administered for six weeks, after which either nevirapine is given as a single drug or the same combination is continued for another 6 weeks in high-risk infants with mothers who are:

* HIV positive, not on ART

* Mother diagnosed with HIV 72 hours after delivery.

* On ART with viral load > 1000 copies/mL

* With unknown viral load, hasn't been on ART for >4 consecutive weeks.

Option C: Abacavir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) approved for the treatment of HIV-1 infectionThe most serious adverse effect is a hypersensitivity syndrome characterized by fever, maculopapular rash, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal upset, malaise, and fatigue.

Option D: Enfuvirtide is an entry (fusion) inhibitor that binds to the transmembrane gp41 of HIV-1 and blocks its entry into the host cells. It is the only approved parenteral antiretroviral drug, and therefore, injection-site reactions like pain, erythema, induration, and nodules/cysts development are most frequently seen.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not reversed with the administration of glycopyrolate?
options: Muscle weakness due to neuromuscular blockade
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Muscle weakness due to neuromuscular blockade

Glycopyrrolate can reverse all conditions except muscle weakness caused by neuromuscular blockade.

Anticholinergic drugs like glycopyrrolate and atropine are not used to reverse neuromuscular blockade. They only attenuate the undesirable muscarinic effects of anticholinesterase reversal agents.

Reversal agents commonly used in clinical practice:

* Cholinesterase inhibitors - Neostigmine (most common), edrophonium, and pyridostigmine.

* Sugammadex, a cyclodextrin, is the first selective relaxant binding agent for rocuronium and vecuronium.

* L-cysteine causes the inactivation of gantacurium.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: All of the following conditions will have an elevated JVP that rises with deep inspiration except?
questions.explanation: An elevated Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP) that paradoxical rises during deep inspiration is known as Kussmaul's sign. Normally, JVP falls during inspiration as the negative intrathoracic pressure sucks blood into the right heart. Kussmaul's sign indicates impaired filling of the right ventricle. It is a classic finding in Constrictive pericarditis (Option B), Restrictive cardiomyopathy (Option D), and severe right heart failure such as Cor pulmonale (Option C) or right ventricular infarction. HOCM (Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy) (Option A) primarily involves the left ventricle; while it can cause an elevated JVP with a prominent 'a' wave, it does not characteristically cause Kussmaul's sign. HOCM is more commonly associated with a bisferiens pulse and a heaving apex. Differentiating these signs is vital for localizing the pathology to the pericardium, the right heart, or the left-sided conduction and muscle system

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the health insurance package provided for an eligible family per year, in the Ayushman Bharat scheme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 5 Lakhs per family per year

Under the Ayushman Bharat scheme Government provides health insurance cover of upto 5 Lakhs per family, per year.

Ayushman Bharat-National Health Protection Mission: To build a comprehensive need-based health care service. Dr R.S. Sharma is the Chief Executive Officer of the AB- NHPM.

Components: The target of the two initiatives mentioned below are to build a New India 2022.

* Creation of 1,50,000 Health and Wellness Centres- These centres will provide Comprehensive Primary Health Care (CPHC), covering both maternal and child health services and non-communicable diseases, including free essential drugs and diagnostic services. The first Health and Wellness Centre was launched by the Prime Minister at Jangla, Bijapur, Chhatisgarh on 14 April 2018.

* The second component is the National Health Protection Mission (NHPM) which provides health protection cover to poor and vulnerable families. The Health and Wellness Centres will play a critical role in creating awareness about AB-NHPM, screening for non-communicable diseases, follow-up of hospitalisation cases among others.

Beneficiary Level:

* Government provides health insurance cover of up to Rs. 5,00,000 per family per year.

* More than 10.74 crore poor and vulnerable families (approximately 50 crore beneficiaries) covered across the country.

* All families listed in the SECC database as per defined criteria will be covered. No cap on family size and age of members.

* Priority to girl child, women and and senior citizens.

* Free treatment available at all public and empaneled private hospitals in times of need.

* Covers secondary and tertiary care hospitalization.

* 1,350 medical packages covering surgery, medical and day care treatments, cost of medicines and diagnostics.

* All pre-existing diseases covered. Hospitals cannot deny treatment.

* Cashless and paperless access to quality health care services.

* Hospitals will not be allowed to charge any additional money from beneficiaries for the treatment.

* Can reach out for information, assistance, complaints and grievances to a 24X7 helpline number - 14555

Ayushman Bharat Diwas is being celebrated across the country on April 30.

On 12 December 2012, the United Nations General Assembly endorsed a resolution urging countries to accelerate progress toward universal health coverage (UHC) – the idea that everyone, everywhere should have access to quality, affordable health care - as an essential priority for international development. International Universal Health Coverage Day aims to raise awareness of the need for strong and resilient health systems and universal health coverage

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old patient had a tooth extraction three days back. He now presents with a mass in the submandibular region which is otherwise asymptomatic. There is no ulcer on the oral mucosa. On drainage of the discharge, it was foul-smelling with a lot of yellow granules. They showed gram-positive filamentous rods on grams staining. What is the most likely implicated pathogen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Actinomycetes israelli

This is a case of Cervicofacial actinomycosis caused by Actinomyces israeli. It presents as a painless nodule that indurates with purulent discharge that contains sulfur granules giving it a yellow color. Sulfur granules are composed of a matrix of bacteria, calcium phosphate, and host tissue.

Actinomycosis is an indolent, slowly progressive suppurative and granulomatous infection that produces pyogenic lesions with interconnecting sinus tracts that contain sulfur granules. It is an anaerobic or microaerophilic bacteria.

It presents as one of the following clinical types:

• Cervicofacial actinomycosis- (most common site) fluctuant mass in the jaw area producing draining fistulas. (lumpy jaw)
• Thoracic actinomycosis- pulmonary infection with fever, cough, and purulent sputum. It usually occurs following aspiration or trauma leading to inoculation of the infective material.
• Abdominal actinomycosis- following ruptured appendix or ulcer. It may involve multiple organs.
• Pelvic actinomycosis- due to the colonization of intrauterine contraceptive devices.
• Actinomycosis can spread to bones and surrounding tissue and produce multiple discharging sinuses.

Diagnosis is by Gram staining of sulfur granules that shows a dense network of thin gram-positive filaments, surrounded by club-shaped structures. (sunray appearance). Culture shows the "molar tooth" appearance of the colonies. On solid media, A. israeli produces spidery colonies.

Penicillin G is the drug of choice and the duration of therapy is between 6-12 months. The other drugs that can be used include amoxicillin, erythromycin, tetracycline, doxycycline, clindamycin, and minocycline.

The image below shows the "molar tooth" appearance of the Actinomyces colonies.

The image below shows gram-positive filaments of Actinomyces.

• Characterized by flexion of the upper extremities at the elbow and extensor hyperactivity in the lower extremities.
• The flexion can be explained by active rubrospinal excitation of flexor muscles in the upper extremities; the hyperextension of lower extremities is due to the same changes that occur after midcollicular decerebration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman with a history of beta- thalassemia develops anxiety, hypotension, and fever during a blood transfusion. What is the next appropriate step in managing this transfusion reaction?
options: Stop the blood transfusion and restart after stabilization
Continue the blood transfusion and perform an ECG
Investigate for clerical errors in the blood transfusion process
Administer corticosteroids and monitor vital signs
questions.explanation: The patient develops fever, hypotension, and anxiety during transfusion, which strongly suggests an acute transfusion reaction (possibly acute hemolytic or severe febrile reaction). This is a medical emergency. The first and most critical step in managing any suspected transfusion reaction is to immediately stop the transfusion to prevent further exposure to the offending blood product. After stopping: 1. Maintain IV access with normal saline 2. Assess vitals and stabilize the patient 3. Send blood samples and the transfused unit for investigation Once the patient is stabilized and the cause is identified, further transfusion (if needed) can be considered cautiously. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Continue transfusion → Dangerous; worsens reaction (C) Clerical check → Important but not the first step (D) Corticosteroids → May be used later, not initial action

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the marked bond:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydrogen bond

The marked bond represents a hydrogen bond between thymine and adenine.

The complementary nitrogenous bases of the 2 strands of the DNA double helix are linked by hydrogen bonds. Adenine and thymine are linked by two hydrogen bonds (A=T) whereas three hydrogen bonds are present between cytidine and guanine (C≡G). Van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions are present between the stacked adjacent base pairs.

A β-N-glycosidic bond is present between the nitrogenous base and deoxyribose sugar. C1 of deoxyribose/ribose sugar is joined covalently to N1 of pyrimidines and N9 of purines by β-N-glycosidic bond. An ester bond is present between the sugar and phosphate group of the same nucleotide. An acid anhydride bond is present between two phosphate groups.

A polymer of nucleotides is joined by 3’-5’ phosphodiester bond. The bond is present between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate group of another.
questions.learning: Hydrogen bond — The marked bond represents a hydrogen bond between thymine and adenine. The complementary nitrogenous bases of the 2 strands of the DNA double helix are linked by hydrogen bonds.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following condition is depicted in the given CT image?
questions.explanation: (CAH) The CT image shows bilaterally enlarged adrenal glands with a lobulated / cerebriform appearance, which is a classic radiological finding of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. In CAH, chronic ACTH stimulation leads to diffuse adrenal hyperplasia, typically involving both adrenal glands symmetrically. (B) Hepatitis – Causes diffuse liver changes, not adrenal enlargement. (D) Cirrhosis – Shows a shrunken, nodular liver with portal hypertension features (splenomegaly, ascites), not this appearance

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: On indirect ophthalmoscopy the examiner noticed a concave shaped out bulging of the outer layer in the posterior part of the eye. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Posterior Staphyloma

Posterior staphyloma is a localized outpouching of the posterior sclera, commonly seen in pathological (high) myopia.

• Concave bulging of posterior segment on ophthalmoscopy
• Associated with axial elongation of eyeball
• Leads to progressive visual deterioration

Pathophysiology:

• Thinning and stretching of sclera → outward bulging of posterior pole
• Predisposes to retinal degeneration, maculopathy, and retinal detachment

Why not other options:

B. Hypermetropia

• Short eyeball → no posterior bulging
• Retina lies anterior, not outpouched

C. Astigmatism

• Due to unequal corneal curvature
• No posterior segment abnormality

D. Corneal ulcer

• Anterior segment pathology
• Seen on cornea, not on fundus/ophthalmoscopy

questions.text: Which of the following features are characteristic of the Bezold–Jarisch reflex? 1. Hypotension 2. Bradycardia 3. Hypopnea 4. Tachycardia Which among the options are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

The Bezold–Jarisch reflex is triggered by ventricular mechanoreceptor stimulation, often during inferior wall ischemia. Classic triad-

• Bradycardia

• Hypotension

• Hypopnea (reduced respiration)

It causes increased vagal tone leading to bradycardia and hypotension.

There is also hypopnea due to reflex inhibition of respiration.

The Bezold–Jarisch reflex increases vagal tone, which causes: Bradycardia

Tachycardia is not a feature of this reflex.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which immunoglobulin mediates the clinical features of facial swelling, itching, and hypotension observed after a bee sting in a patient presenting to the emergency department?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of facial swelling (angioedema), itching (urticaria), and hypotension following a bee sting represent a severe Type I hypersensitivity reaction, also known as anaphylaxis. This immediate allergic response is exclusively mediated by Immunoglobulin E (IgE). Upon re-exposure to the bee venom allergen, the allergen cross-links IgE antibodies already bound to the surface of mast cells and basophils. This triggers the rapid release of inflammatory mediators, most notably histamine, which causes systemic vasodilation and increased capillary permeability. IgA (Option A) is involved in mucosal immunity. IgM (Option C) is the primary responder in acute infections. IgG (Option D) provides long-term immunity and is involved in Type II and III hypersensitivities. Therefore, because IgE is the only immunoglobulin class that binds specifically to high-affinity receptors on mast cells to drive acute allergic crises, it is the definitive answer

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted in a school where information regarding vaccination status, gender of students, and their pain scale scores was collected. Mention the types of data taken in the same sequence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nominal, Nominal, Ordinal

The vaccination status and gender are classified as nominal data, since they represent categories without any order. The pain scale is an ordinal variable, because the numbers indicate ranking of severity but No size interval is defined.

Data always forms one of four scales of measurement – nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio scales (mnemonic: NOIR):

Nominal Scale Data

Ordinal Scale Data

Interval Scale Data

Ratio Scale Data

Example

Male/female; red/green; sub-urban/rural

Students ranked 1st/2nd/3rd in their class.

A customer feedback survey using terms like very good, good, poor and very poor or the Likert Scale.

Severity of a disease as mild, moderate, severe

Measurements on the celsius scale.

Pulse rate;

Notes

Have no quantitative value.

They have no order or ratio.

Arranged in a meaningful order.

No size interval is defined

Arranged in a meaningful order with a well defined size interval.

Example: Temperature in Celsius. If temperature in A is 40 deg Celsius and that in B is 20 deg Celsius, then A is 20 deg Celsius hotter than B (taking difference)

Does not have an absolute zero.

For example, Celsius scale has no such thing as “no temperature”. So the value cannot be zero.

Arranged in a meaningful order with a well defined size interval.

Eg: A pulse rate has well defined intervals and is meaningful in comparison. A 100/min pulse is exactly twice of 50 beats/min.

Has an absolute zero.

Eg: There can be a value of zero for pulse.

Type

Qualitative

Qualitative

Quantitative

Quantitative

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which monoclonal antibody is used in cancer treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rituximab

Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody and is used in the treatment of lymphomas.

* Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 B-cell antigen. CD20 is found in cells from the pre–B cell stage through its terminal differentiation to plasma cells and is expressed in 90% of B-cell neoplasms.

* Monoclonal antibody binding to CD20 generates transmembrane signals that produce autophosphorylation and activation of serine/tyrosine protein kinases, induction of c-Myc oncogene expression, and expression of major histocompatibility complex class II molecules.

* Rituximab is approved as a single agent for relapsed indolent lymphomas and significantly enhances response and survival in combination with chemotherapy for the initial treatment of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma(DLBCL).

* It remains effective in patients who relapse after initial treatment with rituximab-based combinations.

* Rituximab improves response rates when added to combination chemotherapy for other indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphomas (NHLs), including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, Waldenström macroglobulinemia, and marginal zone lymphomas.

Note:

Monoclonal antibodies recognize the extracellular domain of the EGFR, inhibit ligand-induced signalling, and can elicit an immune response. Cetuximab is a recombinant, chimeric human/mouse IgG1 antibody that binds to EGFR and prevents ligand-dependent signalling and receptor dimerization, thereby blocking cell growth and survival signals. It is used to treat patients with metastatic colon cancers and Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma(HNSCC)
questions.learning: Rituximab Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody and is used in the treatment of lymphomas. * Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that targets the CD20 B-cell antigen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Hormone responsible for breast pain during breastfeeding is:
questions.explanation: Breast pain during breastfeeding, often associated with the milk-ejection reflex, is primarily mediated by oxytocin. Oxytocin causes the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli, leading to the forceful movement of milk into the ducts, a process known as galactokinesis. While prolactin (Option B) is essential for lactogenesis (milk production) and galactopoiesis (maintenance of milk production), it is not the hormone responsible for the mechanical ejection or the associated "let-down" pain. Estrogen (Option C) and Progesterone (Option D) are vital for mamogenesis (breast growth and development) during pregnancy but actually inhibit the action of prolactin on the breasts until after delivery. The release of oxytocin is triggered by infant suckling through a neuroendocrine reflex arc involving the posterior pituitary gland. Understanding these specific hormonal roles is critical for troubleshooting breastfeeding challenges and managing common issues like painful engorgement or ineffective let-down

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding teeth features and ethnicity?
options: In Africanoids the cusps of molars are wide and deep and shovel shaped cusps in incisors
Upper third molar is most commonly absent in Mongolians
Prominent lingual ridge and labial ridge in mongols
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. In Africanoids the cusps of molars are wide and deep and shovel shaped cusps in incisors

The cusps of molars are wide and deep and cusps of incisors are shovel-shaped in Mongoloid races.

Africanoid races tend to have large teeth and often have more cusps on their molars, even up to eight, with two lingual cusps on the mandibular first premolars as an additional common finding.

In Caucasian races, the lateral incisors in the upper jaw are usually smaller than the central. They also have long pointed canine roots. Small nodules on the lingual surface of maxillary molars, called Carabelli’s cusp are most common in Caucasian races.

In mongoloid teeth, enamel pearls and small nodules of enamel on the tooth surface, are much more frequent. The condition of bull-tooth or taurodontism is most common in Mongoloid people. The pulp cavity of molars is wide and deep, and the roots are fused and bent. A congenital lack of the third upper molar is most commonly seen. The lingual and labial ridges are more prominent.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman who has recently delivered a baby wishes to avoid pregnancy for the next three years. Which contraceptive method would be the most suitable choice for her?
questions.explanation: For a postpartum woman seeking reliable, long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) for a duration of three years, the progesterone-releasing Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD), such as Mirena, is the most appropriate choice (Option B). These devices are safe for breast feeding mothers as they do not contain estrogen, which can interfere with milk production. They offer high efficacy and can remain in place for up to 5–8 years, covering the patient's three-year goal easily. The barrier method (Option A) has a higher failure rate and is less convenient for long-term use. Injectable progesterone (Option C) requires dosing every 3 months, making it less "long-acting" and reliable than an IUD. Lactational amenorrhea (Option D) is only reliable for the first six months postpartum if exclusive breastfeeding is practiced. Therefore, the IUCD provides the best balance of safety, duration, and efficacy
questions.learning: For a postpartum woman seeking reliable, long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) for a duration of three years, the progesterone-releasing Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD), such as Mirena, is the most appropriate choice (Option B).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following substance, facilitate the absorption of dietary iron?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin C

Vitamin C reduces the ferric iron to its ferrous form, thereby helping in the process of absorption of dietary iron from the intestine.

Vitamin C deficiency causes microcytic-hypochromic anemia due to

* Decreased absorption of iron

* Decreased hydroxylation of proline and lysine, which results in defective collagen synthesis and bleeding manifestations.

Note:

Alcohol and fructose also enhance iron absorption.

However, the absorption of both inorganic and heme iron is impaired by calcium. So, a glass of milk with a meal significantly reduces iron availability.

Vitamin C toxicity (>2000 mg/ day): Iron overload can be seen.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which among the following statements is true about keratosis obturans?
options: Failure of migration of desquamated epithelium along posterior meatal wall
Widening of meatus and facial nerve palsy might be seen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

All of the above statements are true regarding keratosis obturans.

Keratosis obturans occurs due to failure of migration of desquamated epithelial cells along the posterior meatal wall (Option A).

It is usually seen between the ages of 5-20 years and is commonly unilateral. Clinical features include severe otalgia and difficulty in hearing. It is associated with systemic conditions like bronchiectasis and chronic sinusitis (Option C).

On otoscopic examination, there is a thickening of the tympanic membrane and a keratin plug appearing like a pearly white mass occluding the canal. The keratin that is shed from the entire circumference of the deep ear canal appears to have an onion skin arrangement. There is also hyperemia of canal skin, sometimes with ulcerations and granulations.

Sometimes, the extent of bone erosion is such that it leaves the facial nerve exposed to injury and subsequent paralysis (Option B). Extensive erosion of the bone can also result in automastoidectomy.

Treatment involves the removal of the plug by syringing or instrumentation. Any recurrence can be prevented with the use of keratolytic such as 2% salicylic acid.
questions.learning: All of the above All of the above statements are true regarding keratosis obturans. Keratosis obturans occurs due to failure of migration of desquamated epithelial cells along the posterior meatal wall (Option A).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a rate-limiting enzyme of HMP pathway?
questions.explanation: The Hexose Monophosphate (HMP) shunt, or pentose phosphate pathway, is essential for generating NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate. The rate-limiting and primary regulated enzyme of this pathway is Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD). It catalyzes the irreversible oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone, while reducing to . Glucose-6-phosphatase (Option A) is the terminal enzyme of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in the liver. Phosphofructokinase-1 (Option C) is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis. Glycogen phosphorylase (Option D) is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis. G6PD deficiency is the most common enzyme-related genetic disorder worldwide. In red blood cells, NADPH is critical for maintaining glutathione in its reduced state, which protects the cells from oxidative damage. Patients with G6PD deficiency are prone to hemolytic anemia when exposed to oxidative stress from infections, certain fava beans, or drugs like primaquine and sulfonamides. This clinical correlation makes G6PD a high-priority topic in biochemistry
questions.learning: The Hexose Monophosphate (HMP) shunt, or pentose phosphate pathway, is essential for generating NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate. The rate-limiting and primary regulated enzyme of this pathway is Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman experiences unilateral, pulsating headaches associated with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia, with relief in a dark room. Which medication is appropriate for preventing and reducing the frequency of future headache episodes?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms—unilateral pulsating headache, nausea, and photophobia—are diagnostic of migraine. The question asks for a medication to reduce the frequency of future episodes, which indicates prophylactic therapy rather than acute treatment. Propranolol, a non-selective beta-blocker, is one of the first-line agents approved for migraine prophylaxis. It works by modulating thalamocortical excitability and vascular tone. Alprazolam (Option B) and Diazepam (Option C) are benzodiazepines used for anxiety and have no role in preventing migraines. Fluoxetine (Option D) is an SSRI used for depression; while some antidepressants like Amitriptyline are used for migraine, Fluoxetine is not a standard prophylactic choice. Prophylaxis is generally indicated if a patient has more than two to three disabling attacks per month. Patients must be counseled that Propranolol is a preventive measure and will not provide relief during an acute attack. Thus, Propranolol is the most appropriate prophylactic agent listed for this 26-year-old female
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms—unilateral pulsating headache, nausea, and photophobia—are diagnostic of migraine. The question asks for a medication to reduce the frequency of future episodes, which indicates prophylactic therapy rather than acute treatment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with acute pain and swelling of the great toe, and laboratory tests show hyperuricemia. To manage her condition, which enzyme should be inhibited by the chosen medication to lower uric acid levels?
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from an acute attack of gout, caused by hyperuricemia. To long-term reduce uric acid levels and prevent further attacks, the standard pharmacological approach is to inhibit the enzyme Xanthine oxidase. This enzyme is responsible for the final steps of purine catabolism, converting hypoxanthine to xanthine and then xanthine to uric acid. Medications like Allopurinol and Febuxostat work by inhibiting this enzyme, thereby lowering the production of uric acid. Urease (Option A) is a bacterial enzyme not found in humans. Homogentisate oxidase (Option B) is the enzyme deficient in Alkaptonuria. Lysyl oxidase (Option C) is involved in collagen cross-linking. While acute gout is treated with NSAIDs or colchicine, xanthine oxidase inhibitors are the mainstay for chronic urate-lowering therapy. Understanding this biochemical pathway is essential for managing metabolic disorders related to purine metabolism and preventing the painful joint destruction and renal stones associated with chronic gout
questions.learning: The patient is suffering from an acute attack of gout, caused by hyperuricemia. To long-term reduce uric acid levels and prevent further attacks, the standard pharmacological approach is to inhibit the enzyme Xanthine oxidase.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Doppler assessment of which fetal vessel is most useful in detecting fetal anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Middle Cerebral Artery

Middle Cerebral Artery Doppler is the most sensitive non-invasive method to detect fetal anemia, especially in Rh Isoimmunization.

Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) peak systolic velocity >1.5 multiples of median indicates fetal anemia. This non-invasive Doppler technique is the gold standard for monitoring fetal anemia, particularly in Rh isoimmunization cases.

anagement if MCA PSV >1.5 MoM

Next step: Cordocentesis (PUBS) to confirm anemia.

Treatment: Intrauterine fetal blood transfusion.
questions.learning: Middle Cerebral Artery Middle Cerebral Artery Doppler is the most sensitive non-invasive method to detect fetal anemia, especially in Rh Isoimmunization.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following options is considered a high-level disinfectant?
questions.explanation: Glutaraldehyde (e.g., Cidex) is classified as a high-level disinfectant. High-level disinfectants are capable of killing all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, when used for a sufficient contact time (chemosterilant). It is widely used for heat-sensitive medical equipment, such as endoscopes and bronchoscopes. Isopropyl alcohol (Option A) is an intermediate-level disinfectant; it kills most bacteria and viruses but is not sporicidal. Iodophors (Option C), like Povidone-iodine, are also intermediate-level disinfectants used primarily as skin antiseptics. Benzalkonium chloride (Option D) is a quaternary ammonium compound, which is a low-level disinfectant that is ineffective against many viruses and spores. High-level disinfection is the minimum requirement for "semi-critical" items that come into contact with mucous membranes. Because glutaraldehyde has a broad spectrum of activity including spores, it is the correct choice
questions.learning: Glutaraldehyde (e.g., Cidex) is classified as a high-level disinfectant. High-level disinfectants are capable of killing all microorganisms, including bacterial spores, when used for a sufficient contact time (chemosterilant).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with congenital severe sensorineural hearing loss. Imaging shows a normal bony labyrinth, but histopathology reveals degeneration of the organ of Corti and saccule, with preservation of the utricle and semicircular canals. Which of the following inner ear malformations best explains this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scheibe aplasia

Scheibe aplasia (cochleosaccular dysplasia) is the most common congenital membranous labyrinth malformation causing severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss.

Key differentiating points among inner ear malformations:

• Scheibe aplasia: Membranous defect of cochlea + saccule (most common; severe SNHL)
• Mondini dysplasia: Incomplete cochlear development (1.5 turns) with bony abnormality
• Michel aplasia: Complete absence of inner ear (most severe)
• Alexander dysplasia: Basal turn cochlear degeneration → high-frequency hearing loss
questions.learning: Scheibe aplasia Scheibe aplasia (cochleosaccular dysplasia) is the most common congenital membranous labyrinth malformation causing severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 38-year-old woman on combined oral contraceptive pills presents with failure of contraception after starting an antiepileptic drug. The antiepileptic accelerates metabolism of estrogens by induction of cytochrome P450 isoenzymes. Which antiepileptic drug is responsible for this contraceptive failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phenytoin

Why: Phenytoin is a well-known potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (particularly CYP3A4, which metabolizes estrogens and progestins). This induction accelerates the metabolism of oral contraceptive hormones, lowering their plasma levels and leading to contraceptive failure (breakthrough bleeding, unintended pregnancy).

Key mechanism:

• Phenytoin → induces CYP3A4 in the liver → ↑ hepatic metabolism of ethinylestradiol and progestins in OCPs → ↓ hormone bioavailability → loss of contraceptive efficacy
• Women on enzyme-inducing antiepileptics are counseled to use higher-dose OCPs, alternative contraception (IUD, barrier methods), or non-hormonal methods

Other classic enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (same category as phenytoin):

• Carbamazepine
• Phenobarbital
• Primidone

Why not the others:

• A. Valproate — Actually a P450 inhibitor, not an inducer; does not cause OCP failure via this mechanism (and interestingly, OCPs can lower valproate levels via a different mechanism — enhanced glucuronidation).
• C. Levetiracetam — Not significantly metabolized by CYP450; minimal drug interaction profile; does NOT affect OCP efficacy. Often preferred in women of childbearing age for this reason.
• D. Ethosuximide — Used for absence seizures; not a significant P450 inducer; not associated with contraceptive failure.
questions.learning: Phenytoin Why: Phenytoin is a well-known potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (particularly CYP3A4, which metabolizes estrogens and progestins).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is typically the first sign of sexual maturation in females?
questions.explanation: Puberty in females typically follows a well-defined chronological sequence. The first sign of sexual maturation is usually Thelarche (Option B), which refers to the beginning of breast development (breast budding). This typically occurs between ages 8 and 10. This is followed by Pubarche (Option C) or Adrenarche, which is the growth of pubic and axillary hair. The final major milestone is Menarche (Option D), the onset of the first menstrual period, which usually occurs about 2 to 2.5 years after thelarche. "Maturation" (Option A) is a general term for the whole process. While there can be individual variations in this sequence, thelarche is the standard physiological "herald" of pubertal onset. Recognition of this sequence is important for pediatricians to identify precocious or delayed puberty. Therefore, breast development is correctly identified as the initial visible marker of female maturation
questions.learning: Puberty in females typically follows a well-defined chronological sequence. The first sign of sexual maturation is usually Thelarche (Option B), which refers to the beginning of breast development (breast budding).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient with diabetic nephropathy develops secondary hyperparathyroidism. Hyperparathyroidism is associated with all of the following conditions, EXCEPT which one?
questions.explanation: Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs as a compensatory response to chronic low serum calcium levels. In Chronic Renal Failure (Option D), the kidney's inability to excrete phosphate and activate Vitamin D leads to hypocalcemia, triggering the parathyroid glands to release more PTH. Similarly, Vitamin D deficiency in Rickets (Option C, children) and Osteomalacia (Option B, adults) results in poor calcium absorption, causing a secondary rise in PTH to pull calcium from the bones. Osteoporosis (Option A), however, is a disease of decreased bone density where serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH levels are typically completely normal. While primary hyperparathyroidism can lead to bone loss, osteoporosis itself is not a cause of elevated parathyroid hormone. Therefore, osteoporosis is the only condition among the choices where parathyroid dysfunction is not a standard physiological feature
questions.learning: Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs as a compensatory response to chronic low serum calcium levels. In Chronic Renal Failure (Option D), the kidney's inability to excrete phosphate and activate Vitamin D leads to hypocalcemia, triggering the parathyroid…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During a routine health assessment using the STEP approach, a physician collects key information from the patient. If a patient reports fatigue and dizziness, which of the following parameters would not usually be evaluated as part of the STEP approach?
questions.explanation: The "STEP" approach in clinical medicine or screening is often utilized to monitor metabolic parameters that contribute to chronic lifestyle diseases. Typical components include checking Blood Pressure (Option B), Blood Sugar (Option C), and Blood Lipids (Option D). These are modifiable risk factors that can explain symptoms like fatigue and dizziness. In contrast, a patient's Blood Group (Option A) is a fixed genetic characteristic that is not routinely assessed as part of a general diagnostic "STEP" screening for symptoms of fatigue or metabolic health. Blood grouping is generally reserved for pre-operative planning, blood transfusion, or obstetric care. When a patient presents with dizziness, assessing for hypertension or diabetes (via pressure and sugar checks) is high-yield, whereas knowing the blood type does not provide immediate diagnostic value for the underlying clinical complaint
questions.learning: The "STEP" approach in clinical medicine or screening is often utilized to monitor metabolic parameters that contribute to chronic lifestyle diseases.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding vaginal epithelium in adult female: 1. From puberty till menopause, the vaginal epithelium is devoid of any gland. 2. The basal epithelial layer contains glycogen. 3. Intermediate and superficial cells become continuous with those covering vaginal portion of cervix. 4. Unlike skin, it does not contain hair follicle. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3 and 4

1. From puberty till menopause, vaginal epithelium is devoid of glands: Correct.

• The vagina has no glands in its epithelium.
• Vaginal lubrication mainly comes from cervical mucus and transudation through the vaginal wall.

2. Basal epithelial layer contains glycogen: Incorrect.

• Glycogen is mainly present in the intermediate and superficial cells under estrogenic influence.
• Lactobacilli metabolize glycogen to lactic acid, maintaining the acidic vaginal pH.

3. Intermediate and superficial cells become continuous with those covering the vaginal portion of cervix: Correct.

• The vaginal epithelium is non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and is continuous with the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix.

4. Unlike skin, it does not contain hair follicles: Correct.

• Vaginal mucosa lacks hair follicles, sebaceous glands and sweat glands
questions.learning: From puberty till menopause, vaginal epithelium is devoid of glands: Correct. • The vagina has no glands in its epithelium. • Vaginal lubrication mainly comes from cervical mucus and transudation through the vaginal wall.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Injury to which brain structure would most likely result in excessive sexual behavior, increased appetite, heightened aggression, and loss of normal fear responses?
questions.explanation: Injury to the amygdala classically produces features of Klüver–Bucy syndrome, which includes hypersexuality, hyperphagia (increased appetite), heightened aggression or placidity, and loss of normal fear responses. The amygdala plays a key role in processing emotions such as fear, aggression, and sexual behavior, so its damage disrupts these functions. Other options are incorrect: (B) Thalamus acts mainly as a sensory relay center, transmitting sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex. Damage to it leads to sensory deficits or altered consciousness, not behavioral changes like hypersexuality or loss of fear. (C) Cingulate gyrus is involved in emotion, motivation, and pain perception, but its injury typically causes apathy or emotional disturbances rather than the classic features described. (D) Hypothalamus regulates autonomic functions, hunger, temperature, and endocrine activity. Although it influences appetite and sexual behavior, it does not produce the full syndrome of fear loss and behavioral disinhibition seen here. Thus, the symptoms strongly point toward amygdala injury
questions.learning: Injury to the amygdala classically produces features of Klüver–Bucy syndrome, which includes hypersexuality, hyperphagia (increased appetite), heightened aggression or placidity, and loss of normal fear responses.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In an asymptomatic individual, what is the most appropriate diagnostic criterion for diabetes mellitus according to the ADA 2023 guidelines?
options: Oral glucose tolerance test: 2 hrs value
questions.explanation: According to the ADA 2023 guidelines, the diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus in an asymptomatic patient include: a Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) , an HbA1c , or a 2-hour plasma glucose during an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT). Therefore, Option A is the only correct diagnostic threshold listed. HbA1c of 5.9% (Option B) falls into the prediabetes range (5.7-6.4%). Fasting glucose (approx. ) (Option C) is completely normal. 2-hour glucose (approx. ) (Option D) is also within the normal or prediabetic range. For an asymptomatic patient, these tests usually require confirmation with a second test result from a different day. Accurate diagnosis is essential to begin early lifestyle and pharmacological interventions to prevent the progression of the disease and its subsequent systemic complications
questions.learning: According to the ADA 2023 guidelines, the diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus in an asymptomatic patient include: a Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) , an HbA1c , or a 2-hour plasma glucose during an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following aneuploidies is most likely to be missed in prenatal neonatal screening? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Klinefelter’s Syndrome

Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is commonly missed during prenatal and neonatal screening because affected individuals often lack obvious congenital abnormalities at birth.

Typical features appear later in life and may include:

• Tall stature
• Small firm testes
• Infertility
• Gynecomastia
• Reduced facial/body hair
• Learning or behavioral difficulties

In contrast:

• Trisomy 21 and Trisomy 18 usually present with characteristic dysmorphic features and congenital anomalies detectable prenatally or neonatally.
• Turner syndrome often presents with cystic hygroma, lymphedema, or cardiac defects.

Thus, Klinefelter syndrome is more likely to remain undiagnosed until adolescence or adulthood.
questions.learning: Klinefelter’s Syndrome Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) is commonly missed during prenatal and neonatal screening because affected individuals often lack obvious congenital abnormalities at birth.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a displaced nasal bone fracture after a road traffic accident (RTA). Which instrument is used for nasal bone reduction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Walsham forceps

Walsham forceps are specifically designed for closed reduction of displaced nasal bone fractures.

They allow controlled elevation and repositioning of the nasal bones with minimal trauma.

Other options:

·     Asch forceps: used for reduction of nasal septal fractures

·     Luc forceps: used for removing tissue (e.g., polyps)

·     Thudiculum/ Killian forceps/speculum: used for nasal examination and septal procedures
questions.learning: Walsham forceps Walsham forceps are specifically designed for closed reduction of displaced nasal bone fractures. They allow controlled elevation and repositioning of the nasal bones with minimal trauma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: How is water collected for bacteriological examination during a disease outbreak?
options: Collect water from already leaking taps
Before collecting, let water flow for at least 1 minute
Water sample container is kept close to the tap avoid spillage
Collect from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Collect from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing

During a disease outbreak, for collection of a water sample for bacteriological examination from a tap in regular use, water is collected from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing.

If water samples are to be collected from a tap that is not regularly used, they should be first sterilized by heating. Then, the tap is cooled and opened fully and the initial water stream is let out to flow before the sample is collected.

The sample bottle must be held near the base with a hand and the stopper and paper cover over it are removed together and held in the fingers.

Other options:

Option A (Collect water from already leaking taps): Collecting water from leaking taps is not recommended as it increases the risk of contamination and may not provide an accurate representation of water quality.

Option B (Before collecting, let water flow for at least 1 minute): This option is close to the correct answer but falls short, as it is recommended to let the water flow for at least two minutes to flush out stagnant water in the pipe.

Option C (Water sample container is kept close to the tap to avoid spillage): While keeping the sample container close to the tap is a good practice to avoid spillage, it is not the main concern during the collection of water samples for bacteriological examination.
questions.learning: Collect from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing During a disease outbreak, for collection of a water sample for bacteriological examination from a tap in regular use, water is collected from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The eye examination of a 20-year-old male shows a golden ring on the iris. What is the next investigation to diagnose the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serum ceruloplasmin

The given image shows a Kayser-Fleischer ring, which is seen in Wilson's disease. Low serum ceruloplasmin level is diagnostic of Wilson's disease.

Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an inherited metabolic disorder resulting due to abnormal copper deposition in tissues (mainly the liver and brain). It is caused by a deficiency of ceruloplasmin (copper-carrying blood protein).

Kayer-Fleischer ring is a brownish-yellow zone of copper deposition that is present in the peripheral Descemet membrane.

The ring is best seen on gonioscopy. Penicillamine therapy may cause the ring to disappear.

Another ocular finding in Wilson's disease is anterior capsular sunflower cataract.

Other options:

Option A: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency leads to lung and liver disease.

Option B: Alpha-fetoprotein is a diagnostic marker in hepatocellular carcinoma.

Option C: Serum iron level is assessed in hemochromatosis which occurs due to increased iron deposition in various tissues. The ocular manifestation includes dry eye and rusty-brown perilimbal and conjunctival discoloration.
questions.learning: Serum ceruloplasmin — The given image shows a Kayser-Fleischer ring, which is seen in Wilson's disease. Low serum ceruloplasmin level is diagnostic of Wilson's disease.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A mother brought her 2-year-old child to the OPD with complaints of lack of weight gain, abdominal pain on eating, and poor eating habits. The child was advised gluten-free diet after which there was improvement in the general condition and weight gain. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Celiac disease

The clinical presentation and the histopathological findings are suggestive of celiac disease.

Celiac disease is an autoimmune gluten-induced enteropathy where HLA DQ2 and DQ8 are expressed. In the small intestine, peptides of gluten are presented to helper T cells which mediate mucosal inflammation. Antiendomysial and anti-tTG antibodies are found in serological studies.

Clinical Features:

• Gastrointestinal Symptoms: Chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, vomiting, weight loss, and failure to thrive.
• Extraintestinal Symptoms: Anemia, fatigue, elevated liver enzymes, neurologic disorders, short stature, dental enamel defects, arthralgia, aphthous stomatitis.

Investigation:

• Serologic Tests: Initial testing for anti-TG2 IgA antibodies and total IgA. If anti-TG2 is positive and IgA levels are normal, CD is likely.
• Genetic Testing: For HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 haplotypes.
• Endoscopy and Biopsy: Multiple biopsies from the small intestine to check for villous atrophy.
• Biopsy Findings: villous atrophy: flattening of the villi in the small intestine, crypt hyperplasia: enlargement of the crypts, intraepithelial lymphocytosis: Increased number of lymphocytes in the epithelium.

Treatment:

Gluten-Free Diet: To manage celiac disease, patients must strictly avoid all foods containing gluten. Safe alternatives include rice, corn, maize, buckwheat, millet, amaranth, quinoa, sorghum, potato, soybean, tapioca, and teff, along with bean and nut flours.

Biopsy findings can be seen below:

Other options:

Option A: Tropical sprue is another malabsorption disorder seen as diarrhoea, steatorrhea, nutritional deficiencies, and weight loss. It is prevalent in some tropical areas hence the name. It is mostly attributed to infectious agents considering its response to antibiotics. It is diagnosed by a small intestinal biopsy which shows a close resemblance to that seen in celiac disease but it’s not specifically triggered by gluten and is more common in adults.

Option C: Whipple Disease is a multisystemic disease caused by T.whipplei. Small intestinal biopsy shows PAS-positive macrophages.

Option D: Intestinal Malabsorption is a general term used for conditions that cause poor nutrient absorption, which could include celiac disease but is not specific enough to explain the clear response to a gluten-free diet.
questions.learning: Celiac disease — The clinical presentation and the histopathological findings are suggestive of celiac disease. Celiac disease is an autoimmune gluten-induced enteropathy where HLA DQ2 and DQ8 are expressed.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presented with complaints of bleeding gums. Blood investigations showed iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies do you expect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

Dietary deficiency of vitamin C can lead to scurvy which can manifest as microcytic anemia, defective collagen synthesis, and bleeding manifestations.

Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin. It is mainly required for the hydroxylation of prolyl and lysyl residues of collagen reactions. It also maintains vitamin E and many metal cofactors (eg. copper) in a reduced state. It also facilitates the absorption of iron by reducing it from a ferric to a ferrous state.

Hence, vitamin C deficiency leads to defective collagen synthesis, fragile blood vessels, and iron deficiency anemia. Other clinical features of scurvy include spongy gums, loose teeth, swollen joints, subcutaneous hemorrhage, and bone fractures.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Kinesin, Dyenin and Myosin proteins are examples of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Molecular motors

Kinesin, dynein, and myosin are examples of molecular motors.

The molecular motors are the force-generating proteins as they move proteins, organelles, and other cell parts (collectively referred to as “cargo”) to all parts of the cell.

Kinesin:

* The conventional form of kinesin is a double-headed molecule that moves its cargo toward the plus (“+”) ends of microtubules.

* Some kinesins are associated with mitosis and meiosis.

* Other kinesins perform different functions, and may also move cargo to the minus (“–”) end of microtubules.

Dyneins:

* They have two heads, with their neckpieces embedded in a complex of proteins.

* Cytoplasmic dyneins are similar to conventional kinesin, except they move particles and membranes to the minus (–) end of the microtubules.

* Axonemal dyneins are present with the axonemes of the cilia. An axoneme consists of a unique arrangement of nine outer microtubule doublets and two inner microtubules ("9+2" arrangement). The coordinated dynein–microtubule interactions within the axoneme are responsible for the ciliary and sperm movement.

Myosins:

* There are about 18 classes of myosins.

* The heads of some myosin molecules (myosin II) bind to actin and produce motion by bending their neck regions.

* Some myosin molecules (myosin V) may move the cargo, by walking along microfilaments, one head after the other.
questions.learning: Molecular motors Kinesin, dynein, and myosin are examples of molecular motors. The molecular motors are the force-generating proteins as they move proteins, organelles, and other cell parts (collectively referred to as “cargo”) to all parts of the cell.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is indicative of severe pre-eclampsia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)

Severe preeclampsia is diagnosed when preeclampsia is associated with severe hypertension or evidence of end-organ dysfunction. Features suggesting severe disease include:

• BP ≥160/110 mm Hg
• Thrombocytopenia
• Elevated liver enzymes
• Pulmonary edema
• Renal insufficiency
• Neurologic symptoms
• Fetal growth restriction (IUGR)

Intrauterine growth restriction occurs due to uteroplacental insufficiency caused by abnormal placental vascular remodeling and is considered a marker of severe placental disease.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Diastolic BP 90 mm Hg → mild hypertension
• Systolic BP 145 mm Hg → not severe range
• Proteinuria 2 g/24 h alone does not define severe preeclampsia
questions.learning: Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) Severe preeclampsia is diagnosed when preeclampsia is associated with severe hypertension or evidence of end-organ dysfunction.

questions.text: All of the following can be given to a pregnant woman with SLE except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mycophenolate mofetil

Management of SLE in pregnancy requires use of drugs that are safe for the fetus while maintaining disease control.

Drugs considered safe in pregnancy:

• Hydroxychloroquine → continue in all patients (reduces flares, improves outcomes)
• Azathioprine → safe immunosuppressant (≤2 mg/kg/day)
• Sulfasalazine → safe with folic acid supplementation
• Low-dose steroids if required

Contraindicated in pregnancy:

• Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF)

o    Highly teratogenic

o    Causes congenital malformations (ear, facial, cardiac defects) and miscarriage

o    Must be stopped before conception

questions.text: A patient presented with right hypochondriac pain. He had an episode of diarrhea 1 week prior. CT scan of the abdomen reveals a liver abscess of around 25 ccs. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medical therapy

This patient with an abscess in the liver with a history of diarrhea most likely has an amebic liver abscess. The initial treatment of choice for an amebic liver abscess is medical therapy with metronidazole.

Ingestion of Entamoeba histolytica cysts causes intestinal diseases like diarrhea. Following this, the trophozoites reach the liver mostly through the portal venous system and cause amebic liver abscess. The common presenting features are right upper quadrant pain, tenderness, fever, hepatomegaly, and diarrhea.

CT abdomen is helpful in differentiating amebic from a pyogenic abscess. A rim enhancement is noted in case of a pyogenic abscess.

The mainstay of treatment for amebic abscesses is metronidazole, which is curative in more than 90% of patients. Luminal agents such as iodoquinol, paromomycin, or diloxanide furoate can be administered to treat the carrier state.

Aspiration of abscess is recommended in case of

• Diagnostic uncertainty
• Failure to respond to metronidazole therapy
• Abscesses larger than 5 cm in diameter and in the left liver, since they are thought to carry a high risk of rupture
